t: Article 90 — Introduction: how this Code is set up
x: Article 90 is the front door of the Code. It explains why the Code exists, what kinds of installations it covers, what it leaves out, and how its chapters fit together. It also explains the difference between a rule you must follow and background material that only helps you understand a rule. Start here when a question is really about whether the Code applies at all, who enforces it, or whether a note in the book is a requirement. Most day-to-day wiring questions are answered in Chapters 1 through 7, not in Article 90 itself. Florida enforces NEC 2020 through the Florida Building Code, 8th Edition (2023). NEC 2023 is not yet adopted in Florida.

t: Purpose of the Code
x: The point of the Code is to protect people and property from the hazards that come with using electricity. Following it, together with proper maintenance, produces an installation that is largely free from hazard. The Code is not a design manual for beginners, and meeting the Code does not promise the most efficient or most convenient system — it sets the safety floor. When a plan meets the Code but works poorly, that is a design problem, not proof the Code failed. When a shortcut works but is hazardous, the Code still controls. Build to the safety floor first, then to good design above it.

t: Scope — what is covered and what is not
x: This section lists the kinds of installations the Code covers, such as premises wiring in buildings, yards, parking areas, and similar locations, and the kinds it does not cover, such as most utility-owned generation and distribution installations, ships, railway rolling stock, and mining equipment. It also covers installations where the Code applies only with special permission from the authority having jurisdiction. Smoke and carbon monoxide alarms in a house are handled by the building code, not by this article. The line that matters most in the field is the utility line: work on the customer side of the service point is generally Code work; the utility's own system generally is not. If a

t: How the chapters are arranged
x: Chapters 1 through 4 apply broadly to electrical installations. Chapters 5, 6 and 7 cover special places, special equipment and special conditions, and they add to or modify the general chapters. Chapter 8 covers communications systems and stands apart — the general chapters only apply to it where a Chapter 8 rule points back to them. Chapter 9 holds tables used by the rest of the book, and the annexes at the back are explanatory, not requirements. For a normal house or light-commercial job you live in Chapters 1 to 4. Open Chapter 5, 6 or 7 only when the occupancy or equipment is special, and when you do, read that rule together with the general rule it modifies.

t: Enforcement and the AHJ
x: The authority having jurisdiction — the AHJ, usually the local building department and its inspectors — enforces the Code and approves equipment and installations. The AHJ can grant special permission where the Code allows it, and can interpret how a rule applies to a local situation. An inspector's reading on your job carries weight that a handbook, an app or a study guide does not. If a rule could be read two ways on a real job, ask the AHJ before rough-in, not at inspection. Write down who said what and when. This book is a reference aid; the AHJ and the printed NEC govern. Local amendments and AHJ positions always win over a statewide summary, especially on items where enforcement has va

t: Mandatory rules, permissive rules, and explanatory material
x: Mandatory rules use shall or shall not language — they must be followed. Permissive rules use shall be permitted language — they allow an option, they do not require it. Explanatory material, including Informational Notes, is there to explain or point to other material; a note by itself does not create a requirement you can be failed for, and you cannot use a note to override a rule. When someone cites a note as the reason for a red tag or a change, ask for the rule section behind it. Notes are where good explanations live, but the enforceable requirement is always in the rule text or in another standard the rule points to.

t: Formal interpretations
x: Where there is a genuine dispute about what a Code rule means, there is a formal process for getting an official interpretation from NFPA. That process is slow and is meant for real disagreements about the text, not for settling a question on one job. One job's question goes to its AHJ. You will almost never use this section in the field. Know that it exists so you do not treat a magazine article or a forum post as an official interpretation.

t: Examination of equipment for safety
x: This section explains how equipment gets examined for safety, normally by being tested and listed or labeled by a qualified testing laboratory. It is the background for the approval, listing and labeling language used all through Article 110. Equipment the AHJ accepts has normally been through that kind of third-party check. Look for the listing mark and the label when gear arrives. If a piece of equipment has no mark and no paperwork, raise it before it is installed, not after it is wired.  Sharma standard gear is Siemens (S-02). A listing problem is not solved by a familiar brand name — the specific equipment still has to be listed and used within its listing.

t: Planning for future expansion
x: This section encourages planning an installation so later growth in load does not require tearing the system apart. Allowing room for future circuits and capacity is presented as good practice for convenience and for the life of the installation, not as a hard sizing rule by itself. 90.8(B) covers the number of circuits in enclosures: an enclosure may not be filled beyond the number of circuits it was designed and listed to hold. Spare panel spaces, an accessible junction point, and a raceway path that can be reused are cheap on rough-in day and expensive later. Where the plan allows, leave the next electrician — often us — a workable path.

t: Units of measurement
x: Measurements in the Code are shown with metric values and inch-pound values. Where the two do not match exactly because of rounding or a soft conversion, the section explains which value is treated as the requirement. In United States field work the inch-pound value is the one crews measure with. Measure in inches and feet as printed in the rule you are using. Do not convert a Code dimension yourself and then argue from your conversion at inspection.

t: Article 100 — Definitions: the words the Code uses
x: Article 100 defines the terms that carry a special meaning inside the Code. When a defined word appears in a rule, it means what Article 100 says it means, even if the everyday meaning is broader or narrower. In the 2020 edition the definitions sit in three parts — general definitions, definitions for installations over 1000 volts, and definitions for hazardous (classified) locations — arranged alphabetically inside each part rather than as numbered sections. This chapter covers the job-critical general terms a Sharma helper meets first; it does not attempt every definition in the article. When an argument turns on a single word — accessible, listed, outlet, service — come back to this artic

t: Accessible and readily accessible
x: Accessible, said of equipment, means a person can get close to it to operate, inspect or maintain it, without being blocked by the building's permanent structure. Accessible, said of a wiring method, means it can be removed or reached without tearing out finished construction. Readily accessible is stricter: a person can get to it quickly, without tools other than a key, without climbing over obstacles, and without a portable ladder. A breaker behind a locked door the occupant can open is different from a junction box buried behind drywall. Buried boxes are the classic failure: a wiring method that cannot be reached without demolition is not accessible, and splices belong in accessible boxes

t: Ampacity
x: Ampacity is the most current, in amperes, a conductor can carry continuously in its actual conditions of use without getting hotter than its temperature rating allows. It is not a single number printed on the wire; it depends on the conductor material, insulation rating, ambient temperature, and how many current-carrying conductors share a raceway or cable. Start from Table 310.16, then adjust for the job's real conditions. A conductor that is fine alone in a cool space can be over its limit bundled in a hot Florida attic. Florida attic temperatures make ambient correction a real design step, not a paperwork exercise. S-10: CCA is rated from the aluminum column of Table 310.16, which is why

t: Appliance
x: An appliance is utilization equipment, usually built as a unit, that does a household or similar job — cooking, washing, drying, comfort heating or cooling, and the like — other than a basic luminaire or motor by itself. The word matters because several branch-circuit and disconnect rules turn on whether the load is an appliance. Dishwashers, disposals, ranges, dryers and built-in microwaves are appliances. When a rule says appliance, check whether the equipment in front of you fits that idea before applying a general receptacle rule to it.  S-06 is PENDING. The microwave gets its own 20A circuit. The wire is not settled — 12 AWG copper versus 10 AWG CCA — until Mike Holt rules. If the plan

t: Approved, identified, labeled, and listed
x: These four words form one family. Approved means acceptable to the AHJ. Identified means recognizable as suitable for the specific use in question. Labeled means a testing organization has attached its label after checking samples of the product. Listed means the product appears in that organization's published list of items it has evaluated. A product can be well made and still not be listed, and an unlisted product used where listing is required is a Code problem. Read the box and the device. Breakers must be listed and identified for the panel they go in; a breaker that physically fits a foreign panel is not thereby identified for it.  S-02: all new gear is Siemens. S-03: in an existing S

t: Bonding — bonded, bonding conductor, bonding jumper
x: Bonding means joining metal parts together so they stay at the same electrical potential and have a reliable, low-impedance path that can carry fault current. A bonding jumper is the conductor or fitting that makes that connection. Bonding is not the same job as grounding to the earth; its main safety job is to make fault current flow hard enough to trip the breaker fast. Metal boxes, raceways, enclosures and equipment frames that can become energized need a bonding path back to the source. A loose locknut or paint under a fitting can quietly break that path.

t: Grounded and grounding — telling the conductors apart
x: Grounded means connected to the earth, or to a body that serves in place of the earth. The grounded conductor is the system conductor that is intentionally grounded — in a house, the neutral. The grounding conductor, including the equipment grounding conductor, is the path that ties equipment and enclosures to the grounding system for fault protection. The two words differ by one syllable and do completely different jobs, which is why the Code defines them separately. White is the grounded conductor; green or bare is the grounding conductor. They are bonded together only where the Code permits — at the service — and kept separate downstream in the panels Sharma sets.

t: Branch circuit
x: A branch circuit is the part of the wiring system between the final overcurrent device protecting it — the breaker in the panel — and the outlets it feeds. Everything upstream of that breaker is a feeder or service conductor; everything downstream to the receptacles, lights and equipment is the branch circuit. Article 210 builds its rules on this definition. When you size, protect or troubleshoot a circuit, find its breaker first. The conductor size, the breaker rating and the outlets all have to agree as one branch circuit.  S-01: on commercial work every branch circuit is 20A minimum on 12 AWG copper minimum — no 15A branch circuits on commercial jobs. That is Sharma practice, stricter tha

t: Feeder
x: A feeder is the set of circuit conductors between the service equipment, or another power supply source such as a separately derived system, and the final branch-circuit overcurrent devices. It is the middle layer of the system: service conductors feed the service equipment, feeders carry power onward to panels, and branch circuits run from those panels' breakers to the outlets. Rules for sizing, protection and grounding change depending on which layer a conductor belongs to. The house-to-detached-garage panel run is the everyday feeder: it starts at an overcurrent device in the house panel and ends at the breakers in the garage panel. Call a run by its right layer before applying any sizing

t: Continuous load
x: A continuous load is a load where the maximum current is expected to keep flowing for three hours or more at a stretch. The three-hour line is the whole definition. Continuous loads drive the familiar 125 percent sizing treatment for conductors and overcurrent devices in the articles that use the term. Lighting in a store that stays on all day, an EV charger, and long-running HVAC loads are the usual suspects. Ask how long the load actually runs before deciding whether the continuous-load treatment applies.

t: Dwelling unit
x: A dwelling unit is a single unit that provides complete and independent living facilities for one or more people, including permanent provisions for living, sleeping, eating, cooking and sanitation. All four functions matter. A space with beds but no cooking or sanitation is not a dwelling unit, and many house rules in the Code switch on or off based on this definition. One-family houses and each apartment in a multifamily building are dwelling units. A hotel room without permanent cooking provisions generally is not, which changes which receptacle and protection rules apply to it.

t: Exposed — live parts and wiring methods
x: Exposed has two uses. For live parts, it means a part can be accidentally touched or approached nearer than a safe distance — it is not properly guarded, isolated or insulated. For a wiring method, it means the wiring is on or against a surface, or behind panels meant to allow access, rather than permanently hidden inside the building structure. A cable run on the surface of a garage wall is exposed wiring and needs the protection its article requires. A live bus that a finger can reach is exposed live parts and is a guarding problem under Article 110.

t: Locations — dry, damp, and wet
x: A dry location is one not normally damp or wet, though it can be temporarily damp during construction. A damp location is partly protected from weather or subject to moderate moisture — under a canopy, in some basements and barns, and similar places. A wet location is where water or other liquid can contact the equipment directly, or the installation is underground or in concrete or masonry in contact with the earth. The location decides what equipment and wiring methods are suitable. In Florida, treat exterior work as wet unless it is genuinely sheltered, and slabs and below-grade runs as wet by definition. Use equipment identified for the location you actually have, not the one you wish yo

t: Outlet and receptacle
x: An outlet is any point on the wiring system where current is taken to feed utilization equipment — a receptacle point, a lighting point, a smoke-alarm point and a hardwired equipment connection are all outlets. A receptacle is the contact device installed at an outlet for plugging in a cord-connected load, and a receptacle outlet is an outlet where one or more receptacles are installed. Every receptacle is at an outlet, but not every outlet is a receptacle. Spacing and circuit rules that say outlet usually count lighting and hardwired points too, while rules that say receptacle outlet count only plug points. Mixing the two up is a common cause of a missed required receptacle or a wrong box-f

t: Service — the family of service terms
x: The service is the conductors and equipment that deliver power from the serving utility to the premises wiring. Service conductors run from the service point to the service disconnect. Service equipment is the gear — normally the disconnect and overcurrent devices — that controls and cuts off the supply. The service point is the handoff line between the utility's system and the premises wiring, and most service rules in Article 230 are built from these definitions. Find the service point first on any service change. It decides whose rules govern each run of conductor and where the grounded and grounding conductors are bonded together. The utility serving the job (for example FPL or a municip

t: In sight from — and disconnecting means
x: Two linked terms. A disconnecting means is the device, or group of devices, that disconnects a circuit's conductors from their supply — a breaker or a disconnect switch are the everyday examples. Equipment is in sight from other equipment when it is visible from it and not more than 50 ft away; both halves matter, so a disconnect 20 ft away but hidden behind a wall is not in sight. Many equipment articles require a disconnect to be in sight from the equipment it serves, or to be lockable where they allow it to be out of sight. When you set a condenser or air-handler disconnect, stand at the equipment and look: if you cannot see the disconnect, or it is beyond 50 ft, the in-sight option is no

t: Special permission
x: Special permission is the written consent of the AHJ, given where the Code says the AHJ may allow an alternative. It is not a verbal okay from a plans examiner, a builder or a homeowner, and it is not something an electrician grants himself. Where the Code requires it, get it in writing before the work is done. If a job depends on special permission, paper it: keep the AHJ's written consent with the permit documents so the next inspector sees the same record.

t: Garage, kitchen, and laundry area — how the Code uses area names
x: Of these three area names, only one is a formal Article 100 definition: a kitchen is "an area with a sink and permanent provisions for food preparation and cooking" — both halves must be present, and a portable appliance plugged in on the counter does not create one. Garage and laundry area carry no standalone Article 100 definition in the 2020 Code. The Code uses both terms in its rules — garage receptacles and their GFCI protection in 210.8(A)(2) and 210.52(G), the laundry area branch circuit in 210.11(C)(2) and laundry-area GFCI in 210.8(A)(10) — and they take their ordinary meaning: the garage is the vehicle space and its attached unfinished areas, and the laundry area is where laundry e

t: Article 110 — Requirements for electrical installations
x: Article 110 sets the general rules that apply to almost every installation: use approved and listed equipment the way its listing intends, terminate conductors correctly, do neat and workmanlike work, mark what needs marking, and leave safe working space around equipment. If a habit is wrong on every job, the rule against it is probably in this article. Most Article 110 failures are visible without a meter: wrong-brand breakers, sloppy terminations, unmarked disconnects, blocked panels. A slow walk with this article in mind catches them before the inspector does.

t: Scope of Article 110
x: This short section states that Article 110 covers the general requirements for electrical installations — the approval, installation, ratings, connections, marking and working space of equipment wherever the Code applies. It is not limited to services or to panels; it follows equipment into every occupancy the later articles cover, and the specific articles then add their own rules on top. When a question is about equipment in general rather than one wiring method — a rating, a marking, a clearance — start in Article 110 before hunting through the equipment's own article.

t: Approval of equipment and conductors
x: Conductors and equipment required or permitted by the Code must be approved, which in practice means acceptable to the AHJ. Approval is normally shown through listing and labeling by a qualified testing laboratory. Equipment with no path to approval does not become acceptable because it was cheap, available, or already on the truck. Check approvals at order and delivery time. A non-listed substitute discovered at trim-out costs a return trip and can hold up the whole job.  S-02 and S-03 keep Sharma inside this rule: Siemens gear for new work, and only breakers listed for the panel in existing panels.

t: Examination, identification, installation, and use of equipment
x: When equipment is examined for approval, the things considered include its suitability for the installation, its mechanical strength, wire-bending space, electrical insulation, heating effects, arcing behavior, and how it is classified by type, size, voltage, current capacity and specific use. In plain terms: the right equipment, of the right rating, in the right place, with room for its conductors to land properly. Suitability is decided before installation. A device rated for a dry interior wall does not become suitable on an exterior wet wall because it was the one in the box.

t: Install and use listed equipment per its instructions
x: Listed and labeled equipment has to be installed and used following the instructions that come with its listing and labeling. The manufacturer's instructions are not suggestions where the listing depends on them — a torque value, a conductor material, a temperature rating or a mounting requirement in those instructions has Code force through this section. This is the daily rule behind half of field quality: read the label inside the panel door, the sheet in the device box, and the nameplate on the equipment. If the instructions and a habit disagree, the instructions win.

t: Voltages
x: Equipment is used at the voltage it is rated for, and where the Code states a voltage it means the nominal system voltage the circuit actually operates at, unless a rule says otherwise. A device rated for a lower voltage does not become suitable on a higher-voltage circuit because its terminals fit, and the nominal voltage is what load, protection and clearance rules are keyed to. Check the nameplate voltage against the system in front of you — 120/240 single-phase, 208Y/120 and 480Y/277 three-phase are different worlds for device ratings even when the hardware looks similar.

t: Conductors — general
x: Conductors in the Code are copper unless a rule or an equipment marking provides for another metal. Where other materials such as aluminum or copper-clad aluminum are used, the sizes in the Code's tables and rules are read in the column and on the terms for that material. The metal of the conductor is part of the design, not an afterthought at the supply house. Know which metal is on the spool before you size anything. Ampacity, terminations and the small-conductor limits all change with the metal.  S-10: copper is Sharma's default. When CCA is used, size one AWG larger, use the aluminum column of Table 310.16, land it only on terminations listed for it, and never backstab.

t: Conductor sizes — AWG and circular mils
x: Conductor sizes are expressed in American Wire Gauge for the smaller sizes and in circular mil area for the larger ones. The size designation is a standard language: the same AWG number means the same conductor size whoever made the cable. Size by itself is not ampacity — the rating still comes from the ampacity tables, the termination limits and the conditions of use. Speak sizes in AWG up through 4/0 and in kcmil above that, and never let a breaker handle rating substitute for the ampacity check behind it.

t: Wiring integrity
x: Completed wiring installations must be free from short circuits, ground faults, and any connections to ground other than the ones the Code requires or permits — that is the whole rule of 110.7, and it is why continuity and insulation checks happen before energizing. Do not confuse it with equipment integrity: the rule that internal parts, busbars, wiring terminals, and other parts must not be damaged or contaminated lives at 110.12(B), not here. Before you energize, prove the install: no shorts, no ground faults, no stray grounds. If the gear itself is damaged or contaminated inside, that is a 110.12(B) problem — a different section, with the same stop-and-fix answer.

t: Wiring methods — use only recognized methods
x: Only wiring methods the Code recognizes for the application may be used. A cable or raceway that conducts electricity is not thereby a permitted wiring method for a given location: each method has its own article, its permitted uses and its prohibited uses, and those govern. Improvised assemblies and products used outside their article's limits fail here before any other rule is reached. Before running anything, name the method and its article — NM cable, EMT, PVC, MC and the rest each carry their own use lists. A method allowed indoors is not automatically allowed outdoors or in a wet location.

t: Interrupting rating
x: Equipment meant to interrupt current during a fault has to be able to interrupt the fault current that can actually be delivered at its terminals. A breaker asked to open a fault beyond its interrupting rating can fail violently instead of clearing the fault. The rating is printed on the device and must equal or exceed the available fault current at that point. Check the kAIC marking on breakers against the job's available fault current, especially close to large services and transformers. Series-rated combinations are only valid as tested and documented combinations, not as a field guess.

t: Circuit impedance and fault-current performance
x: The overcurrent devices, the total impedance of the circuit, and the other components have to work together so that, under a short circuit or ground fault, the fault is cleared without extensive damage to the equipment in the circuit. In practice this means a low-impedance fault path, correctly rated devices, and components whose short-circuit current ratings suit the system they are part of. This is the engineering reason behind tight bonding, correct conductor sizing and not mixing untested device combinations. A fault should be a breaker trip, not an equipment failure.

t: Deteriorating agents
x: Equipment must not sit in conditions that will destroy it — dampness, corrosive gases or liquids, heat, mechanical damage and similar agents — unless it is identified for that environment. Ordinary equipment in a corrosive or wet environment fails early and can fail dangerously. Coastal Florida air, pool equipment rooms, fertilizer storage and car washes are the usual traps. Identify the environment first, then pick equipment identified for it. Salt air along Florida coasts is a deteriorating agent. Exterior and coastal gear needs to be identified for the exposure, and corrosion found at service calls should be reported, not just wiped off.

t: Mechanical execution of work — workmanship and unused openings
x: Electrical work has to be done in a neat and workmanlike manner. Unused openings in enclosures, boxes and equipment have to be closed with closures that give protection much like the wall of the equipment itself — a missing knockout blank is an open door for fingers, pests and arc products. Conductors must also be protected where insulation can be damaged. (Keeping water out of enclosures in wet locations is a different rule — see 312.2 and 314.15 — not part of 110.12.) Part (B) covers integrity of equipment and connections: internal parts, busbars, wiring terminals, and other components must not be damaged or contaminated by foreign materials, and there must be no damaged, broken, bent, cut

t: Mounting and cooling of equipment
x: Equipment has to be firmly secured to its mounting surface, and it must not be mounted in a way that blocks the cooling it was designed for. Equipment that depends on air circulation cannot be buried in insulation or boxed in tight. Wooden plugs in masonry are not an acceptable way to secure equipment. Anchor gear with real fasteners into structure or masonry anchors, keep vents and fins clear, and check that a recessed installation still lets the equipment breathe as its instructions require.

t: Electrical connections — terminations in general
x: Most electrical failures start at a connection, and this section is the Code's main defense. Conductors must land on terminals suited to their metal and size, with the connection made by an approved method. Dissimilar metals in contact must be handled only where the device is identified for that combination, because corrosion between unlike metals loosens and overheats a joint over time. Solder, where used, cannot be the thing that holds a joint against pulling apart. Read the lug and device markings before landing wire. CU-only means copper only. A connector for aluminum, copper and CCA together must carry the AL-CU or CU-AL marking, or the intermixed marking where the metals actually touch

t: Temperature limits at terminations
x: A conductor's ampacity may be read from a higher temperature column only if the terminations at both ends are rated for that temperature. For circuits of 100A or less, or using 14 through 1 AWG conductors, the default is the 60 degree C column unless the equipment is marked otherwise. For larger circuits the default is the 75 degree C column. The temperature rating of a conductor cannot be used above the lowest temperature rating of any termination it lands on. This is why 90 degree wire still gets sized from the 60 or 75 degree column at the breaker. Read the breaker and equipment markings; existing v1 item L-033 works the 110.14(C)(1) case in detail.

t: Torque — tighten to the specified value
x: Where a manufacturer gives a torque value for a terminal, the connection has to be tightened to that value using a proper torque tool, unless the equipment has been tested and marked so another method is known to give the same result. Hand-tight by feel is not a value. The specified torque is normally printed on the equipment label or in its instructions. Keep a torque screwdriver and wrench on the truck, use the label value for every lug at trim and service work, and re-check after landing all conductors. Existing checklist item SP-15 covers the field routine.

t: High-leg marking on 4-wire delta systems
x: On a 4-wire, 3-phase delta system, one phase conductor — the high leg — has a higher voltage to ground than the other two. That conductor has to be durably and permanently marked with an orange finish, or identified by other effective means, at the points the section specifies, such as where connections are made and where the grounded conductor is present. The marking is what keeps a 120V load from being landed on the leg that sits at 208V to ground. Sharma meets high legs on older light-commercial services. Before landing any 120V circuit in a delta panel, identify which leg is the high leg, confirm it is orange-marked, and keep 120V loads off it.

t: Arc-flash hazard warning marking
x: Certain equipment that is likely to be examined, adjusted or worked on while energized — such as switchboards, panelboards and motor control centers in other than dwelling settings — must carry a durable field-applied warning marking telling people about the arc-flash hazard. The marking warns; it does not replace safe work practice, and it belongs where a person approaching the gear will see it. On service equipment, 110.16(B) makes the label specific: it must show the nominal system voltage, the arc-flash boundary, and at least one of the available incident energy with its working distance, the arc rating of required clothing, or the site-specific level of PPE. On commercial work, confirm

t: Arcing parts
x: Parts of electrical equipment that can produce arcs in normal operation — switch and breaker contacts, motor brushes and similar devices — have to be enclosed or kept separated and isolated from combustible material. An arc is expected inside properly enclosed equipment; it becomes a fire problem when arcing parts sit open near material that can ignite. Keep enclosures intact around switching equipment, and flag arcing or sparking equipment found open or mounted tight against combustible storage for correction.

t: Light and power from railway conductors (orientation)
x: This section covers the special conditions for taking light and power from railway conductors. It is a legacy, specialized provision that ordinary premises wiring never uses: railway power systems are outside the installations Sharma designs or installs. It is included so the numbering of Article 110 reads complete, not as a working rule. If a job ever genuinely touches railway power conductors, stop and escalate — that is engineered, specialized work, not a field improvisation.

t: Marking — manufacturer marks and field-applied hazard marks
x: Equipment carries the manufacturer's name and its ratings so the user can tell what it is and what it is rated for. Where the Code requires a field-applied hazard marking, it has to be durable enough for its environment, use signal wording everyone recognizes, and not be handwritten where the Code requires a proper marking. A faded or missing rating plate makes equipment hard to approve and harder to service safely. Reconditioned equipment has its own marking rule at 110.21(A)(2): it must be marked with the name or trademark of the business that reconditioned it and the date of reconditioning, identified as reconditioned, and the original listing mark must be removed or voided — reconditione

t: Identification of disconnecting means
x: Every disconnecting means has to be legibly marked to show what it shuts off, unless the purpose is already obvious from where it sits and what it feeds. The marking must be durable for its environment. On a multi-unit or multi-tenant job, each service disconnect and fault-protection device also has to show where its supply side comes from, so no one opens the wrong gear. Label every breaker and disconnect with its actual load — 'condenser', 'air handler 2', 'water heater' — not 'spare' labels on live circuits or a directory copied from another house. Update the directory whenever a circuit changes.

t: Current transformers
x: This section covers current transformers used with electrical equipment, including how unused current transformers mounted in place are to be treated so their secondary circuits are not left in a hazardous state. Current-transformer secondaries behave unlike ordinary branch-circuit conductors: an open-circuited secondary under load can produce dangerous voltage, which is why the section and the equipment instructions govern their handling. On metered commercial services, never open a CT secondary casually and never leave a mounted spare CT with its secondary open — follow the equipment instructions and this section, or hand it to the person who does this work regularly.

t: Available fault current — field marking and documentation
x: At service equipment in other than dwelling units, the equipment has to be field-marked with the available fault current and the date the calculation was made. The calculation has to be documented and available to the people who design, install, inspect and maintain the system. When the utility changes something that raises the available fault current, the marking and the equipment ratings have to be revisited — a service can become under-rated without anyone touching it on site. On service changes, ask for the fault-current figure, mark it with its date, and check it against the interrupting ratings of the gear you are setting under 110.9. Keep the calculation with the job documents. Utilit

t: Lockable disconnecting means
x: Where another rule requires a disconnecting means to be capable of being locked in the open position, this section sets how that capability is provided: the locking means is part of the disconnect installation, stays in place whether or not a padlock is actually applied, and allows the device to be locked open by the person doing the work. An improvised wrap of wire or tape around a handle is not a lockable disconnect. Where a disconnect must be out of sight of its equipment and the rule allows the lockable route instead, confirm the disconnect has a real, permanent lock-off provision before relying on it.

t: Spaces about electrical equipment — the section as a whole
x: Sufficient access and working space must be provided and kept clear around electrical equipment so people can work on it safely and maintain it. The section breaks into the working space itself, clear space, entrance and egress, illumination, dedicated equipment space, and special rules indoors and outdoors. Space that exists on rough-in day and is filled by the plumber's water heater later is not working space. Defend the space from rough-in to final. Coordinate with the other trades early — once a water heater or shelving unit is set inside the panel's space, somebody is moving something, and it is cheaper if it is not us at final.  S-09 back-to-back meter and panel is Sharma's preferred l

t: Working space about equipment
x: Live electrical equipment that may need examination or work while energized has to have a clear working space in front of it. For a typical 120/240V house panel (150V or less to ground), Table 110.26(A)(1) requires 3 ft of depth under all three conditions — what changes the depth is higher voltage to ground, not the house panel case. The space is at least 30 in wide or the width of the equipment, whichever is greater (110.26(A)(2)), and it runs from the floor up to 6-1/2 ft or the height of the equipment, whichever is greater (110.26(A)(3)). The space also has to be arranged so equipment doors and hinged panels can open at least 90°. Measure from the face of the panel, not from the wall behi

t: Depth of working space and the three conditions
x: Depth is read from the table in this section, which sets the distance by the voltage to ground and by what faces the worker. Condition 1 is exposed live parts on one side of the space with no live or grounded parts on the other side. Condition 2 puts a grounded surface, such as a concrete or masonry wall, on the far side. Condition 3 puts exposed live parts on both sides. At 0 to 150 volts to ground the table gives 3 ft for all three conditions; the conditions only change the depth at higher voltages — at 151 to 600 volts to ground the depths are 3 ft, 3 ft 6 in, and 4 ft. The worse the exposure across the aisle, the deeper the space must be once voltage makes the conditions diverge. For a h

t: Clear space, entrance and egress, and illumination
x: Working space cannot be used for storage. Entrances must let a worker get in and out without squeezing past live parts, and on large equipment (110.26(C)(2)) a second entrance/exit path is required once the service disconnects total 1,200A or more. Personnel doors within 25 ft of the working space have their own rule at 110.26(C)(3): the door must open in the direction of egress and carry listed panic hardware or fire-exit hardware. Working spaces also have to be illuminated so the work is not done by flashlight, and the lighting must not be controlled by automatic means only (110.26(D)) — automatic control may supplement a switch, but it cannot be the only control. If the panel room doubles

t: Dedicated equipment space
x: The floor space equal to the footprint of indoor electrical equipment, from the floor up to 6 ft above the equipment or the ceiling if lower, is dedicated to the electrical installation. Foreign pipes, ducts and other systems cannot pass through that zone except where the section allows, and suspended ceilings with removable panels do not count as the structural ceiling for this purpose. Outdoor equipment has a matching dedicated zone with its own clearances. Foreign systems installed ABOVE that dedicated zone are handled at 110.26(E)(1)(b): they need protection against leaks and condensation so nothing drips onto the electrical equipment below. This is the rule behind 'the plumber cannot ru

t: Guarding of live parts
x: Live parts that a person might contact have to be guarded — by covers, enclosures, elevation, location in a room only qualified people can enter, or partitions that keep unqualified people from reaching them. The method depends on the voltage and the setting, but the idea is constant: nobody unqualified should be able to reach out and touch an energized part. Replace every cover you remove, the same day. An open panel with live bus exposed in an occupied building is a guarding failure even if it was only meant to be open for an hour.

t: Enclosure types
x: Enclosures are selected by type for the environment they will live in, and this section's table matches enclosure types to the exposures they are built to withstand — indoor dust and dripping liquid, outdoor rain and sleet, hose-directed water, corrosion, and the like. The common field types run from a general indoor enclosure, through the outdoor rain-tight type crews see on house disconnects, to the corrosion-resistant types used in washdown and coastal work. The type marked on the enclosure, not its appearance, is what it is rated for. Match the type to the real exposure: indoor-type equipment does not go on an exterior Florida wall, and a corroded or wrong-type enclosure found on a servi

t: Equipment over 1000 volts — enclosure and access (overview)
x: Part III of Article 110 adds stricter rules for installations over 1000 volts, nominal, starting with how electrical equipment in such installations is enclosed and how access to it is controlled. Metal-enclosed gear and vault-type installations have to keep unqualified people away from high-voltage parts with real physical barriers, locks and warning signs. Sharma rarely installs this class of work, so this page is an orientation marker rather than a working guide. If a commercial job crosses into over-1000V equipment, stop and escalate — design, guarding and access rules change materially, and this work is engineered and permitted differently from ordinary premises wiring.

t: Grounded conductors — how they are identified
x: Article 200 is about the grounded conductor, which in a house is usually the neutral. Its job in this article is identification: how a worker can tell, by color, marking, or terminal, which conductor is grounded so nobody lands it in the wrong place. It does not size the neutral — that work lives in Articles 210, 215, 220, and 250. Treat white and gray as a warning label, not a suggestion. Before you splice, land, or re-mark a conductor, check what it is actually connected to at both ends.

t: How a grounded conductor is marked
x: This section gives the ways a grounded conductor may be identified, and the method changes with conductor size. Smaller insulated conductors use a continuous white or gray outer finish, or white or gray with colored stripes other than green. Larger conductors may use that same finish, or be identified at terminations and accessible points in the ways the section allows. On rough-in, pick the right roll — do not plan to tape your way out of the wrong insulation color on small branch wiring. On larger feeders, mark every accessible point, not just the end you happen to be landing today.

t: What white or gray insulation may be used for
x: White or gray insulation is reserved for the grounded conductor, with narrow exceptions the section spells out. The familiar field examples are a re-identified conductor in a cable assembly used as a hot for a switch loop or a 240V circuit, and flexible cord uses — and re-identification has to be permanent and visible where required. A white conductor is never free to be a ground; equipment grounds are green, green with yellow stripes, or bare. If you re-identify a white wire as a hot, mark it at every box where it appears and tell the trim crew. If you open a box and find an unmarked white on a switch or breaker, stop and trace it instead of assuming.  Never backstab and never guess a re-id

t: Branch circuits — the circuits that feed the load
x: Article 210 governs the final run of wiring that delivers power to lights, receptacles, and appliances. It sets circuit ratings, the protection people need from shock and arc faults, which dedicated circuits a dwelling must have, where receptacles and lights must go, and how much load a circuit may carry. Most of Sharma's rough-in and trim work is judged against this article. Read a house plan through Article 210 first: protection, dedicated circuits, receptacle layout, then lighting outlets. That order catches the expensive misses before wire is pulled.  S-01: on commercial work Sharma runs 20A minimum branch circuits — stricter than this article requires for dwellings.

t: Multiwire branch circuits
x: A multiwire branch circuit shares one grounded conductor between two or three ungrounded conductors taken from different phases or legs. Because the shared neutral only carries the unbalanced current when the hots are on opposite legs, landing both hots on the same leg can overload a neutral that has no breaker of its own. The article also requires a way to disconnect all the hots together at the panel and grouping so the shared set can be identified. Before you share a neutral, confirm the breakers are on opposite legs and tied or on a common-trip / handle-tied arrangement as required. In a 120/240V house panel, that means adjacent positions are not automatically opposite legs in every pane

t: Ground-fault protection for people
x: This section requires ground-fault protection in the places where a person, water, concrete, or the outdoors make a fault to ground most dangerous. Protection can be provided at the receptacle, at the breaker, or by a device feeding through to downstream outlets, as long as the outlet that needs protection actually gets it. The 2020 dwelling rule reaches further than older editions — see the next pages. Walk the job location by location, not room name by room name. A receptacle in an unfinished part of a basement, within reach of a sink, or in a laundry area is judged by where it sits, not by what the plan calls the room. Florida enforces NEC 2020 through the FBC 8th Edition (2023). A local

t: Dwelling locations that need GFCI protection
x: For dwellings, this list covers receptacles in bathrooms, garages and certain accessory buildings, outdoors, crawl spaces, basements, kitchen areas covered by the list, near sinks, in boathouses, near tubs and showers, in laundry areas, and in indoor damp or wet locations. In NEC 2020 the rule applies to receptacles rated 125V through 250V on single-phase circuits of 150V to ground or less — that is why a 240V dryer or garage receptacle is no longer outside the rule. Measurement points matter: distances are taken from the sink, tub, or shower feature the list names. Use the existing lookup items for the full location list instead of working from memory on a walk-through. Pay special attentio

t: Laundry areas — including the dryer receptacle
x: Item (10) on the dwelling list is laundry areas. Read together with the 2020 voltage range in 210.8(A), it covers the 250V dryer receptacle as well as the 120V washer receptacle. That is the code reason a modern Sharma dryer circuit needs ground-fault protection even though older Florida houses were built without it. Do not treat the dryer as exempt because it is 240V, and do not protect only the washer outlet. Check the whole laundry area, including a laundry closet in a hallway or garage layout.  S-08: dryer circuit is a Siemens Q230GF, 30A 2-pole GFCI breaker. That is the locked Sharma catalog number — do not substitute an older dryer breaker note.

t: GFCI locations outside dwellings
x: Non-dwelling occupancies have their own GFCI list, covering bathrooms, kitchens, rooftops, outdoors, areas near sinks, indoor damp or wet locations, locker rooms with showers, garages, accessory buildings and service bays (other than vehicle exhibition halls and showrooms), crawl spaces at or below grade level, unfinished areas of basements, laundry areas, and bathtub and shower stall areas where receptacles sit within 6 ft of the outside edge of the tub or stall. The voltage and size limits in this subsection are not identical to the dwelling list, so a commercial job cannot be roughed from house habits alone. Kitchens in commercial work are judged by the article's own definition and equipm

t: Specific appliances that need GFCI protection
x: Beyond location lists, this subsection points to 422.5(A): specific appliances need ground-fault protection wherever they are installed, in any occupancy, when rated 150 volts or less to ground and 60 amps or less. The 2020 list is automotive vacuum machines, drinking water coolers and bottle fill stations, cord-and-plug-connected high-pressure spray washers, tire inflation machines, vending machines, sump pumps, and dishwashers. The test is the appliance and its rating, not the room. When an appliance is on the list, moving it to a room that is not on the 210.8(A) list does not remove the requirement. Check the appliance schedule, not just the room finish. If a listed appliance will be cord

t: Outdoor outlets other than receptacles
x: This subsection reaches outdoor outlets that are not receptacles — the hardwired outdoor equipment case, within the rating limits it states. The condenser is the example Sharma runs into: a hardwired outdoor unit can be an outlet for this rule even though there is no plug and no receptacle at the unit. For a one- or two-family dwelling, Florida resolves the condenser question directly: FBC-Residential §E3408.1 amends 210.8(F) with Exception No. 2 — GFCI protection is not required for listed and labeled HVAC equipment. Ask the AHJ's current position before finalizing a condenser circuit on a job where this has not already been settled. Do not promise a homeowner or a builder either answer unt

t: Branch circuits a dwelling must have
x: This section is the circuit-count backbone of a house: enough branch circuits for the load, plus the named dwelling circuits the next pages cover. General circuits are spread so the load is divided, and the required small-appliance, laundry, bathroom, and garage circuits have their own limits on what else they may feed. A panel schedule that only counts spare spaces has not answered this section — the named circuits have to exist and serve the right outlets. Build the panel schedule from this section outward: named circuits first, then general area circuits, then spares. If a named circuit is feeding lights or another room, that is a rough-in error, not a labeling fix.  Sharma often uses mod

t: The named dwelling circuits: kitchen, laundry, bathroom, garage
x: This subsection names four things. At least two 20A small-appliance circuits serve kitchen, pantry, breakfast, and dining receptacles, with tight limits on other outlets. At least one 20A laundry circuit serves the laundry receptacle and nothing else outside that area. At least one 20A bathroom circuit serves bathroom receptacles, or — for a single bathroom only — may carry that bathroom's other outlets. And the 2020 edition adds a dedicated 20A garage circuit for the required garage receptacles, with a limited allowance for readily accessible outdoor receptacles. Label these four on the panel schedule by their code job, not by a room nickname, and check the 'no other outlets' limits before

t: Arc-fault protection
x: Arc-fault protection guards against damaged, pinched, or deteriorating wiring and loose connections that can arc long before a breaker sees an overload. The protection may be provided by a listed combination-type breaker or by one of the other arrangements the article permits, but the outlets in the listed rooms have to end up protected. Arc-fault and ground-fault protection do different jobs; one does not replace the other. Think of this as a room list applied at the panel. When a plan adds a room or changes a room's use, re-check the list instead of copying the last house's schedule.  S-07: Sharma's dual-function breaker provides both arc-fault and ground-fault protection on every 120V cir

t: Rooms where dwelling circuits need AFCI protection
x: For dwellings, this subsection applies to 120V, single-phase, 15A and 20A branch circuits supplying outlets or devices in the listed rooms and areas — kitchens, family rooms, dining rooms, living rooms, parlors, libraries, dens, bedrooms, sunrooms, recreation rooms, closets, hallways, laundry areas, and similar rooms or areas. A bathroom, garage, or unfinished basement is not on this list. The rating limits matter too: a 240V appliance circuit is outside this subsection's stated range. On the panel schedule, mark every 15A and 20A 120V circuit with the rooms it serves, then test that list against this subsection. Mixed circuits that touch a listed room need the protection for the circuit.  S

t: Extending or modifying an existing circuit
x: Work on an existing circuit can pull arc-fault duties with it. This subsection deals with branch circuits that are modified, replaced, or extended in the listed dwelling areas, and with a panel or device change that has a similar effect. There is an exception connected with a short extension — its exact length and conditions are flagged below and must be checked in the printed code before a crew relies on it. On service work, ask first whether the job is a repair in place or an extension or modification. If wire is being added or the circuit is being reworked, assume this subsection is in play and confirm the exception in the book before quoting it to an inspector.

t: Sizing branch-circuit conductors
x: Conductors and breakers for a branch circuit are sized for the load the circuit will actually carry, and a continuous load — one that runs at its maximum for three hours or more — is counted at 125 percent for that sizing unless the assembly is listed for continuous operation at its rating. That is why a load that looks like it 'fits' a breaker on nameplate amps alone can still need the next size up. Multi-outlet circuits supplying receptacles for cord-and-plug loads are also sized by the rating rules in this section and in 210.23. Find the continuous loads first: EV charging, fixed heating, some lighting and equipment. Do the 125 percent math on paper in the job file, not in your head at th

t: Outlet devices and receptacle ratings on a circuit
x: This section matches the device to the circuit: lampholders, receptacles, and cord-and-plug equipment may not be loaded beyond their own ratings, and a receptacle's rating must fit the circuit it sits on. On a 20A multi-outlet circuit, 15A duplex receptacles are permitted because the load is spread across outlets; a single receptacle on an individual 20A circuit is a different case and must match the circuit. The existing lookup item carries the rating table in plain form. When a plan calls for a single dedicated receptacle — a fridge, a microwave, a shop tool — check the device rating against the circuit rating before trim. Do not let a trim bin of 15A devices decide the question.  S-06: th

t: How much load a branch circuit may carry
x: This section caps what may be put on a circuit by its rating. A single cord-and-plug appliance that is not fastened in place may not take more than 80 percent of a circuit that also serves other outlets, and fastened-in-place equipment has its own limit when it shares a circuit with lighting or portable loads. Motor and specific-appliance loads are sent to their own articles instead of being judged by a general percentage. Do the percentage math for the big plug-in loads: space heaters, window units, and shop equipment are where a shared 20A circuit quietly goes over. If a load is fastened in place and shares the circuit, check the second limit too.

t: Where dwelling receptacles must go
x: This is the placement section: it decides where receptacles are required in a dwelling, room by room and surface by surface, so that cords stay short and extension cords stay out of daily use. It does not set circuit ratings — 210.11 does that — and it does not set a general mounting height for ordinary wall receptacles. The subsections that follow walk the house in the order Sharma roughs it: walls, counters, bathrooms, outdoors, laundry, garage, halls, and foyers. Rough from this section with a tape and the floor plan, not from habit. Most placement callbacks are a missed wall, a missed bay, or a counter run measured from the wrong edge.  S-04: where the plan is silent, receptacles are set

t: Wall spacing in habitable rooms
x: In kitchens, family rooms, bedrooms, and the other rooms this subsection lists, receptacles are placed so that no point along the floor line of a wall is more than 6 ft from a receptacle — which works out to 12 ft maximum between receptacles on a run. Wall space is counted from 2 ft wide upward, and the section explains how fixed panels, sliding panels, and room dividers count, and when a floor receptacle may count toward the requirement. A receptacle behind a fixed appliance or too far above the floor does not do the job this spacing is meant to do. Measure along the floor line around corners and breaks, the way a lamp cord actually travels. Mark the 2 ft wall pieces — beside a door, betwee

t: Kitchen countertops, islands, and peninsulas
x: Countertop receptacles are placed so no point along the wall line of a counter is more than 24 in from a receptacle, and a counter run 12 in or wider needs one. Islands and peninsulas are handled by counter area in the 2020 edition: one receptacle for the first portion of countertop area and one more for each additional stated increment — the existing checklist item carries the 2020 numbers. This subsection also limits how far above a counter a receptacle may sit and restricts receptacles placed face-up in a work surface to listed assemblies. A peninsular countertop also needs at least one receptacle within 2 ft of its outer end, measured from the connecting wall (210.52(C)(2)). Count island

t: Bathroom receptacles
x: Each bathroom needs a receptacle close to every basin: within 3 ft of the outside edge of the basin, on a wall or partition next to it, or in one of the other positions this subsection permits. A double vanity has two basins and needs the requirement met for each one. This placement rule works alongside the bathroom circuit rule in 210.11(C)(3) and the GFCI list in 210.8(A) — all three have to be satisfied at the same sink. Measure from the basin's outside edge, not from the center of the faucet and not from the cabinet edge. On a long double vanity, one receptacle in the middle may not be within 3 ft of both basins — check both.

t: Outdoor receptacles for a dwelling
x: A one- and two-family dwelling needs readily accessible outdoor receptacles at the front and at the back, no more than 6.5 ft above grade, and additional rules cover balconies, decks, and porches that are accessible from inside. Multifamily buildings have their own version of this requirement. 'Readily accessible from grade' is part of the rule — a receptacle that can only be reached by a ladder or through a locked gate area does not serve the purpose. The requirement applies to a balcony, deck, or porch of 20 sq ft or more in overall area that is accessible from inside the dwelling. Place the front and back receptacles where a person standing on the ground can actually use them, and check p

t: Laundry receptacles
x: At least one receptacle is required in the laundry area of a dwelling, and it is served by the laundry branch circuit covered in 210.11(C)(2). A laundry closet counts the same as a laundry room for this placement rule. The dryer receptacle is a separate, larger outlet — this subsection is about the general laundry receptacle, usually the washer. If the washer location moves on a plan revision, move this receptacle with it and keep it on the laundry circuit. A receptacle borrowed from an adjacent hallway circuit fails both placement and circuit rules.

t: Garage receptacles — one per vehicle bay
x: In the 2020 edition, a dwelling garage with power needs at least one receptacle in each vehicle bay, placed no more than 5.5 ft above the floor. Attached and detached garages are both addressed, and garages without electric power are outside the requirement. The bay rule replaced the older single-garage-receptacle habit — a three-bay garage is not finished with one receptacle by the door. Count bays from the door layout on the plan, not from how the owner says they will park. Put one receptacle in each bay at rough-in; adding the third bay's receptacle at trim is a drywall patch.

t: Hallway receptacles
x: A dwelling hallway that is 10 ft or longer needs at least one receptacle. Length is measured along the centerline of the hallway, following its turns, without going through a doorway into another room. Short halls need none under this subsection, which is why the measurement — not a guess at 'about ten feet' — decides it. Run the tape down the centerline and around the bend of an L-shaped hall before deciding. Vacuum and night-light use is exactly what this receptacle is for.

t: Foyer receptacles
x: A foyer that is not part of a hallway and is greater than 60 sq ft has its own receptacle rule: a receptacle outlet is required in each wall space 3 ft or more in width, on walls not interrupted by door openings, other openings, or similar architectural features. A smaller foyer, or a foyer that forms part of a hallway, is judged under the hallway rule in 210.52(H) or the spacing rule for the room it opens into instead. Measure the foyer as its own space when it is separated by doors or cased openings. Do not count a wall segment that is mostly doorway as usable wall space.

t: A service receptacle near heating and air-conditioning equipment
x: Equipment that needs servicing needs a receptacle close to it: a 125V, 15A or 20A receptacle on the same level and within 25 ft of heating, air-conditioning, and refrigeration equipment. It may not be wired to the load side of the equipment disconnect, so it stays live for a work light and tools while the unit is shut off. Rooftop and attic equipment are the cases Sharma meets most. At rough-in, locate the air handler and condenser, then place the receptacle and prove the 25 ft with a tape — following the access path, not through a wall. Keep it off the equipment circuit's load side.

t: Lighting outlets and wall switches
x: Habitable rooms, kitchens, and bathrooms need a wall-switched lighting outlet; in some living areas a switched receptacle may stand in for it, and the subsection separates those cases. Hallways, stairways, attached garages, and entries have their own switch-location rules, and rooms and spaces used for storage or equipment, plus attics and similar spaces, have lighting requirements of their own. The point throughout is that a person should never have to cross a dark room or a dark stair to reach a switch. Walk the plan as a person arriving at night: front door, hall, stairs, each room. If any leg of that walk is in the dark, a switching rule has probably been missed.  S-05: switch boxes at 4

t: Feeders — power between the service and the final panels
x: A feeder carries power from service equipment, a transformer, or another source to the panelboards where branch circuits begin. Article 215 is short: it covers feeder conductor sizing, overcurrent protection, and ground-fault protection for certain large feeders. Most feeder questions on a Sharma job are really answered together with Article 220 for the load, Article 240 for the protection, and Article 250 for the grounding conductor that runs with it. Name the run correctly on the schedule — service conductors, feeder, or branch circuit — because the sizing and grounding rules change with the name. A subpanel feed is a feeder, and it is wired like one.  S-02 and S-09 frame Sharma feeder wor

t: Feeder conductor size and the continuous-load rule
x: Feeder conductors must have ampacity at least as large as the noncontinuous load plus 125 percent of the continuous load, before derating and correction are worked through, unless a listed assembly rated for continuous operation is used. Feeders supplying a dwelling's whole load may also be sized under the dwelling service and feeder table covered in Chapter 3, which is why a house feeder is not always sized from the general ampacity table alone. The calculated load itself comes from Article 220. Do the Article 220 number first, then size the feeder — never size from the size of the panel that happens to be on the truck. Write the continuous portion down separately so the 125 percent step ca

t: Feeder overcurrent protection
x: A feeder is protected by an overcurrent device rated not over the ampacity of its conductors, subject to the allowances in Article 240 — including the next-higher-standard-rating allowance where it applies and the tap rules where it does not. The breaker at the start of the feeder is therefore a conductor-protection question first and a load question second. Where a feeder continues to a subpanel, the equipment grounding conductor and the neutral treatment at that subpanel are Article 250 questions, covered later in this chapter. Match three numbers before energizing: feeder conductor ampacity, breaker rating, and the Article 240 rule you are relying on. If the middle number is larger than t

t: Load calculations — proving the service is big enough
x: Article 220 is the arithmetic of the trade: it turns floor area, appliance nameplates, and heating and cooling equipment into a number that sizes branch circuits, feeders, and services. It offers a standard method that counts loads item by item and, for dwellings, an optional method that uses demand factors on the whole house. Sharma's house services are normally proved with the optional dwelling method, and the app's load calculator is built on it. Never size a service from the breaker that was there before or from a neighbor's house. Run the calculation, keep it in the job file, and let it pick the service size.

t: General lighting load by floor area
x: For dwellings, the general lighting load is taken at 3 volt-amperes for each square foot of floor area, measured from the outside dimensions of the building, with the exclusions and inclusions the table and its notes describe — open porches and unfinished spaces not adaptable for future use are treated differently from living area and adaptable space. This is the starting block of both the standard and the optional dwelling calculations. It covers general lighting and general-use receptacles; named circuits and appliances are added on top of it. Measure the house the way the calculation does — outside dimensions — and do not subtract for hallways or closets. When a plan shows a finished bonu

t: The optional method for a dwelling service or feeder
x: Where a feeder or service supplies an entire dwelling, this optional method lets the load be totaled with demand factors instead of adding every load at full value. The method has conditions: it is for a dwelling, the service or feeder must carry the entire load, and the rating must meet the minimum this section sets. The general-loads part and the heating-and-cooling part are calculated separately and then added, and the existing calc table 220.82 in the app carries the rule rows and worked test cases for the method. Use the app calculator, then hand-check the two parts before you order gear: the demand-factored general load, and the larger heating-or-cooling figure. Save the printout or wo

t: Optional method — the general loads
x: The general-loads block starts with floor area at 3 VA per square foot, adds 1,500 VA for each small-appliance circuit and for the laundry circuit, and adds the nameplate ratings of the appliances and motors the subsection lists. The first 10 kVA of that total is taken at full value and the remainder at 40 percent. That demand step is the whole advantage of the optional method, and it only applies to the loads this block covers — heating and cooling are handled separately in the next part. Count circuits, not appliances, for the 1,500 VA blocks: two small-appliance circuits are required, and a third one that is installed also counts. Use nameplate VA where a rating is given in amps and volts

t: Optional method — heating and cooling
x: Heating and cooling do not run at full load together, so this part takes the largest of several stated options rather than the sum — air conditioning at full value is one option, fixed electric space heating is treated by count of units, and heat pumps with supplementary heat have their own sub-cases. Because those heat-pump sub-cases were only summarized in the v1 material, this page states the structure and not item-by-item percentages for them. Mike must confirm the sub-cases against the printed code before any calculator logic or exam answer depends on them. In Florida the air-conditioning figure usually wins this comparison, but a house with strip heat or a heat pump with auxiliary heat

t: Outside branch circuits and feeders
x: Article 225 covers wiring that runs outside — between buildings, across a yard, or overhead or underground to a detached structure. Its recurring themes are clearances, support, a disconnect at the building being supplied, and limits on how many supplies a building may have. Sharma meets it on detached garages, barns, pool houses, and site lighting fed from a house or a main building. When a run leaves a building, switch articles. A feeder inside one building and the same feeder continued to a second building are judged by different pages, and the second building needs its own disconnect and grounding treatment.

t: How many supplies may feed one building
x: The general rule is one: a building or structure gets a single feeder or branch circuit, or a single set of feeders, subject to the exceptions the section lists for things such as emergency and standby systems, fire pumps, and certain large or separately controlled installations. Two ordinary feeders run to the same detached garage because two panels were convenient is not one of the ordinary cases. Where an exception is used, the building must carry a permanent plaque or directory showing where the other disconnects are. Before running a second supply to a structure that already has one, name the exception in writing in the job file. If you cannot name one, redesign to a single larger feede

t: A disconnect at the building being supplied
x: A feeder or branch circuit supplying another building must have a disconnecting means at that building, located and grouped as this section and the following sections require, suitable for use as service equipment where required, and rated as those sections set out. The disconnect is what lets a person at the detached building kill its power without walking back to the main building. Its rating and location rules sit in the sections immediately after this one, so read them together on a real job. Mount and label the disconnect at rough-in, not at final. If the feeder feeds a subpanel inside the building, confirm which device is the building disconnect and that it is grouped and marked as suc

t: Services — where utility power enters
x: Article 230 governs the service: the conductors and equipment that bring utility power to the building and end at the service disconnect. It covers how many services a building may have, conductor clearances, where the disconnect goes and how many there may be, how big a dwelling service must be, and two 2020 additions Sharma sees on every house — surge protection and an outdoor emergency disconnect. The meter and panel layout a builder notices most is decided here and in Article 250. Plan the service as one assembly at rough-in: drop or lateral clearances, meter position, disconnect, SPD, emergency disconnect, grounding electrode system. Finding one piece missing at final is a re-inspection

t: Clearances for service conductors
x: Service conductors that run where people, windows, doors, and vehicles can reach them need clearance. Overhead conductors near a building must keep the distances this section sets from windows, doors, porches, and similar features, with a stated allowance where conductors run above an opening. Underground and other service arrangements are handled by their own parts of the article and by Article 300 burial rules. Check the drop against the finished building, not the framing: a window that will open, a porch roof, and a balcony added on a plan revision all change the clearance picture. Use the existing lookup item for the window rule crews ask about most. The utility's own service standards a

t: Surge protection on the service
x: New in the 2020 edition, this section requires surge protection when a service supplies a dwelling: a listed Type 1 or Type 2 surge protective device, installed in or next to the service equipment, with the rating and connection rules the section states. It also applies when service equipment is replaced. It protects the house's electronics against surges arriving on the service; it is not lightning protection and it is not a substitute for equipment-level protection on sensitive gear. Confirm the SPD is on the material list for every new house service and every service change, and that its location — integral to the panel or in an enclosure next to it — is drawn before rough-in. A surge dev

t: Where the service disconnect goes
x: The service disconnect must be readily accessible and in one of the locations this section allows: outside the building, or inside near the point where the service conductors enter, subject to the 2020 wording and to what the AHJ accepts for conductor length inside. Every occupant also needs access to disconnecting means for their own space in the occupancies the section covers. The disconnect is what everything downstream is judged from — it is where the service ends and feeders and branch circuits begin. Decide the disconnect location with the inspector's local practice in mind before the service is built, especially on a service change where an older inside location is being reused. Keep

t: How many service disconnects, and how they are grouped
x: The 2020 edition reorganized this rule: a service may have two to six disconnecting means, and 230.71(B) permits four arrangements — (1) separate enclosures for each disconnect; (2) panelboards, each with its own main disconnect; (3) a switchboard with each disconnect in a separate barriered vertical section; or (4) switchgear or metering centers with each disconnect in its own compartment. The disconnects must be grouped as 230.71(A) requires. A single multi-switch assembly is not automatically wrong — it counts where it fits one of these four arrangements. On a service with more than one disconnect, show the arrangement on the plan — separate enclosures, panelboards with mains, barriered s

t: Minimum size for a one-family dwelling service
x: A one-family dwelling service disconnect is rated at least 100 amperes, 3-wire. That is a floor, not a recommendation: the Article 220 calculation governs whenever it comes out higher, which on a modern Florida house with electric range, dryer, water heating, and air conditioning it usually does. Other occupancies and uses have their own minimums in the surrounding subsections of 230.79. Never quote a 100A service because it is the minimum. Run the calculation, and if the result is close to a standard size, say so with the worksheet in hand.

t: An outdoor emergency disconnect for dwellings
x: Also new in 2020, this section requires one- and two-family dwellings to have an emergency disconnect in a readily accessible outdoor location, marked as the emergency disconnect in the way the section requires. It exists so firefighters and first responders can kill power to the house without entering it. Where the service equipment itself is outdoors and meets the section, the arrangement may already satisfy it; where the disconnect is indoors, a separate outdoor device is the usual answer. Add the emergency disconnect to the service material list and the plan notes at the same time as the SPD — the two 2020 items are missed together. Mark it as required, not with a generic label.  S-02: t

t: Overcurrent protection — breakers and fuses
x: Article 240 is the protection article: it decides where overcurrent devices go, what standard ratings exist, how conductors are protected, when the next higher rating may be used, how tap conductors work, and where panels may and may not be located. A breaker has two jobs that must not be confused — it protects the conductor, and only through that does it protect the equipment and the building. Most of Article 240 that Sharma uses daily is in 240.4 and 240.24. For every circuit, ask the Article 240 question out loud: what conductor am I protecting, at what ampacity, and which rule lets me use this breaker size? If the answer is a shrug, the circuit is not designed yet.  S-03: in an existing

t: Protecting a conductor at its ampacity
x: The starting rule of the article is simple: conductors are protected against overcurrent at their ampacity, in the ways this section then refines. It points to the special cases handled elsewhere — motors, air conditioning, welders, transformers, and others — where the nameplate or a specific article changes the protection picture. It also contains the two allowances Sharma uses most, covered on the next two pages: rounding up to the next standard rating in limited conditions, and the small-conductor caps. When equipment has a nameplate that states its own maximum protection, follow that equipment article and the nameplate — the general rule here is not permission to upsize. Write the specia

t: When the next higher breaker size may be used
x: Where a conductor's ampacity does not land on a standard rating, the next higher standard overcurrent device may be used only when the conditions in this subsection are all met: the conductor is not part of a multi-outlet branch circuit supplying receptacles, the ampacity is not over the stated ceiling for this allowance, and the next higher device does not exceed that same ceiling. It is an allowance with fences, not a general right to round up. The existing lookup item works the common examples. State all three conditions when you use this allowance on a feeder or an equipment circuit. If the circuit feeds receptacles on a multi-outlet branch circuit, stop — the allowance is not available.

t: The small-conductor caps
x: Whatever the ampacity table allows at a higher temperature rating, this subsection caps overcurrent protection for small conductors: 14 AWG copper at 15A, 12 AWG copper at 20A, and 10 AWG copper at 30A, with tighter caps for aluminum and copper-clad aluminum — 12 AWG at 15A and 10 AWG at 25A. Specific equipment articles can direct otherwise for their own equipment, but for general branch wiring these caps are the numbers that decide the breaker. They are also why a 12 AWG conductor on a 25A breaker fails inspection even when a table column seems to allow the ampacity. Memorize the copper row and the aluminum/CCA row separately.
