On a CCA job, a 20A circuit means 10 AWG wire — check the roll b

t: Standard ratings for breakers and fuses
x: Overcurrent devices come in standard ampere ratings, and this section lists them — the familiar steps from small branch ratings through the large service ratings, plus the additional standard ratings it names for fuses. Nonstandard ratings exist only in the limited cases the Code allows. A calculation that lands between two standard ratings is resolved by the protection rules, not by ordering a breaker in the calculated size. When a load calculation lands at a nonstandard number, write the next step as a choice between the standard ratings on either side and record which rule you used. Do not write a nonstandard breaker size on a material list.

t: Where overcurrent devices may be located
x: Overcurrent devices must be readily accessible, protected from damage, and within the height limit this section sets — the operating handle, at its highest position, no more than 6 ft 7 in above the floor or working platform, with exceptions for the cases the section names. The same section bars overcurrent devices from the vicinity of easily ignitable material, from clothes closets, and, in dwellings, from bathrooms. The exception wording under subsection (A) is flagged below; the height number and the closet and bathroom prohibitions are covered by the checked v1 items linked here. Measure handle height to the top breaker in the panel as installed, including a raised floor or platform chan

t: Grounding and bonding — the fault-current path
x: Article 250 is the longest and most argued article in this chapter. Grounding connects a system to earth through electrodes; bonding connects metal parts together so a fault has a low-impedance path back to the source that trips the breaker fast. Earth itself is not that fault path — the breaker trips because bonding carries the fault home. The pages that follow walk the service bond, the electrodes, the sizing tables, and the piping and intersystem bonds in that order. On every job, trace one imaginary fault with your finger: from a hot wire touching a metal box, through the ground or bond, back to the source, and out on the hot again. If any link in that loop is missing, painted over, or l

t: What grounding and bonding must accomplish
x: This general section states the performance the rest of the article builds: grounded systems are connected to earth in a way that limits voltage from lightning and surges and stabilizes voltage to ground, and electrical equipment and enclosures are bonded together into a continuous, low-impedance path that can carry fault current long enough for the overcurrent device to open. It also states plainly that the earth is not to be used as the sole equipment grounding conductor. When a specific installation rule is unclear, this section is the test it has to pass. Use this page when a field argument starts: 'will it trip the breaker, fast, every time?' is the question this section asks. If the ho

t: Grounding at the service — and nowhere downstream
x: At the service, the grounded conductor is connected to the grounding electrode system and to the equipment grounding conductors through the main bonding jumper, in the service equipment. That is the one place in a premises system where neutral and ground meet. Downstream of the service — in subpanels and feeders — the grounded conductor is kept isolated from equipment grounds and enclosures, so normal neutral current never travels on metal parts and fault current has one clear path home. In every subpanel: neutral bar isolated and not bonded to the can, ground bar bonded to the can, grounds and neutrals on their own bars, and no bonding screw or strap left in place by habit. Photograph the f

t: Main and system bonding jumpers
x: The bonding jumper is the conductor or connection that ties the grounded conductor, the equipment grounding system, and the enclosure together at the service, and the system bonding jumper does the same job for a separately derived system. This section covers their material and how they are sized — for the main bonding jumper, by reference to the same sizing table used for the grounding electrode conductor, with the limits the section states. A jumper that is present but undersized or poorly landed does not do the job. Factory-installed straps and screws count only when they are the listed means for that equipment and actually installed. On a service change, verify the jumper exists before y

t: A separate building fed by a feeder
x: When a feeder supplies a second building or structure, that building needs its own grounding electrode system and a disconnect, and an equipment grounding conductor is run with the feeder in modern work. The grounded conductor at the separate building is not bonded again in the ordinary case — the bond stays at the service — and the narrow exception for existing installations has conditions that must all be met. This is the Article 250 companion to the Article 225 pages earlier in this chapter. Treat a detached garage panel as a subpanel that also needs electrodes: four-wire feeder, isolated neutral, ground bar bonded, rods driven at the building. Do not re-bond the neutral because the build

t: The grounding electrode system — all of it, bonded together
x: Every grounding electrode that is present at a building must be bonded together into one grounding electrode system: metal underground water pipe, building steel, a concrete-encased electrode, a ground ring, rods and pipes, plates, and the other electrodes the next section lists. 'Present' is the deciding word — an electrode that exists on the job may not be skipped because another one was easier to connect. The grounding electrode conductor connects that system to the service. Inventory the electrodes on the site walk: water service material, foundation steel or rebar, and what will be driven. A concrete-encased electrode has to be caught before the pour — after it, the chance is gone.

t: Electrodes that are permitted — and the ones that are not
x: This section lists what may serve as a grounding electrode, from underground water pipe with its conditions, through building steel and concrete-encased electrodes — at least 20 ft of the stated rebar or bare copper conductor encased in the foundation — to rods, pipes, and plates. It also lists what may not be used, which includes metal underground gas piping and aluminum electrodes. A water pipe electrode has its own supplementing rule, covered with the installation section. The concrete-encased electrode is the one to coordinate with the builder: 20 ft of qualifying rebar or conductor, encased as the section requires, with an accessible connection. Confirm it with the concrete crew before

t: Installing electrodes — rods, depth, and the second rod
x: Electrodes must be installed as this section requires: driven or buried to the depths it states, kept as close as practicable to each other and to the service, and supplemented where a single rod, pipe, or plate does not meet the stated resistance to earth — 25 ohms or less — or is not tested at all. In practice that means a second rod, spaced at least 6 ft from the first, on almost every job. Rod connections must be accessible or of the irreversible or exothermic type the article allows where they are buried. Drive two rods at least 6 ft apart unless you have a tested 25-ohm-or-less result in the job file. Keep the grounding electrode conductor run short, straight, and protected where it is

t: Sizing the grounding electrode conductor
x: The grounding electrode conductor is sized from Table 250.66 by the size of the largest service-entrance conductor, not by the amperage of the service disconnect alone. The section then caps what is actually required for particular electrodes: a run that goes only to rods needs no larger than the stated maximum, and a run to a concrete-encased electrode has its own larger cap — the existing checklist and quiz items carry those numbers. Aluminum and copper-clad conductors used for this purpose have material and installation limits in the surrounding sections. The caps, stated plainly: the portion of the GEC that is the sole connection to a rod, pipe, or plate electrode never has to be larger

t: Connections to electrodes — accessibility and continuity
x: Grounding electrode conductor connections must be made so they stay effective: clamps and connectors listed for the electrode and the conductor, connections to a water pipe made at an accessible point within the stated distance of where the pipe enters the building, and the conductor kept continuous or spliced only by the methods this section allows. Interior metal water piping farther into the building is a bonding question, not a substitute electrode connection point. Land the water-pipe clamp where it can be inspected, on clean metal, and do not bury a mechanical splice in the grounding electrode conductor run. If a run is cut short on a remodel, replace it or use an allowed irreversible

t: The intersystem bonding termination
x: Other systems — telephone, cable, antenna, and similar communications systems — need a place to bond to the electrical grounding system, and this section requires an intersystem bonding termination at the service or metering equipment, accessible for connection, with room for the stated number of terminations. It is the small bar or bridge by the meter that keeps a cable installer from clamping onto a random pipe. It does not replace the bonding those systems' own articles require; it gives them the listed place to land. Install it where the other utilities actually arrive at the house, and leave it accessible after siding and landscaping. Point it out on the final walk — half its failures a

t: Bonding metal piping systems
x: Metal water piping in a building supplied by a grounded system must be bonded, sized and connected as this section directs, and other metal piping that is likely to become energized — gas piping is the standard example — must be bonded as well. The bonding jumper is sized by the circuit or service that could energize the piping, using the tables this section points to. Bonding a pipe is a different job from using it as an electrode, and a pipe can need both treatments in different places. Trace the water piping bond from the panel to clean pipe, and check any jumper over a water meter or filter so the path stays continuous when the meter is removed. For gas piping, bond per this section and

t: Sizing the equipment grounding conductor
x: The green or bare conductor that runs with a circuit is sized from Table 250.122 by the rating of the overcurrent device ahead of it — not by the size of the current-carrying conductors, except that when circuit conductors are upsized, the equipment ground must be upsized in proportion. It must be able to carry fault current back to the source for as long as the breaker takes to open, which is why a long, upsized run with a standard ground is a defect even though every receptacle tests 'grounded.' The existing quiz items carry the table's common values. When you upsize a run for voltage drop, upsize the ground in the same proportion and write both sizes on the plan. Cable assemblies do this

t: Frames of ranges and dryers on existing circuits
x: Older installations were permitted to ground the frames of ranges and clothes dryers to the neutral on a 3-wire circuit, and this section keeps that arrangement lawful only for existing installations that meet all of its conditions. New work is 4-wire: two hots, an insulated neutral, and a separate equipment ground, with the appliance's bonding strap removed. This page is a tip for service work, not a design rule — and its detailed conditions are flagged below. On a service call, identify what is actually in the wall before quoting a receptacle swap. If the circuit is being replaced or extended as new work, pull 4-wire and set a 4-wire receptacle and cord; never create a new 3-wire installat

t: Wiring methods — general rules
x: Article 300 is the rulebook that sits over every wiring method in this chapter. Whichever cable or raceway you pick later — NM, MC, EMT, PVC — these general rules still apply: protect the wiring from damage, give underground runs enough cover, support what you install, and leave enough free wire at every box to make a proper joint. Read this article first, then go to the article for the specific method. Before you choose a method, ask three questions: Where does it run (dry, damp, wet, underground, exposed)? What can hit it? How will it be supported? The answers pick the method and trigger the 300 rules.

t: Protecting wiring from physical damage
x: This is the nail-and-screw section. Where cable or raceway passes through or runs alongside wood or metal framing, it has to sit far enough back from the face of the framing that drywall screws and nails miss it — or be shielded by a steel plate. It also covers cables run across the top of joists, through notches, and parallel to framing, where the same idea applies: keep the wiring out of the fastener zone, or armor it. Center your holes, keep the 1-1/4 in setback in 300.4(A)(1), and plate anything that ends up closer. Kick plates / nail plates are not extras — if the cable is in the strike zone, the plate goes on before drywall, every time.  Kick plates are always in Sharma takeoffs — stoc

t: Bored holes in wood framing
x: A hole bored through a wood stud or joist for cable or raceway must be drilled so the edge of the hole is at least 1-1/4 in from the nearest edge of the wood. If that distance cannot be kept, the cable must be protected by a steel plate at least 1/16 in thick, of a suitable length and width, installed to protect the wiring. Drill in the middle third of the stud width where you can. Check both faces — a hole can be legal from the front and too close from the back on a shallow stud. Plate first, then pull cable, so the plate is not forgotten.

t: Cables and raceways parallel to framing members and furring strips
x: This is the along-the-framing companion to the bored-hole rule. In exposed or concealed work, where a cable or raceway runs parallel to a framing member — a joist, rafter or stud — or parallel to furring strips, it has to be installed and supported so the nearest outside surface of the cable or raceway is at least 1-1/4 in from the nearest edge of the framing member or furring strip, wherever nails or screws are likely to penetrate. Where that distance cannot be kept, the cable or raceway must be protected from nail or screw penetration by a steel plate, sleeve or equivalent at least 1/16 in thick; a listed and marked thinner steel plate that provides equal or better protection is also permi

t: Protecting large conductors where they enter enclosures
x: Conductors 4 AWG and larger entering a cabinet, box or raceway have to be protected from abrasion at the entry — by a fitting, bushing or adapter that gives them a smooth, rounded surface to bear on, in the cases this subsection describes. Big conductors are stiff, heavy and expensive; a sharp knockout edge plus one hard pull is insulation damage you cannot see after the cover goes on. The research notes this protection was expanded and clarified for 2020; the exact fitting language is Mike's to confirm. Fit the insulating bushing before the pull, not after you see the scrape. On service and feeder entries, check every entry edge with a fingertip before conductors go in.

t: Underground wiring — cover, protection and sealing
x: Underground runs have to be in a wiring method approved for burial and buried deep enough that digging, traffic and frost do not reach them. Cover is measured from the top of the cable or raceway to finished grade, and the required depth depends on the method and what is above it — a yard, a driveway and a slab are not the same row of the table. Risers coming out of the ground need protection from damage. Under 300.5(G), a raceway through which moisture could contact energized live parts has to be sealed or plugged at either or both ends, with a sealant identified for use with the cable or conductor insulation; the separate seal for a raceway that passes between different temperatures, where

t: Securing and supporting — general
x: Wiring methods must be secured in place and supported at the intervals their own article requires. Raceways and cables cannot hang off other raceways, pipes or ceiling wires unless the rule for that method specifically allows it, and in a fire-rated ceiling the support has to be independent so the wiring does not fall when the ceiling does. When in doubt, support it yourself: your own strap, on structure, at the spacing in the method's article (334.30 for NM, 330.30 for MC, 358.30 for EMT, 352.30 for PVC). Never lay cable on a ceiling tile or tie it to a sprinkler pipe.

t: Free conductor length at boxes
x: At every outlet, junction and switch point, leave at least 6 in of free conductor, measured from where the conductor comes out of its raceway or cable sheath. Where the box opening is smaller than 8 in in any direction, the conductors also have to stick out of the opening by at least 3 in, so devices can be made up and folded back without fighting short wires. Conductors that pass straight through a box without a splice or termination are not counted by this rule. Strip and make up with the full 6 in in hand. If you are short, the fix is a bigger pull or a re-pull — not a wire nut buried with 2 in stubs. Leave the same working length on the spare conductors you cap off.

t: A box or fitting at each splice, outlet and junction
x: Where the wiring method is conduit, tubing, Type AC cable, Type MC cable, Type MI cable, nonmetallic-sheathed cable or another cable method, a box or conduit body has to be installed at each conductor splice point, outlet point, switch point, junction point, termination point and pull point — unless one of the exceptions in 300.15(A) through (L) permits otherwise for that case. A fitting identified for the use may be used in place of a box or conduit body where conductors are not spliced or terminated inside the fitting, and that fitting has to stay accessible after installation unless it is listed for concealed installation. Boxes themselves have to stay accessible under 314.29, without tea

t: Firestopping penetrations of rated construction
x: Where wiring passes through a fire-rated floor, wall or ceiling, the opening around it has to be firestopped with an approved system so fire and smoke do not travel through the penetration. The electrical work does not end at the conduit — the annular space around it is part of the rated assembly's performance. Ordinary expanding foam from the truck is not a firestop system unless it is listed as one for that assembly and penetration. On commercial and multi-family work, plan the firestop with the run: listed system for the assembly, the raceway type and the opening size, installed before the wall is signed off. Photograph it — the next inspector cannot see inside a closed wall either. Fires

t: Wiring in ducts, plenums and other air-handling spaces
x: Spaces made for moving environmental air — ducts, plenums and the space above a ceiling used as a return-air plenum — restrict what wiring may run there and how, because anything burning or smoldering in that space feeds the whole building's air. Only the wiring methods and materials this section allows may be installed, and equipment in those spaces is limited to what the section and the mechanical rules permit. The field trap is the plenum ceiling that looks like an ordinary ceiling: before you run a method through a ceiling space on commercial work, ask whether that space is a return-air plenum. If it is, the method list shrinks — when in doubt, ask the AHJ before rough-in, not at inspect

t: Wiring in exit enclosures
x: Exit enclosures — the protected stair towers and exit passageways people escape through — may contain only the wiring that serves the exit enclosure itself and the limited other wiring this section permits. Ordinary branch circuits passing through a stair tower on their way somewhere else do not belong there. This section was new in the 2020 NEC, which is why older study material and older habits do not mention it. On multi-family and commercial work, route around the stair tower by default. If a run must enter it, stop and check what it serves before it goes in.

t: Conductors for general wiring
x: Article 310 is about the conductors themselves: what they are made of, how they are insulated, and — most used of all — how much current they may carry. The ampacity work lives in 310.12 for dwelling services and feeders, 310.15 for correction and adjustment, and Table 310.16 for the ampacity values themselves. Termination temperature limits live back in 110.14(C) in Chapter 1; this article hands you the number, Chapter 1 tells you which column you may actually use. Start every sizing question here in this order: load, then Table 310.16 column allowed by the terminations, then correction/adjustment in 310.15, then the small-conductor caps in 240.4(D) from Chapter 2.

t: The dwelling 83% rule for services and whole-load feeders
x: For a single-phase dwelling service rated 100A through 400A that carries the entire load of the house, the service conductors may be sized at 83% of the service rating instead of the full Table 310.16 ampacity. The same idea applies to a feeder that carries the entire dwelling load, such as the feeder from an outside meter-main to the inside main panel. It does not apply to a partial-load feeder, and it does not apply when temperature correction or bundling adjustment is in play. The pair Sharma uses daily: a 200A house service is 2/0 copper or 4/0 aluminum when this rule applies. A feeder to a garage subpanel that carries only part of the house load gets sized at full value from Table 310.1

t: Ampacity correction (temperature) and adjustment (bundling)
x: Table 310.16 assumes no more than three current-carrying conductors together and a 30°C (86°F) surrounding temperature. When reality is hotter, or more conductors share a raceway or cable, the ampacity goes down: an ambient correction factor for temperature, and an adjustment factor for the count of current-carrying conductors — 80% for 4 to 6, 70% for 7 to 9, 50% for 10 to 20, 45% for 21 to 30, 40% for 31 to 40, and 35% for 41 or more. Equipment grounding conductors do not count, and a neutral that carries only the unbalanced load of its circuit usually does not count either. You may start the math from the conductor's insulation rating (for example the 90°C column for THHN or NM conductors

t: Table 310.16 — how to read the ampacity table
x: Table 310.16 gives the allowable ampacity of an insulated conductor by size, material and temperature column: 60°C, 75°C and 90°C, for copper on the left and for aluminum and copper-clad aluminum together on the right. Read it in four steps. One, find the size. Two, pick the material column — CCA is read in the aluminum columns, never the copper columns. Three, pick the temperature column your terminations allow under 110.14(C); most house equipment is 75°C, and the 90°C column is mainly a starting point for correction and adjustment. Four, apply 310.15, then check the small-conductor caps in 240.4(D): copper 14/12/10 AWG is capped at 15/20/30A, and aluminum/CCA 12/10 AWG is capped at 15/25A

t: CCA in every calculation — ampacity, voltage drop, fill, terminations, sizing
x: Copper-clad aluminum is a material choice inside the same calculations, not a separate code. Run every calculation the same way and pick the CCA line where the table has one: (1) Ampacity — CCA is read in the aluminum column of Table 310.16, with the 240.4(D) caps for aluminum, and the minimum conductor sizes in the cable articles apply — in 2020 work the smallest CCA branch conductor you will meet is 12 AWG, and there is no 14 AWG CCA NM. (2) Voltage drop — Chapter 9 Table 8 lists copper and aluminum resistances only; there is no CCA row, so no CCA resistance figure is given on this page for design use. A CCA voltage-drop figure has to come from the cable maker's data for the actual product

t: Medium-voltage conductors and cable
x: Article 311 covers the use, installation, construction specifications and ampacities for medium-voltage conductors and cable, Type MV — a single or multiconductor solid-dielectric cable rated 2,001 volts up to and including 35,000 volts, nominal. It was new in the 2020 NEC, built from material formerly in Articles 310 and 328, and Article 328 was deleted. In the 2023 NEC this material was moved and expanded as Article 315, and Article 305, the general article for systems over 1,000 volts, is also a 2023 addition — 315 and 305 are not 2020 numbers. Sharma does not pull medium-voltage cable on ordinary work; this page exists so the book's map is complete and nobody cites the wrong edition's nu

t: Cabinets, cutout boxes and meter socket enclosures
x: Article 312 covers the enclosures the conductors in Article 310 land in: panel cabinets, cutout boxes and meter sockets. Its job is room and protection inside the enclosure — enough space to deflect and bend conductors entering the top or bottom, no sharp edges cutting insulation, doors and covers that close properly, and enclosures kept out of damp and wet locations unless they are rated for them. Working space in front of the enclosure is a Chapter 1 rule (110.26), not this article. On a Sharma house this is the meter enclosure and the panel cabinet. Check conductor bending room before you land a 4/0 service conductor, not after, and keep the enclosure plumb so the deadfront and door seat

t: Conductor bending and deflection space in enclosures
x: Large conductors cannot be bent around a thumb. This section sets the minimum space inside cabinets, cutout boxes and meter enclosures for conductors to deflect and bend where they enter and land — figured from tables in the section by conductor size, number of conductors per terminal, and whether the conductor turns or runs straight through. An enclosure can be big enough on the wall and still be too small for the 4/0 or 250 kcmil that has to land in it. Size the enclosure from the conductor, not the wall space: check the bending-space table for the largest conductor and the entry direction (top, bottom, side) before the gear is ordered. Forcing a feeder into too-tight a bend is damaged ins

t: What may live inside an enclosure for switches and overcurrent devices
x: An enclosure that houses switches or overcurrent devices is not a general-purpose junction box, but it is not sealed against all other wiring either: this section allows conductors to run through and splice inside it within set limits — commonly taught as the wiring space used by feed-through conductors being limited to a share of the enclosure's cross-sectional wiring space (40%), and splices and taps to a larger share (75%), with the exact conditions in the section. The 2020 changes also addressed power-monitoring and energy-management equipment installed in these enclosures. Do not treat a panel as free splice space on a remodel. If feed-through or splices are planned in an overcurrent en

t: Outlet, device, pull and junction boxes
x: Article 314 is the box article: which box, how big, how it is set, how it is supported, and what may live in it. The sizing heart is 314.16 — a box is big enough only if its marked volume holds every conductor, device, clamp and ground the counting rules charge against it. The placement rules around it (setback, repair, support, fan rating, accessibility) are what inspectors check after the volume math passes. Run the fill math before the rough-in, not at trim. A box that fails fill in the wall fails the same way on paper — cheaper to catch it on paper.

t: Box fill — volume, allowances and counting
x: A box may not be filled past its volume. Start with the box volume: for a standard metal box use Table 314.16(A); for a nonmetallic or marked box use the volume marked on the box itself. Then charge the contents using Table 314.16(B) allowances — 2.00 cu in for each 14 AWG, 2.25 for each 12 AWG, 2.50 for each 10 AWG. The counting rules in 314.16(B)(1) through (5) decide how many allowances each thing costs — including the 2020 grounds rule on the next page (up to four grounds count once, each one past four adds a quarter) — and the total charge may not exceed the box volume. The five counts, in field order: (1) each conductor that enters from outside and ends or is spliced in the box counts

t: The five counting rules, one by one
x: 314.16(B)(1) Conductors: each conductor from outside the box that is spliced or terminated counts once; a conductor that runs through unbroken counts once; an unbroken loop or coil of conductor not less than twice the minimum free-conductor length required by 300.14 — so 12 in or more of loop — counts twice; pigtails that originate in the box count zero. (B)(2) Clamps: where one or more internal cable clamps are present, all of them together count once, at the largest conductor in the box; a cable connector with its clamping mechanism outside the box counts zero. (B)(3) Support fittings: where luminaire studs or hickeys are present, count one allowance for each type of fitting — all studs to

t: Conductors and cables entering boxes
x: Cables entering a box have to be secured to it, or the cable has to be fastened close enough that the box entry stays put, and the cable sheath has to continue into the box so the conductors are protected where they enter. The v1 field rule (L-065): the sheath extends at least 1/4 in inside the box past any clamp, and with single-gang nonmetallic boxes the cable is fastened within 8 in of the box while the sheath still goes 1/4 in in. Strip the sheath outside the box, not inside it: 1/4 in of sheath past the clamp is protection; 2 in of sheath inside the box is fill you did not count and a make-up fight at trim.

t: How a box sits in a wall or ceiling
x: How far a box may sit behind the finished surface depends on what that surface is made of. In concrete, tile, gypsum board (drywall), plaster, or other noncombustible material, the front of the box, plaster ring, extension ring, or listed extender may be back no more than 1/4 inch. In wood or other combustible material, the box or extender has to reach the finished surface or project past it. Drywall is noncombustible for this rule even when it is screwed to wood studs. A box buried farther than the rule allows is both a device problem — the yoke ears cannot reach — and a code problem. Set box depth off the stud face for the finish that is actually going on that wall: 1/2 in drywall is not t

t: Repairing the surface around a box
x: Where a box is set in a noncombustible wall or ceiling, the broken or chipped surface around it has to be repaired so there is no gap or open space bigger than 1/8 in around the box. The plate cannot be the patch — the surface itself has to come back to the box. On remodel work, check the gap before you set the device. A 1/4 in crater around a cut-in box is a fail here and a wobbly device later; use the right box or repair the opening.

t: Supporting boxes
x: A box has to be supported — screwed, nailed, braced or hung by a method the article allows for that box type — rigidly enough that it does not move when devices are plugged in and pulled out for twenty years. Surface boxes, pendant boxes and boxes in walls and ceilings each have their own allowed supports in this section, and a box supported by a raceway alone is allowed only in the narrow cases the section describes. Wiggle test at rough-in: grab the box and push. If it moves, the device will move at trim and the plate will never sit flat. Add the brace or bracket now.

t: Boxes at ceiling-fan outlets
x: Where an outlet in a habitable room ceiling is in a spot that could support a ceiling fan — wired and placed the way a fan location is — the box has to be listed for fan support, and the maximum weight it may carry is marked on it. A fan over 35 lb up to 70 lb needs a box marked for that weight; a fan heavier than 70 lb is supported independently of the box. If there is a ceiling outlet in a bedroom or living room with a switch leg, rough it in with a fan-rated box whether or not the plan shows a fan today — the next owner will hang one there. That is checklist BL-09.

t: Pull and junction boxes for conductors 4 AWG and larger
x: Once conductors reach 4 AWG and larger, box sizing stops being a cubic-inch question and becomes a geometry question: the box must be big enough to pull and bend stiff conductors without damaging them. For a straight pull — in one wall, out the opposite wall — the distance from the entry to the opposite wall must be at least eight times the trade size of the largest raceway. For an angle pull, a U pull or splices, that distance must be at least six times the largest raceway in the row, plus the sum of the trade sizes of the other raceways in the same row on the same wall; and the distance between raceways that enclose the same conductor must be at least six times the larger raceway. These ru

t: Boxes must stay accessible
x: A junction or pull box has to remain accessible without removing any part of the building — no drywall, no tile, no fixed cabinetry over the cover. If reaching the splice means cutting the building open, the box was in the wrong place when the walls were open. Before close-in, walk the job and photograph every junction box location. If a cover will be behind a fixed finish, move the box or move the splice now.

t: Armored cable — Type AC
x: Type AC is a factory cable with its conductors inside a flexible metal armor, with an internal bonding strip in contact with the armor so the armor can serve as the equipment ground path. Sharma meets this article most often through one cross-reference: 334.23 sends NM cable in accessible attics to the attic protection rules written here in 320.23. The cable itself shows up on Sharma jobs mainly in older work and the occasional commercial job. Do not confuse AC with MC: AC carries its bonding strip and uses fittings listed for AC; MC (Article 330) usually carries a separate green ground conductor. The fittings are not interchangeable by habit — use the fitting listed for the cable in your ha

t: Flat cable assemblies — Type FC
x: Type FC is a factory flat-cable assembly of parallel conductors formed integrally with an insulating web, made to be field-installed in a surface metal raceway identified for the use — a specialized method, not a substitute for NM run loose in a wall. It is permitted only as branch circuits, with a branch-circuit rating not exceeding 30 amperes, to supply suitable tap devices for lighting, small appliances, or small power loads, where installed for exposed work in locations where it will not be subject to physical damage, and protected by a cover identified for the use where it is installed less than 8 ft above the floor or a fixed working platform. The cable, raceway, tap devices and fittin

t: Flat conductor cable — Type FCC
x: Type FCC is a flat conductor cable system designed to be installed under carpet squares and similar finishes, with its own shields, boxes and transition fittings. It is a different method from Type FC flat cable assemblies (Article 322) — the two are not interchangeable, and neither is ordinary branch wiring in a flat jacket. Encountered almost only in specialized commercial fit-outs. Identify the system by its listing before touching an existing FCC installation.

t: Integrated gas spacer cable — Type IGS
x: Type IGS is a specialized underground cable: a factory assembly of one or more individually insulated conductors — solid aluminum rods laid parallel — enclosed in a loose-fit nonmetallic flexible conduit, insulated with dry kraft paper and pressurized sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) gas, and rated 0 through 600 volts. It is a below-grade method for service conductors, feeders, and branch circuits, including direct earth burial. It must not be used as interior wiring, must not be exposed in contact with a building, and must not be used above ground. It exists in the book so the map is complete, far outside house and light-commercial branch work. No Sharma field use. If IGS appears on a drawing, it

t: Metal-clad cable — Type MC
x: Type MC is a factory assembly of insulated conductors inside a metal sheath — smooth, corrugated or interlocked armor — with its own equipment grounding arrangement. It is the commercial counterpart to NM: it can be used exposed or concealed, in dry locations and the other locations its listing allows, fished in existing walls, and run where NM cannot go, such as many commercial ceilings and walls. It may not be used where it will be subject to physical damage, in wet locations unless the specific cable is listed for it, or in the other prohibited uses its article lists. Cut MC with the right tool and use listed MC connectors — a Romex connector is not an MC connector. Support and securing f

t: Mineral-insulated, metal-sheathed cable — Type MI
x: Type MI is a copper or alloy sheath packed with mineral insulation around its conductors — a cable chosen where extreme heat, fire survival or mechanical abuse rules out ordinary methods, such as fire-pump and critical circuits and harsh industrial spots. Its terminations are specialized sealed fittings, and moisture control at the ends is part of the installation, not an afterthought. Sharma meets MI mainly as existing work in older or specialized installations. Do not cut or terminate it with NM/MC habits — the sealing fitting and its instructions govern.

t: Nonmetallic-sheathed cable — Types NM, NMC, NMS (Romex)
x: This is Sharma's house cable. NM is two or more insulated conductors with an equipment ground, factory-wrapped in a nonmetallic sheath. Article 334 says where it may be used (334.10), where it may never be used (334.12), how it is protected and run (334.15, 334.17, 334.23), how it is bent (334.24), how often it is secured and supported (334.30), and how its ampacity is limited (334.80). Almost every Sharma rough-in decision — staple spacing, attic runs, the 60°C ampacity limit — traces back to this one article. If you learn one article in this chapter cold, learn this one. The other methods are variations; NM is the daily work.

t: Where NM may be used
x: NM may be used exposed or concealed in normally dry locations, in one- and two-family dwellings and their garages, and in the other buildings and construction types this section allows. 'Normally dry' is the load-bearing phrase: the cable is a dry-location method, and the building type limits in this section are why a method that is fine in a house may not be fine in a larger commercial building. House, garage and accessory work in dry interiors: NM is the default. Anything wet, damp, underground or in a bigger occupancy: stop and check 334.12 and pick another method.

t: Where NM may not be used
x: NM may not be used in wet or damp locations — including inside a raceway that is itself underground or outdoors, because the inside of that raceway is a wet location — as service-entrance cable, embedded in concrete or masonry, in areas subject to physical damage without protection, or in the other locations this section lists. It is a dry, protected, interior method. The classic fail: NM sleeved in PVC down an outside wall and underground to a yard light. The PVC does not make the location dry. Use UF or conductors in raceway for that run (Articles 340 and 352). Florida's humidity does not reclassify an interior dry location, but any exterior or underground raceway interior is wet — plan th

t: NM in exposed work and through framing
x: Exposed NM has to follow the surface it is run on and be protected where it can be hit. Where it passes through a floor, a wall or framing, the Article 300 protection rules ride along: bored-hole setbacks and nail plates from 300.4, and protection where the cable passes through slots or notches. In unfinished basements and crawl spaces, this section sets how larger cables may run through joists and how smaller cables are run on running boards or through bored holes. The basement and crawl-space case has its own subsection, 334.15(C): where cable runs at angles with the joists, a cable at least as large as two 6 AWG or three 8 AWG conductors may be secured directly to the lower edges of the j

t: NM in accessible attics — the scuttle rule
x: For accessible attics, this section points NM cable at the attic rules written for AC cable in 320.23: 334.23 says the installation of cable in accessible attics or roof spaces shall also comply with 320.23. Under 320.23(A), cable run across the top of floor joists, or within 7 ft of the floor or floor joists across the face of rafters or studding, has to be protected by substantial guard strips that are at least as high as the cable; where the space is not accessible by permanent stairs or ladders, that protection is required only within 6 ft of the nearest edge of the scuttle hole or attic entrance. Under 320.23(B), cable installed parallel to the sides of rafters, studs, or ceiling or flo

t: Bending radius of NM cable
x: NM may not be bent so sharply that the bend damages the sheath or the conductors inside it; the rule of this section is expressed as a minimum radius measured to the inner edge of the bend — commonly taught as five times the cable diameter. A kinked flat cable at a tight stud turn is exactly the damage this section is aimed at. Make wide, lazy turns. If you have to force it around a corner with your thumb creasing the sheath, the bend is too tight — re-route or move the hole.

t: Securing and supporting NM
x: NM must be secured and supported at intervals not exceeding 4-1/2 ft, and within 12 in of every box, cabinet and fitting. Cable run through bored holes or notches in framing counts as secured and supported by that framing. Flat cable may not be stapled on edge, and the staple has to hold the cable snug without crushing the sheath. Staple pattern on a stud run: within 12 in of the box, then at least every 4-1/2 ft, snug not crushed. A staple that deforms the sheath is a damage point, not a support point.

t: Ampacity of NM cable — the 60°C limit
x: The conductors inside NM are 90°C rated, but the cable's ampacity is limited to the 60°C column of Table 310.16. You may still start correction and adjustment math from the 90°C value — that is what makes a bundled or hot-attic NM run survivable on paper — as long as the final ampacity after 310.15 does not exceed the 60°C value, and the 240.4(D) small-conductor caps still apply on top. Field translation: 14 AWG NM on a 15A breaker and 12 AWG NM on a 20A breaker, full stop — and if you derate a bundle of home runs, do the math from 90°C, then cap the answer at the 60°C column (25A for 12 AWG before the 20A breaker cap).  S-10 still governs the wire choice: copper by default; CCA one size up.

t: Power and control tray cable — Type TC
x: Type TC is a factory assembly of power or control conductors with an overall jacket, listed for installation in cable tray (Article 392) and the other uses its article permits. Tray-rated is the load-bearing word: a cable in a tray must be a cable type Article 392 allows, and TC is the common one. Certain TC constructions carry additional ratings (such as exposed-run ratings) only when the cable is marked for them. On a light-commercial tray job, read the jacket print before the cable leaves the shop: TC alone is not every rating — check for the marking that matches the actual installation.

t: Type P cable
x: Type P is a rugged, flexible cable construction originating in marine and drilling work, listed in the 2020 NEC for the applications its article describes, including certain hazardous-location uses noted in the 2020 changes. It is not a house or ordinary commercial branch-circuit cable. No Sharma field use on ordinary work. Its presence on a drawing signals a specialized, engineered specification.

t: Service-entrance cable — Types SE and USE
x: Type SE cable is a single-conductor or multi-conductor assembly, primarily used for services. Type SE has a flame-retardant, moisture-resistant covering and is the above-ground form. Type USE is identified for underground use, has a moisture-resistant covering, but is not required to have a flame-retardant covering. On a house, SE is the cable that can carry the service where individual conductors in a mast or raceway are not used. Where SE is used for interior branch-circuit or feeder wiring, 338.10(B)(4) makes the Article 334 installation rules apply to that run — see the 338.10(B)(4) page. Type SE and Type USE are not interchangeable: SE shall not be used underground, with or without a ra

t: SE cable used as interior wiring
x: Type SE cable is a service-entrance cable first, but 338.10(B)(4) also lets it be used as interior wiring for branch circuits and feeders inside a building. When it is used that way, the installation has to follow Part II of Article 334 for NM cable — excluding 334.80. The routing, protection and support rules of Part II therefore apply to the indoor SE run, but the NM ampacity rule in 334.80 does not. SE has its own narrow ampacity rule instead: for ungrounded conductor sizes 10 AWG and smaller, where installed in contact with thermal insulation, the ampacity is in accordance with the 60°C conductor temperature rating. An SE cable feeding a subpanel inside the house is roughed and protected

t: Underground feeder cable — Type UF
x: UF is NM's underground sibling: the conductors are embedded in a solid moisture-resistant covering so the cable itself is rated for direct burial and wet locations, and for sunlight exposure where it is marked sunlight resistant. It is used for yard lights, outbuildings, pool and landscape feeds and other underground branch circuits and feeders, buried at the cover depth Article 300.5 sets for it — 24 in for direct burial in the general case, with the 12 in residential GFCI exception L-061 teaches. UF is stiff and unforgiving to strip — score the covering carefully and do not nick the conductors. Above ground, protect it where it can be damaged, the same as any exposed cable, and sleeve rise

t: Intermediate metal conduit — IMC
x: IMC is the middle-weight steel raceway: thinner wall than rigid metal conduit, heavier and stronger than EMT, threaded like RMC and usable in most of the same places, including many wet and exposed locations with the right fittings. Sharma meets it mainly on commercial and service work where EMT is not tough enough and full rigid is not needed. One trade size note that matters in the field: IMC and RMC share the same outside diameter, but IMC's thinner wall gives it a larger inside area, so its Chapter 9, Table 4 fill values are its own — do not use the RMC row for an IMC run. Link to Chapter 9 for the actual numbers; do not re-derive them here.

t: Rigid metal conduit — RMC
x: RMC is the heavy-wall threaded steel raceway — the toughest common raceway in this chapter. It may be used in nearly every location, including underground (where its 6 in cover in the general open-ground row of Table 300.5 is the payoff for its strength. Under a one- or two-family dwelling driveway that same rigid metal conduit needs 18 in, the same as PVC and direct-burial cable. Streets, roads, and other driveways and parking lots demand 24 in for every method), wet locations, and places subject to physical damage, with fittings and supports made for it. Underground, corrosion protection and the soil conditions govern how long it lasts. The 6 in burial depth is why RMC still earns its cost

t: Flexible metal conduit — FMC ('Greenfield')
x: FMC is a flexible spiral metal raceway used for short, bendy final connections — inside equipment, across a vibration gap, or fished where a rigid method cannot go. It is not a wet-location method in its basic form (that is LFMC, Article 350), it needs fittings listed for it, and when it is used as the ground path its length and overcurrent limits are restricted — on Sharma work, pull a green ground and do not rely on the spiral. Keep FMC whips short and supported, bond with a real conductor, and switch to LFMC the moment the location is wet or outdoors.

t: Liquidtight flexible metal conduit — LFMC
x: LFMC is FMC with a liquidtight plastic jacket over the metal core — the flexible method for wet locations, outdoors, and vibrating equipment. On Sharma work this is the condenser whip: LFMC from the disconnect to the outdoor unit, with listed liquidtight fittings, supported close to each end, and a separate equipment ground inside. The whip is not the support for the disconnect and the disconnect is not the support for the whip — strap both, keep the whip off the ground where it will be weed-eaten, and seal the outdoor end with the listed fitting, hand-tight plus the manufacturer's turn, not channel-locks. 210.8(F) GFCI enforcement on outdoor HVAC outlets has varied by AHJ and amendment — se

t: Rigid polyvinyl chloride conduit — PVC
x: PVC is the nonmetallic rigid raceway Sharma uses underground and in wet and corrosive spots: services and feeders in the yard, pool-area runs, and sleeves. Schedule 40 is the standard wall; Schedule 80 is the heavier wall used where the run is exposed to physical damage. PVC may not be used where ambient or conductor heat will exceed its temperature rating, in the hazardous and theater-type locations its article bars, or as a support for fixtures and equipment hanging off it. Underground cover for PVC is 18 in in the general Table 300.5 case. Two field behaviors define the method: it expands and contracts a lot with temperature, and its joints are solvent-welded, not threaded (except at list

t: High-density polyethylene conduit — Type HDPE
x: HDPE conduit is the coiled, flexible nonmetallic raceway used mainly for long underground runs — directional-bored and trenched duct for utilities, site feeders and communications — joined by fusion or listed couplings rather than solvent cement. Its strength is the continuous long run with no joints in the bore. Sharma meets HDPE most often as the duct the utility or site contractor provides. Confirm what is actually in the duct and who owns it before planning a pull through it.

t: Nonmetallic underground conduit with conductors — Type NUCC
x: NUCC is a factory assembly: conductors already installed inside a nonmetallic underground conduit, supplied and installed as one listed system for direct burial work. Because it arrives as a system, its fittings, splices and repairs follow its own article and listing — it is not field-pulled PVC with a head start. Rare on Sharma work. Treat any NUCC found underground as a system to be identified before it is cut or extended.

t: Reinforced thermosetting resin conduit — Type RTRC
x: RTRC is a fiberglass-reinforced resin raceway chosen where corrosion resistance and strength matter and metal raceways would rot or are barred — chemical, wastewater and harsh outdoor industrial environments. It is joined with its own fittings and adhesives and supported under its own article. Its baseline support table, Table 355.30, carries the same spacings as PVC's Table 352.30 — 3 ft for trade sizes 1/2 through 1, rising to 8 ft for trade size 6 — and conduit listed for support at a different spacing is permitted to be installed in accordance with that listing. Specialized work only. If a corrosive-environment job specifies RTRC, its support table and joining instructions come with the

t: Liquidtight flexible nonmetallic conduit — LFNC
x: LFNC is the all-plastic liquidtight flexible raceway — no metal core — used for short flexible connections in wet and outdoor locations where a nonmetallic method is wanted, including many pool and equipment connections. It comes in listed types with different fittings and limits, has a maximum supported length pattern similar to other flex methods, and may not be used where subject to physical damage or beyond its temperature and listing limits. On pool and outdoor equipment, confirm the specific LFNC type and its fittings are listed for the location before it goes on the truck — 'liquidtight' on the box is a listing claim, not a description.

t: Electrical metallic tubing — EMT
x: EMT is the thin-wall steel raceway that carries most of Sharma's light-commercial work: unthreaded, joined with set-screw or compression couplings and connectors, bent on the job with a hand or mechanical bender. It may be used exposed or concealed, in dry, damp and wet locations — in wet locations with fittings that comply with 314.15 and with supports, straps, bolts and screws of corrosion-resistant material or protected against corrosion. Galvanized steel and stainless steel EMT may be installed in concrete, in direct contact with the earth, and in areas subject to severe corrosive influences where protected by corrosion protection and approved as suitable for the condition; aluminum EMT

t: How many conductors fit in EMT — the Chapter 9 handoff
x: This section does not carry its own fill numbers: the number of conductors in EMT is whatever Chapter 9 allows — Table 1 percentages (53% for one conductor, 31% for two, 40% for more than two, 60% for a nipple 24 in or shorter), Table 4 areas for the raceway, and Table 5 areas for the conductors. Worked example from the v1 Chapter 9 tables: 1/2 in EMT has a 40% area of 0.122 sq in; a 12 AWG THHN conductor occupies 0.0133 sq in; 0.122 / 0.0133 = 9.17, so nine 12 AWG THHN fit. Equipment grounds count toward fill. Do the area math, do not eyeball a stuffed pipe at trim time. When all conductors are the same size, Annex C gives the same answer as a shortcut — but the tables are the rule, Annex C

t: EMT bends — radius and the 360-degree rule
x: Bends in EMT have to be made so the tubing is not damaged and its inside diameter is not effectively reduced. The radius of the curve of any field bend, measured to the centerline of the tubing, must not be less than the radius shown in Chapter 9, Table 2 for that trade size. Offsets and saddles count toward the run's total bend. Between pull points, the total bend in one run may not exceed 360 degrees: the equivalent of four quarter bends, in any combination. A run that needs more than 360 degrees needs a pull point — a box or conduit body — not a stronger pull. Count every bend on your fingers as you lay out: stub-up 90, offset 30 + 30, three-point saddle 22.5 + 45 + 22.5 — you are at 240

t: Securing and supporting EMT
x: EMT must be securely fastened within 3 ft of each outlet box, junction box, device box, cabinet, conduit body or other tubing termination, and securely fastened and supported at intervals not exceeding 10 ft. Where structural members do not readily permit fastening within 3 ft of a termination, an unbroken length of EMT — a length without couplings — may be fastened up to 5 ft from that termination. For concealed work in finished buildings or prefinished wall panels where securing is impracticable, unbroken lengths without a coupling may be fished. Horizontal runs supported by openings through framing members at intervals not exceeding 10 ft, and securely fastened within 3 ft of a terminatio

t: EMT couplings and connectors — tight, and listed for the location
x: EMT couplings and connectors must be made up tight so the raceway is mechanically continuous and electrically continuous as a ground path. Where buried in masonry or concrete, they must be of the concrete-tight type. Where installed in wet locations, they must comply with 314.15 — listed for use in wet locations and installed so moisture does not enter or accumulate in the enclosure. The Code rule is the listing for the location, not the fitting style: use the type, compression or set-screw, that is listed concrete-tight or listed for wet use for the job in front of you. Match the fitting to the location on the purchase order, not at the truck: a fitting listed concrete-tight for masonry or

t: Flexible metallic tubing — Type FMT
x: FMT is a small, flexible metallic tubing method for specific limited applications — not a general raceway and not the same thing as FMC (Article 348), despite the similar name and look. Its permitted uses are narrow and its size range is small. Name-check before use: FMT on a print is a specific listed method. Do not substitute FMC, EMT or LFMC for it by appearance.

t: Electrical nonmetallic tubing — ENT ('smurf tube')
x: ENT is a pliable, corrugated nonmetallic raceway used concealed in walls, floors and ceilings, in slab on grade and in other locations its article allows — common on Sharma-adjacent work for low-voltage and island/concrete runs in houses, and as a sleeve where a future pull is wanted. It is not a general substitute for PVC conduit: its locations, support rules (commonly every 3 ft and within 3 ft of boxes, per its article) and temperature and damage limits are its own. Island receptacle in a slab house is the classic ENT case: stub it accurately, cap it, photograph it with measurements before the pour — a lost stub in concrete is a saw-cut later.

t: Auxiliary gutters
x: An auxiliary gutter is a sheet-metal enclosure hung at switchboards, panelboards and service equipment to give conductors room to enter, turn and distribute where the equipment's own wiring space runs out. It supplements the equipment — it is not a raceway run across a building, and its conductor fill and splicing room follow its own article. On larger services and multi-meter work, a gutter is what makes a clean, legal lineup possible. Size it for the conductors and their bending, like 312.6, before the gear is set.

t: Busways
x: A busway is a factory-built distribution system: busbars in a metal housing, with plug-in units that tap power off along the run — the backbone distribution of larger commercial and industrial buildings. Sections are joined, supported and tapped as a listed system; overcurrent protection and grounding follow its article and the system design. Outside Sharma's ordinary scope, but common in the larger commercial spaces Sharma works in. Never open, move or tap a busway as if it were a big wireway — it is energized distribution equipment.

t: Cablebus
x: Cablebus is an engineered power-distribution assembly: insulated conductors supported in a ventilated metal enclosure, built to a specific design for large feeders, typically between major equipment. It is designed and supplied as a system for that job, not assembled from shelf parts in the field. Industrial and large-commercial work only. Field changes to a cablebus run are engineering changes, not electrician improvisation.

t: Cellular concrete floor raceways
x: This article covers raceways formed in cellular concrete floor systems in larger commercial buildings, where the floor structure itself contains the distribution cells and header ducts. Outlets are activated from the cells with system fittings. Encountered in existing commercial buildings, not new Sharma construction. Identifying the floor system correctly is the whole job before any outlet work.

t: Cellular metal floor raceways
x: The metal counterpart to Article 372: raceways formed by the cells of a cellular steel floor deck in commercial construction, with header ducts and system outlet fittings. Bonding and continuity of the metal system are part of its article. Existing-building work. As with 372, the system has to be identified before it is extended or abandoned in place.

t: Metal wireways
x: A wireway is a sheet-metal trough with a hinged or removable cover, used in light commercial work to carry feeders and branch circuits where conductors need to be laid in and remain accessible along a run — above panels, along shop walls, in electrical rooms. Conductors are limited by fill and by the number of current-carrying conductors before adjustment applies, splices and taps are allowed inside where the wireway stays accessible, and the cover is what makes the system legal: no cover, no wireway. Wireway is the tidy alternative to a forest of parallel conduits leaving a panel — plan its size for the conductors plus their derating, not just their bulk.

t: Nonmetallic wireways
x: The nonmetallic counterpart to Article 376's metal wireways: a trough with a removable cover for laying in conductors, used where a nonmetallic system is wanted, within the locations and limits its article sets. Fill, splices and support follow the same wireway logic in a plastic system. Use where corrosion makes metal wireway a poor choice and the location is permitted. The cover still makes the system — no cover, no wireway.

t: Multioutlet assemblies
x: A multioutlet assembly is a surface, flush or freestanding raceway designed to hold conductors and receptacles, assembled at the factory or in the field — the hard-wired strip over a workbench or lab counter, in metal or nonmetallic form. It is permitted in dry locations only. It may not be installed concealed — except that a metal assembly may be surrounded on its back and sides by the building finish and a nonmetallic one may be recessed in a baseboard — and it is barred where subject to severe physical damage, in hoistways, and in the other locations its article lists. A metal assembly may pass through a dry partition if no outlet sits inside the partition and the cover can be removed on

t: Nonmetallic extensions
x: Nonmetallic extensions are listed surface extension wiring systems that start from an existing outlet to serve additional outlets along a wall surface — a narrow, specific method with its own fittings and limits, not a license to surface-run ordinary cable. They are barred in many of the places people first think of using them. Rarely the right answer on Sharma work; a proper raceway (386/388) or a new circuit is usually both legal and better. Know the article mainly to recognize the method.

t: Strut-type channel raceway
x: A strut-type channel raceway is a listed wiring system built on metal strut channel with covers and fittings made for electrical use — the channel is the raceway. Ordinary structural strut by itself is a support, not a raceway; the listed covers, fittings and conductor limits of this article are what turn it into one. Common confusion on commercial jobs: strut holding conduits is support work; strut carrying conductors inside it is this article. Keep the two apart in the takeoff and the inspection conversation.

t: Surface metal raceways
x: Surface metal raceway is the low-profile metal channel system mounted on walls and ceilings in finished spaces — the office and retail retrofit standard — carrying branch circuits to surface boxes and devices made for the system. Fill, fittings and grounding are the system's own; it is a raceway, not a decorative cover for loose cable. The retrofit answer where walls cannot open. Plan device boxes and fittings from the same system — mixing ordinary boxes defeats the listing.

t: Surface nonmetallic raceways
x: The nonmetallic counterpart to Article 386: surface-mounted plastic raceway systems for finished spaces, common for both power and low-voltage in offices and homes. Power and communications sharing one system is allowed only where the system is listed and arranged for it. Neat retrofit work, within its damage and location limits — it is surface wiring, so it lives where people and furniture can reach it. Protect or re-route accordingly.

t: Underfloor raceways
x: Underfloor raceways are distribution ducts set in or under a concrete floor — the older office-building system of floor ducts and junction boxes feeding floor outlets. New work is uncommon; existing systems are met on commercial remodels, where inserts and outlets must match the system. On a remodel, find the junction boxes before promising floor outlets. An abandoned duct with no access is archaeology, not distribution.

t: Cable tray systems
x: Cable tray is a support system, not a raceway: an open ladder, ventilated or solid-bottom structure that supports the wiring methods listed in Table 392.10(A) — including tray-rated Type TC, metal-clad cable, raceways, and, where identified for the use, nonmetallic-sheathed cable in the structures Article 334 permits. Single insulated conductors are the restricted case: outside the industrial-establishment rules of 392.10(B) they do not belong in tray. The tray itself must be bonded and grounded as the article requires, and fill is figured by the cable-area and sum-of-diameters rules of 392.22, not by the Chapter 9 conduit tables. If Sharma reaches for tray on a light-commercial job, the cab

t: Low-voltage suspended ceiling power distribution systems
x: This article covers listed low-voltage power systems that use the suspended ceiling structure to distribute power to ceiling-supported equipment — a specific engineered system, not permission to treat ceiling grid as a raceway or support. Components, connections and loads are the system's own. Specialized commercial systems only. Ordinary ceiling work stays under 300.11 and 300.22 — this article does not loosen either.

t: Concealed knob-and-tube wiring
x: Knob-and-tube is the oldest method in the chapter: single conductors run open on porcelain knobs and through porcelain tubes, found in older Florida houses. This article governs its (very limited) permitted extensions and uses today; new knob-and-tube installations are effectively a closed door, and insulation contact with it is a known fire concern that other codes also address. On remodels in older houses, Sharma practice is identification and safe handling: document it, do not bury it in new insulation or extend it casually, and put replacement options in front of the customer.

t: Messenger-supported wiring
x: Messenger-supported wiring carries cables or conductors on a steel messenger strand strung between structures — overhead spans to outbuildings, site lighting and similar runs, using cable assemblies listed for the method. The messenger carries the load; the electrical cable is not its own support. Overhead spans live outdoors and age outdoors: check the strand, attachments and clearances as one system at every service call.

t: Open wiring on insulators
x: Open wiring on insulators — individual conductors run exposed on insulators with set separations — is a legacy and specialized method (agricultural and industrial settings are its remaining home), governed by its own clearances and protection rules. It is not a shortcut version of knob-and-tube and not a method for new house work. Know it to recognize it. New Sharma work does not start here.

t: Outdoor overhead conductors over 1,000 volts
x: The chapter's last article covers outdoor overhead conductors operating over 1,000 volts on premises wiring — the campus- or plant-style medium-voltage distribution a property owner owns, not the serving utility. It is a short, engineered article, not a clearance table: it sets no prescriptive clearances of its own, 399.30 requires the supporting structures to be designed and documented by a licensed professional engineer, and the detailed clearance and construction rules live in the National Electrical Safety Code. Utility installations under a utility's exclusive control sit outside the NEC altogether under 90.2(B)(5). (Note the number: in the 2020 NEC this article is 399, not 395 — the re

t: Flexible cords and cables — article intro
x: Article 400 covers cords and flexible cables used to connect equipment, not wire that is installed as part of a building. It sorts cord types by construction and permitted use, and it draws a hard line against using a cord as a substitute for permanent wiring. If the wire is meant to stay in the building, it belongs in a Chapter 3 wiring method, not in a cord. When you reach for a cord, ask whether the equipment is meant to move, be serviced, or be exchanged. If the answer is no, run a permanent wiring method instead. Check the cord jacket marking for the type letter before you trust it in a damp or hard-use location.

t: What flexible cords may be used for
x: Section 400.10 lists the jobs a flexible cord is allowed to do: hanging fixtures, connecting portable equipment, appliances that need to be moved for cleaning or service, and similar uses where flexibility is the point. The common thread is that the equipment, not the building, is what moves. A cord feeding a fixed outlet box or a permanent load is outside this list. Before you plug or hard-wire a cord to anything, name the 400.10 use out loud. If you cannot name one, stop and run conduit or cable. Watch especially for cords run through walls, ceilings, or doorways, which this article does not allow.

t: Uses not permitted — flexible cords and cables
x: Section 400.12 is the stop list for flexible cords and cables — in the 2017 edition this list was numbered 400.8, and the 2020 reorganization of Article 400 moved it here. Unless 400.10 permits the use, a flexible cord, flexible cable, cord set, or power-supply cord may not be used: (1) as a substitute for the fixed wiring of the structure; (2) run through holes in walls, structural ceilings, suspended or dropped ceilings, or floors; (3) run through doorways, windows, or similar openings; (4) attached to building surfaces, except that cords used for temporary wiring under 590.4 may be attached; (5) concealed by walls, floors, or ceilings, or located above suspended or dropped ceilings, excep

t: Fixture wires — article intro
x: Article 402 covers the small conductors used inside fixtures and equipment, called fixture wires. They are for wiring within a luminaire or similar equipment and for connecting that equipment over a limited distance, not for general branch-circuit runs through a building. Sizes run smaller than branch wiring, which is exactly why they must stay inside the equipment they belong to. If you find a fixture wire run acting like a branch circuit through a wall or ceiling, flag it. Replace that run with a Chapter 3 method sized for the circuit. Keep fixture-wire splices inside the fixture or its listed outlet box.

t: Switches — article intro
x: Article 404 covers switches: the devices that open and close a circuit, from a simple single-pole snap switch to motor-circuit switches. It handles which conductor a switch may interrupt, where a grounded (neutral) conductor must be available at a switch box, how high and how accessible a switch must be, and how switch terminals are marked for conductor materials. Start here whenever a switching question is about the device itself rather than the circuit feeding it. On rough-in, the two 404 questions to settle before the walls close are neutral availability at switch boxes and switch height. Both are cheap at rough-in and expensive after drywall.  S-05: when the plan is silent, Sharma sets s

t: Three-way and four-way switching — what the switch may control
x: Section 404.2(A) deals with which conductor a switch interrupts. In plain terms, switching belongs in the ungrounded (hot) conductor, and three-way and four-way arrangements must be wired so the load is never left connected to a hot conductor with the switch appearing to be off in a way that leaves lampholder shells energized. The traveler system exists to let two or more locations control one load while keeping that rule intact. Wire 3-way/4-way runs by function, not by color habit: common, travelers, switched leg, neutral, ground. Test every switch position at trim and confirm the load is fully controlled from each location before you leave. Never borrow a neutral from another circuit to m

t: A neutral must be available at most switch locations
x: Section 404.2(C) requires a grounded conductor — the neutral — to be present at most switch locations in a dwelling and in general lighting control. The reason is practical: modern controls, timers, occupancy sensors, and smart switches often need a neutral to power themselves. There are listed exceptions, including some raceway installations where the neutral can be added later and certain replacement or retrofit situations, so read the exception list for the exact job instead of assuming. At rough-in, pull the neutral through every switch box even when the planned device is a plain snap switch that does not use it today. Cap it neatly in the back of the box. That one habit prevents the mos

t: Switches in damp or wet locations — and out of the tub/shower wet location
x: Article 404 requires switches installed in damp or wet locations to be in enclosures suited to the location, and it separately restricts switches in a bathtub or shower space: a switch may not be installed within the wet location of a tub or shower unless it is part of a listed tub or shower assembly made for that purpose. The rule parallels the receptacle and luminaire zones in 406.9(C) and 410.10(D) — the wettest part of the room is kept free of devices a wet person would operate. A switch on the dry wall outside that space is an ordinary installation. At layout, treat the tub/shower wet location as a no-switch zone the same way you treat it as a no-receptacle zone. Exterior and patio swit

t: Switches must be reachable — operating handle height
x: Section 404.8(A) requires switches to be readily accessible and sets a ceiling on height: the center of the operating handle, in its highest position, may not be more than 6 ft 7 in. above the floor or working platform. The point is that a person standing on the floor must be able to operate the switch without a ladder or a reach tool. It does not set the normal mounting height for a house switch — that comes from the plan or company practice. Measure to the handle in its up position, not to the top of the box. Special cases exist for switches next to equipment they serve and for busway-type installations, so check the exceptions before you relocate a switch that looks too high.  S-05: Sharm

t: Snap switch ratings and the loads they may control
x: Section 404.14 ties a general-use snap switch to the kind of load it controls. A switch marked for AC only, or for AC/DC, has different limits for motor, inductive, and tungsten-type loads, and a switch may not be loaded past the rating that applies to that load type. In plain terms: the amp number on the yoke is not a promise for every load — the load type decides which limit applies. Read the yoke marking before you put a snap switch on a motor, a ballast bank, or a heater. Where the load is a motor or is otherwise hard on contacts, use a switch rated for that duty or control it through a rated contactor or relay.

t: Switch terminal markings for conductor materials (CO/ALR)
x: Section 404.15(C) carries the CO/ALR marking rule for switches — the switch-side twin of 406.3(C) for receptacles: a switch designed for the direct connection of aluminum conductors must be marked CO/ALR. The terminal rules that go with the marking, stated for the 2020 NEC in NEMA Engineering Bulletin No. 122 from the UL guide information for snap switches: terminals of 15A and 20A snap switches are for use with copper and copper-clad aluminum conductors only, unless marked CO/ALR, which adds aluminum; terminals of switches rated 30A and above are for copper only, unless marked AL/CU. Plain aluminum never lands on an unmarked device terminal. Check the device itself: read the terminal markin

t: Receptacles, cord connectors, and attachment plugs — article intro
x: Article 406 covers receptacle outlets and the plugs and cord connectors that go into them: how receptacles are rated and grounded, when a replacement must upgrade protection, where face-up devices may be used, what damp and wet locations demand, the tub and shower exclusion zone, and where tamper-resistant receptacles are required. It is the article behind most device-level corrections on a residential final. At trim, work 406 as a checklist room by room: correct replacement type, WR where the location needs it, in-use cover where the location is wet, TR where 406.12 requires it, and nothing inside the tub/shower zone.  S-07: points marked GFI on a Sharma plan get a standard tamper-resistant

t: Replacing a receptacle — the replacement must meet today's rules for that location
x: Section 406.4(D) governs what you must do when you swap out an existing receptacle. Where current code requires GFCI, AFCI, tamper-resistant, or weather-resistant protection at that location, the replacement has to provide it. Where there is no equipment grounding conductor in the box, the permitted paths are a non-grounding-type replacement, a GFCI-type replacement marked as having no equipment ground, or a grounding-type receptacle fed through a GFCI device and marked accordingly. You may not simply install a standard grounding receptacle on an ungrounded circuit and leave it looking grounded. On a service swap, test for a real ground first, then pick the replacement path and apply the req

t: Receptacle assemblies in countertops and work surfaces — listed for the surface
x: A receptacle assembly installed in a countertop surface has to be listed for countertop applications — an ordinary receptacle in a cut-in box does not become countertop equipment by being set into the surface. Where the assembly is required to provide GFCI protection under 210.8, it is permitted to be a GFCI receptacle assembly listed for countertop applications. Section 406.5(F) applies the same listing rule to receptacle assemblies in work surfaces. Whether a receptacle may sit face-up in that surface at all is the next rule, 406.5(G). On a kitchen or bath counter, put the listed pop-up or countertop assembly on the material list — do not plan on a standard duplex in the surface. If that l

t: Face-up receptacles in countertops — the prohibition is 406.5(G)
x: Section 406.5(G) carries the face-up rule for receptacles in counters and work surfaces. Under (G)(1), a receptacle may not be installed in a face-up position in or on a countertop or work surface unless it is listed for countertop or work surface applications. Under (G)(2), a receptacle may not be installed face-up in the area below a sink at all — the listed-assembly exception does not apply there. The hazard is the position itself: a face-up device collects spills, crumbs, and liquids directly into its face. The separate listing rule for receptacle assemblies made for these surfaces is at 406.5(E) and (F), covered on the previous page. Do not cut a standard duplex into a countertop face-u

t: Receptacles in damp locations
x: Section 406.9(A) covers receptacles in damp locations — places that are protected from direct weather but can be damp, such as a covered porch or a carport. The receptacle must be weather-resistant type, and the enclosure must keep moisture out of the wiring connections when no plug is inserted; a cover that is weatherproof when the plug is out is the usual way this is met. Damp is the middle category: not dry indoors, not taking direct rain. Look up before you decide: if the device can get rained on with the cover open or closed, treat it as wet, not damp, and use the 406.9(B) in-use arrangement. When in doubt, install the wet-location setup — it satisfies the damp case too.

t: Receptacles in wet locations — in-use covers and weather-resistant devices
x: Section 406.9(B) covers receptacles in wet locations, where water can reach the device whether or not something is plugged in. The enclosure must stay weatherproof while a plug is inserted and the cord is in use — the bubble or in-use cover — and 15A and 20A, 125V and 250V receptacles in wet locations must be weather-resistant (WR) type.
