An unattended wet-location receptacle, such as one on a house exterior, needs that in-use protection; the rule has specific treatment for receptacles that are attended while in use. Stock both parts on the truck: a WR receptacle and an extra-duty in-use cover. A flat flip lid on an exterior receptacle that runs a pump, a charger, or landscape equipment is a

t: No receptacles inside the tub or shower zone
x: Section 406.9(C) keeps receptacles out of the zone directly inside and immediately around a bathtub or shower stall. In the 2020 arrangement this zone is measured 3 ft horizontally and 8 ft vertically from the top of the bathtub rim or the shower stall threshold, and no receptacle may be installed within that zone. The rule exists because a person in water is in the worst possible position to contact a device or a cord connected to it. On layout, mark the zone on the floor plan before you place bath receptacles, not at trim. Vanity receptacles belong outside the zone even when the counter runs close to the tub. If the only wall space is inside the zone, move the discussion to the builder bef

t: Tamper-resistant receptacles in dwellings and other listed occupancies
x: Section 406.12 requires tamper-resistant receptacles in dwelling units and in a list of other occupancies where children are present, such as guest rooms, childcare and preschool areas, dormitories, and certain medical and office waiting areas. A TR receptacle has internal shutters that only open when both blades of a plug go in together, so a key or paperclip pushed into one slot does not reach a live contact. The requirement applies at the receptacle locations the article covers, generally those at normal reachable height rather than the listed exceptions such as receptacles high above the floor or inside a luminaire. Use TR devices as the default dwelling device and check the exception be

t: Switchboards, switchgear, and panelboards — article intro
x: Article 408 covers the boards themselves: switchboards, switchgear, and the panelboards Sharma installs on nearly every job. For residential and light commercial work the live parts of this article are the circuit directory, identification of circuits, closing unused openings, overcurrent protection of the panelboard, and the rule that breakers be the type listed for the panel they sit in. The industrial switchboard sections matter on larger commercial gear; the directory and listing rules matter everywhere. Treat the panel as a document, not just a box: directory filled in, circuits identified at every disconnect, unused openings closed, and only listed breakers installed. An inspector can

t: The circuit directory — specific, on site, and kept current
x: Section 408.4(A) requires every circuit and circuit modification to be identified at the panelboard with enough detail to tell circuits apart, and a circuit directory (or circuit identification) must be provided at the board. Generic labels like 'plugs,' 'lights,' or 'bedroom' written for a different house do not meet the intent; the identification has to describe the actual purpose or use of each circuit in that building. Spare positions must be marked as spares, and the directory must be updated when circuits change. Fill the directory at trim, from the actual panel schedule, and have the person who wired the house check it circuit by circuit with a tester or by switching. A directory copi

t: Identification of the source of supply
x: Section 408.4(B) addresses panelboards supplied by a feeder: the board must be marked to identify where its supply comes from when that source is in a different location or is not obvious, so that a person standing at the panel can find the disconnect that kills it. Companion identification rules in Article 408 also require disconnects and circuits to be marked for their purpose where they are not self-evident. The theme of the whole part is that nobody should have to guess what feeds what. On a sub-panel, label the feeder source (for example, 'Fed from Main Panel, Garage') at the sub-panel and label the feeder breaker at the source panel. Do the same for any panel fed from a generator or a

t: The equipment's short-circuit current rating must cover the available fault current
x: Section 408.6 requires switchboards, switchgear, and panelboards to have a short-circuit current rating (SCCR) at least equal to the available fault current where they are installed. A panel that matches the job on volts and amps can still be the wrong panel if its SCCR is below the fault current the service can deliver into a short. This requirement was added in the 2020 edition, which is why older change-out habits never asked the question. On a service change or a commercial panel set, get the available fault current (from the utility or the design documents) and compare it with the SCCR marked on the gear before the gear is ordered. Record both numbers in the job file. If the fault curre

t: Unused openings must be closed
x: Section 408.7 requires unused openings in a panelboard (and in switchboards and switchgear) to be closed with closures that give protection substantially equal to the wall of the enclosure. An open breaker space with a missing filler plate is an exposed live-part opening, a dust and vermin path, and an automatic correction. Tape is not a closure. Keep listed filler plates for the panel brand on the trim truck. Before final, open every panel, run a finger check for open spaces, blank plates, and missing knock-out closures, and close them with the manufacturer's part.  S-02/S-03 apply to the closure as well: use the filler listed for that panel, not a near-fit from another brand.

t: The panelboard itself must be protected
x: Section 408.36 requires a panelboard to be protected by an overcurrent device rated no higher than the panelboard's rating, located in or ahead of the board, with listed exceptions such as certain existing installations and mains supplied under specific service rules. In plain terms, a 100A panel may not sit behind a 200A breaker just because the feeder wires are large. The bus has its own limit and something must enforce it. When you set a sub-panel, check three numbers together: panel bus rating, feeder conductor ampacity, and the breaker feeding it. The smallest applicable limit governs. Record all three on the panel schedule for the office file.

t: Each grounded (neutral) conductor gets its own terminal
x: Section 408.41 requires each grounded conductor in a panelboard to terminate in its own individual terminal that is not used for any other conductor, unless the terminal is specifically identified for more than one. Doubling two neutrals under one screw is a classic correction: when one circuit is worked on, loosening the shared terminal can open the neutral of a live circuit sharing it. Equipment grounding conductors follow their own termination rules and the panel's listing; the one-per-terminal discipline on this page is about the grounded conductors. At trim, land neutrals one to a screw and torque them; never park a second neutral under a screw 'temporarily.' On a panel change-out, budg

t: A panelboard may not be installed face-up
x: Section 408.43 prohibits installing a panelboard in a face-up position. A load center belongs on a vertical surface with its breakers oriented as the listing intends; a face-up board collects debris and water, and its breakers do not operate or indicate as designed. The rule was added in the 2020 edition and most often matters on custom commercial millwork and unusual equipment layouts, not on a standard house panel. If a plan or a cabinet detail shows a panel lying flat, stop at rough-in and raise it with the builder — the fix is a layout change, not a field workaround. Check orientation on any pre-built equipment package before it is set.

t: Industrial control panels — article intro
x: Article 409 covers industrial control panels: the factory- or field-assembled panels that control industrial machinery, with their short-circuit current rating (SCCR) marking, supply conductor sizing, and internal wiring rules. The SCCR is the headline item — a panel may not be installed where the available fault current exceeds the rating marked on it. Sharma meets this article on light commercial and equipment work rather than in houses. Read the SCCR on the panel label and compare it with the available fault current at its supply before you set the panel. If the panel has no SCCR marking or the fault current is unknown, stop and take it to Mike — that is an engineering check, not a field

t: Luminaires, lampholders, and lamps — article intro
x: Article 410 covers light fixtures in the broad code sense: luminaires, lampholders, and lamps, including where they may be installed, how they are supported, temperature limits near combustible material, and the special zones in bathtubs, showers, and clothes closets. The two pages Sharma hits constantly are the tub/shower zone and the closet rules. Fixture listing and its instructions (110.3(B)) do half the work in this article — the box and the spec sheet are part of the code answer. Read the fixture's own listing before you rough the box: weight, temperature rating, damp/wet rating, and closet or shower suitability are all on the label or the cut sheet, not in the field manual.  Sharma ba

t: Luminaires in the bathtub and shower zone
x: Section 410.10(D) controls fixtures inside the zone measured 3 ft horizontally and 8 ft vertically from the top of the tub rim or the shower threshold. Inside that zone a luminaire must be listed for damp locations, and for wet locations where it is subject to shower spray, and certain fixture types — including hanging fixtures, pendants, and ceiling-suspended fans — are not permitted in the zone at all. A fixture outside the zone is not governed by this subsection even if it is in the same bathroom. Mark the zone on the plan at rough-in and check every bath fixture against it, including the shower light and any fan/light combo. Confirm the damp or wet marking on the fixture label matches wh

t: Luminaires in clothes closets — permitted types and clearances
x: Section 410.16 controls what may light a clothes closet and how far it must sit from the closet storage space — the volume defined in 410.2: 24 inches out from the side and back walls, from the floor up to 6 feet or the highest clothes-hanging rod, and 12 inches out from the walls, or the width of the shelf if greater, from there up to the ceiling. Permitted types [410.16(A)]: surface-mounted or recessed incandescent or LED luminaires with a completely enclosed light source; surface-mounted or recessed fluorescent luminaires; and surface-mounted fluorescent or LED luminaires identified as suitable for installation within the closet storage space. Not permitted [410.16(B)]: incandescent lumin

t: Recessed luminaires — insulation contact and thermal protection
x: Section 410.116 covers recessed luminaires: the clearance they must keep from combustible material, the thermal protection that shuts the fixture down if it overheats, and the difference between fixtures listed for direct contact with insulation (Type IC) and those that must keep insulation away. An IC rating is a property of the specific fixture, not of recessed fixtures in general. The fixture's marking also decides whether it may be installed in a ceiling that will be insulated after the fact. Read the housing label before the ceiling closes: IC or non-IC, and the insulation clearance if it is non-IC. In an insulated Florida attic ceiling, a non-IC can buried in blown insulation is both a

t: Lighting systems operating at 30 volts or less — article intro
x: Article 411 covers low-voltage lighting systems operating at 30 volts AC or 60 volts DC or less — and only 15 volts AC or 30 volts DC where contact with water is likely: the listed system, its power supply, and the secondary wiring that feeds the fixtures. These systems are installed as a listed assembly, not assembled from loose parts in the field, and the secondary conductors have their own rules distinct from ordinary branch wiring. Sharma meets this article mainly in landscape-style and specialty accent lighting inside a project. Install the system as the listed package: listed power supply, listed fixtures, and the manufacturer's wiring instructions. Do not extend a 30V secondary with b

t: Appliances — article intro
x: Article 422 covers appliances: water heaters, dishwashers, disposals, ranges and cooktops, dryers as appliances, space heaters that plug or hard-wire as appliances, and similar equipment. Its working parts are branch-circuit sizing for specific appliances, permitted cord-and-plug connections, overcurrent protection, and the disconnecting means that lets a servicer kill the appliance safely. Where an appliance is also a motor load or also HVAC equipment, Articles 430 and 440 may govern instead or in addition — check the appliance's own article first. For every appliance on a job, settle three things from the nameplate before rough-in is closed: circuit size, cord-and-plug or hard-wired, and w

t: GFCI protection required for specific appliances
x: Section 422.5 names the appliances that must have Class A GFCI protection for personnel wherever they are installed — the duty travels with the appliance, on top of the room rules in 210.8, and meeting one does not erase the other. The 2020 list at 422.5(A) is: automotive vacuum machines provided for public use; drinking water coolers and bottle fill stations; cord-and-plug-connected high-pressure spray washing machines; tire inflation machines provided for public use; vending machines; sump pumps; and dishwashers. It reaches appliances rated 150 volts or less to ground and 60 amperes or less, single- or 3-phase, cord-and-plug-connected or hardwired, and 210.8(D) points to this same list. Th

t: Storage water heaters — treat the load as continuous for circuit sizing
x: Section 422.13 sizes the branch circuit for a fixed storage water heater of 120 gallons or less at not less than 125 percent of the heater's nameplate rating. In practice that is why a common 4500W, 240V heater (18.75A) lands on a 25A minimum calculation and is conventionally wired on a 30A circuit with 10 AWG copper — the arithmetic must be run for the actual nameplate on the actual job, not copied from the last house. The heater is treated this way because it can run for long stretches recovering a tank. Do the division every time: nameplate watts divided by voltage, times 1.25, then choose the standard breaker and conductor that cover it. Write the result on the panel schedule so the next

t: Cord-and-plug connection for range hoods
x: Section 422.16(B)(4) is the provision the brief assigns to cord-and-plug-connected range hoods: a listed range hood may be connected with a cord and plug where the conditions of that subsection are met, including that the hood is marked for that connection method and the receptacle arrangement matches the rule. Cord connection is what lets the hood be removed for service without unwiring it, but it is only permitted because the appliance and the installation meet the listed conditions — not as a general shortcut for any fixed appliance. Confirm the hood's instructions allow cord connection and that the receptacle location matches the plan before rough-in. If the hood is listed for hard-wirin

t: Disconnecting means for permanently connected appliances
x: Section 422.31 covers how a permanently connected appliance is disconnected for service. Depending on the appliance's rating, the disconnect may be a switch or breaker that meets the article's conditions, and for larger appliances the disconnect must be capable of being locked in the open position or meet the subsection that applies to its size. The intent is simple: the person servicing the appliance must be able to cut its power and keep it cut. The branch-circuit breaker can serve this role only where the conditions for doing so are met. At rough-in, decide where each hard-wired appliance's disconnect lives and confirm a servicer can reach it. A water heater, an air handler, or a cooktop

t: Fixed electric space-heating equipment — article intro
x: Article 424 covers heating that is built into the building: baseboard heaters, wall heaters, radiant panels and cables, duct heaters, and boilers used for space heat. Its core ideas are that heating loads are treated as continuous, that the equipment must be listed and installed to its instructions, and that disconnects and controls must let the heater be serviced and shut off safely. In Florida houses Sharma meets this article most often at duct heat strips in an air handler and at the occasional wall or bath heater. Size every heater circuit from the nameplate as a continuous load, and confirm the disconnect and control arrangement before the air handler or heater is set. Heat strips are a

t: Branch-circuit sizing for fixed space heat — 125 percent
x: Section 424.4(B) is where this rule lives in the 2020 edition — it was 424.3(B) in 2017, before the Article 424 reorganization. The 2020 text states the sizing directly instead of using the old 'shall be considered continuous load' sentence: the branch-circuit conductors for fixed electric space-heating equipment and any associated motors shall be sized not smaller than 125 percent of the load. Overcurrent protection is sized at the same 125 percent through the continuous-load rules of 210.19(A)(1) and 210.20(A), so in practice both the conductors and the breaker come out at 125 percent of the total load connected to the circuit, heater plus any blower or fan motor in the same equipment. t: Disconnecting means for fixed space-heating equipment
x: Section 424.19 requires a disconnecting means for fixed space-heating equipment that disconnects the heater and its controller, placed so the equipment can be serviced safely, with provisions for locking or for the breaker arrangement depending on the installation. A duct heater inside an air handler is normally disconnected at the air handler's disconnect, which is why the 440/424 boundary matters on an HVAC change-out: the heat strips and the blower are one piece of equipment at service time. Confirm the disconnect kills the strips and the blower together, and that it is within reach of the person servicing the unit. On a change-out, if you move the disconnect, re-verify the heat-strip cir

t: Fixed resistance and electrode industrial process heating equipment — article intro
x: Article 425 covers electric heating used for an industrial process rather than for comfort: process tanks, ovens, and similar equipment. Sharma's residential and light commercial work rarely installs it, so this first pass gives the article a place in the book and a scope page only. Where a commercial job includes process heat, work the article with the equipment listing and ask Mike before treating it like space heat under 424. Do not borrow 424 rules for a 425 load by habit. Identify the article from the equipment's use, then apply that article plus the listing.

t: Fixed outdoor electric deicing and snow-melting equipment — article intro
x: Article 426 covers fixed electric equipment that melts snow and ice outdoors: heated pavements, walks, and similar surfaces. It is a later-pass article for a Florida book — Sharma does not install snow-melting in its territory — and it is included here so Chapter 4 walks the NEC in complete official order. Ground-fault protection of equipment is a central theme of this article when it does apply, as with its sister heating articles. If a Florida job somehow specifies deicing equipment (a northern builder's standard detail copied onto a Florida plan is the usual way), flag it to the office rather than installing or deleting it silently. Florida note: no snow load in Sharma's territory; treat

t: Fixed electric heating equipment for pipelines and vessels — article intro
x: Article 427 covers electric heat tracing and heating for pipes and vessels: the cable or panel that keeps a pipe from freezing or keeps a process fluid at temperature. Sharma meets its Florida cousin in the form of pipe heat trace on exposed commercial plumbing and in freeze protection details, not in ordinary house work. Ground-fault equipment protection is again a central requirement because the heating element runs where people and water are both present. Install heat trace exactly to its listing: correct cable for the pipe, correct controller and sensor location, and the required ground-fault equipment protection in place and tested. Photograph the controller setting at turnover.

t: Motors, motor circuits, and controllers — article intro
x: Article 430 is the longest working article in Chapter 4 and the one most often misapplied, because it is a system, not a single rule: conductors sized from table full-load current, separate overload protection sized from the nameplate, short-circuit and ground-fault protection sized from its own tables and percentages, a controller, and a disconnect within sight. Each of those five jobs has its own sizing basis, and using one number for all five is the classic 430 error. Air-conditioning equipment is pulled out of parts of 430 by Article 440, which has its own nameplate-driven rules — always check which article governs the equipment in front of you. Work a motor in this order, every time: (1

t: Which current do you size from — table values vs. nameplate
x: Section 430.6 is the traffic rule for the whole article. For sizing conductors, disconnects, controllers, and short-circuit/ground-fault protection, you use the full-load current values from the Article 430 tables for the motor's horsepower and voltage — not the amps printed on that particular motor's nameplate, because the next replacement motor may differ. Overload protection is the exception: it is sized from the actual nameplate current of the motor installed, because it protects that specific machine. Mixing those two bases up is the single most common motor calculation error. Keep two numbers on your worksheet and label them: 'Table FLC' and 'Nameplate FLA.' If a number on your page is

t: Conductors for a single motor — 125 percent of table full-load current
x: Section 430.22 sizes the branch-circuit conductors feeding one continuous-duty motor at not less than 125 percent of the motor's full-load current as taken from the Article 430 tables. The extra quarter covers the heating of a motor that runs for long periods at full load. Intermittent and short-time duty motors are treated under their own parts of this section, so the duty rating on the nameplate decides which rule you are in before you do any arithmetic. Take the table FLC for the horsepower and voltage, multiply by 1.25, then select the conductor from the ampacity table using the correct temperature column for the terminations. Do not size the wire from the nameplate amps and do not round

t: Conductors feeding several motors
x: Section 430.24 sizes conductors that feed two or more motors (or motors with other loads): take 125 percent of the full-load current of the largest motor, add the full-load currents of the other motors at 100 percent, and add any other loads under their own rules, all using the Article 430 table values. The largest motor gets the continuous-duty margin; the rest are added at face value, on the reasonable basis that the feeder sees the sum. It is the feeder-level companion to the single-motor rule in 430.22. Build the sum in a labelled column — largest motor first at 125 percent, then each additional motor at 100 percent — so the next person can audit it. Do not apply 125 percent to every mot

t: Overload protection — protects the motor from running too hot
x: Section 430.32 requires overload protection for continuous-duty motors over the small sizes the article sets, sized from the motor's nameplate full-load current with the percentage depending on the motor's service factor and temperature-rise markings. The overload device watches running current over time and trips before the windings cook; it is not there to clear a short circuit, which is the branch protective device's job. A motor with built-in thermal protection meets this requirement through its own device where the article allows it. Read service factor and rise off the nameplate before you select or set an overload. If the overload trips repeatedly, measure the running amps and find th

t: Branch-circuit short-circuit and ground-fault protection for motors
x: Section 430.52 sizes the device that clears a fault on a motor branch circuit, using the percentages in Table 430.52 applied to the table full-load current, with the device type (fuses, inverse-time breaker, instantaneous-trip breaker, and so on) deciding which column applies. These percentages are deliberately far above running current, because the device must ride through motor starting inrush without opening, while still clearing a fault. That is why a motor circuit can legally have a breaker that looks oversized for its wire — the overload device, not the breaker, is protecting the motor and, through its sizing rules, the circuit against overload. Never judge a motor circuit by house-cir

t: The motor disconnect must be within sight
x: Section 430.102 places the disconnecting means for a motor and its controller within sight from the equipment it disconnects — visible and not more than 50 ft away, the Article 100 meaning of 'in sight.' The person servicing the machine must be able to see the disconnect, or the disconnect must be of a type that can be locked open under the conditions the article allows. A breaker in a panel across the building, with no lockable arrangement, does not give a servicer control of the machine in front of them. Stand at the motor and point at its disconnect before you call the job done. If you cannot see it, either move it, add the local disconnect, or confirm the lockable arrangement the article

t: What may serve as the motor disconnect
x: Section 430.109 lists the types of switches and devices permitted to serve as a motor disconnect, including horsepower-rated switches and listed circuit breakers, with the permitted type depending on the motor's size and duty. A general-use switch that is fine for a lighting load is not automatically a motor disconnect; the device must be rated for interrupting a motor circuit of that horsepower. Small fractional-horsepower motors have their own permitted arrangements under this section and 430.111. Read the horsepower rating on the switch, not just the amp rating, before you land a motor on it. When the disconnect is a breaker in a panelboard, confirm it is a permitted type for that motor a

t: Rating of the motor disconnect — at least 115 percent
x: Section 430.110 sizes the disconnecting means for a motor circuit: a general-use switch used as a motor disconnect must have an ampere rating of at least 115 percent of the motor's full-load current as taken from the Article 430 tables, and horsepower-rated devices are selected by their horsepower rating for the motor served. The disconnect is a switching device that must safely make and break motor current, which is why its sizing basis is its own rule and not simply 'match the breaker.' Combined with 430.102 (within sight) and 430.109 (permitted types), this completes the disconnect picture. Check two markings on a motor disconnect: the amp rating against 115 percent of table FLC, or the h

t: Air-conditioning and refrigerating equipment — article intro
x: Article 440 takes hermetic refrigerant motor-compressors and air-conditioning equipment out of the general motor rules and gives them a nameplate-driven system. The equipment nameplate states the minimum circuit ampacity (MCA) and the maximum overcurrent protection (MOCP, sometimes marked MOP or 'max fuse/breaker'), and those two printed numbers — not a horsepower table — size the circuit. Article 440 also sets the disconnect rule Sharma's crews use daily: within sight, readily accessible, at the equipment. Where 430 and 440 disagree for a compressor, 440 governs. Florida settles the common condenser question for houses: FBC-Residential §E3408.1 amends 210.8(F) with Exception No. 2 — GFCI pr

t: Reading the HVAC nameplate — MCA and MOCP do the sizing
x: Section 440.4(B) covers the nameplate marking for equipment with a hermetic refrigerant motor-compressor: the plate carries the rated-load current and the branch-circuit selection current, and the manufacturer's marked minimum circuit ampacity and maximum overcurrent device rating are built from them. In field language: MCA tells you the smallest conductor ampacity the circuit may have; MOCP tells you the largest fuse or breaker you may protect it with. A breaker smaller than MOCP is allowed; a conductor smaller than MCA is not. The plate, not a tonnage rule of thumb, is the calculation. On every condenser and air handler: record MCA, MOCP, voltage, and phase from the plate. Wire to at least

t: Short-circuit current rating of air-conditioning and refrigerating equipment
x: Section 440.10 requires motor controllers and industrial control equipment used with air-conditioning and refrigerating equipment to have a short-circuit current rating suitable for the available fault current, with the rating marked as the article requires. It is the Article 440 companion to 408.6 and 409: modern packaged HVAC gear and its control panels carry an SCCR, and a unit installed where the available fault current exceeds it is a mismatch even when MCA and MOCP are perfect. The issue arises on commercial rooftops and larger services, rarely on a house condenser. On commercial HVAC work, add SCCR to the nameplate photograph set: MCA, MOCP, and SCCR, plus the available fault current

t: The HVAC disconnect — within sight and readily accessible
x: Section 440.14 requires the disconnecting means for air-conditioning and refrigerating equipment to be within sight from the equipment and readily accessible to it, with an exception for certain industrial/process installations where conditions are met. 'Within sight' carries the Article 100 meaning: visible and within 50 ft. The disconnect may be on the equipment or separate from it, but a person servicing the unit must be able to reach it and see the unit from it. A breaker inside the house panel does not satisfy this by itself. The disconnect also may not be mounted on a panel that is designed to allow access to the equipment itself, and it may not be placed where it obscures the equipmen

t: Short-circuit and ground-fault protection for a compressor circuit
x: Section 440.22 sizes the branch-circuit short-circuit and ground-fault protection for a hermetic motor-compressor circuit and ties it to the equipment's rated-load or branch-circuit selection current, with the marked MOCP on a listed unit's nameplate being the number the installer works to in practice. As with motors generally, this device is allowed to be larger than the conductor's plain ampacity, because equipment overload protection inside the unit does the running protection and the breaker must ride through compressor starting current. That allowance only exists inside Article 440's system — never borrow it for a general circuit. If a condenser trips a breaker sized at or below its MOC

t: Conductor sizing for a single motor-compressor
x: Section 440.32 sizes conductors for a single hermetic motor-compressor at not less than 125 percent of the compressor's rated-load current or branch-circuit selection current, whichever is greater. On listed equipment the manufacturer has already done this work and printed it as the MCA, so the field rule and the nameplate rule agree: the conductor ampacity must be at least the MCA. Where you are sizing from a compressor's own data rather than a unit plate, this section is the arithmetic behind the plate. When the plate is present, wire to the MCA and do not re-derive it. When the plate is missing or illegible on existing equipment, stop and get the data from the manufacturer rather than est

t: Generators — article intro
x: Article 445 covers generators themselves: their marking, conductor ampacity, overcurrent protection, and shutdown controls. The transfer equipment and the optional-standby-system rules that decide what a generator may feed live mainly in Chapter 7 (Article 702), and required standby systems in 700/701 — this article is about the machine. Sharma meets 445 on whole-house generator work in dwellings, where the 2020 outdoor shutdown rule on the next pages is the item inspectors ask about. Separate the two questions on a generator job: is the machine itself installed to 445, and is the system it feeds wired and sized to Chapter 7? Passing one does not pass the other. Cross-link to Chapter 7 for t

t: Stationary generators must be listed (2020 addition)
x: Section 445.6, added in the 2020 edition, requires stationary generators operating at 600 volts or less to be listed. Before this edition a generator could arrive on a job with no listing requirement stated in Article 445 itself; now the machine's listing is a code item, checked the same way as any other equipment's. The listing carries the installation instructions that 110.3(B) makes enforceable, including clearances, exhaust, and the shutdown arrangement in 445.18. At quote stage for a standby generator, confirm the exact model is listed and get its installation manual into the job file before the pad is poured. An unlisted or grey-market unit is a stop, not a discount. Florida note: hurr

t: Generator conductors — 115 percent of nameplate current
x: Section 445.13 sizes the conductors from a generator to its first distribution device or devices at not less than 115 percent of the generator's nameplate current rating, with the article's own provisions for cases where design prevents overloading. The margin exists because a generator can be asked to carry its full rating for the whole duration of an outage. Neutral conductor treatment has its own paragraphs in this section, so do not assume the neutral is automatically the same size as the ungrounded conductors on every system type. Size from the nameplate on the actual machine, and confirm whether the installation is a separately derived system before you settle the neutral and grounding

t: Outdoor shutdown for a generator at a one-family dwelling
x: Section 445.18(D) is the 2020 provision the brief assigns to the emergency shutdown of a generator installed outdoors at a one- or two-family dwelling: in addition to the shutdown provisions that apply to generators generally, a dwelling unit generator located outside must have a readily accessible disconnecting/shutdown device located outside the dwelling, so the machine can be shut down by occupants or first responders without entering the building or standing at the machine itself. Read it together with the rest of 445.18, which governs shutdown of the prime mover generally. On a dwelling generator job, locate the outdoor shutdown where a responder would look for it — at the normal entry

t: Transformers and transformer vaults — article intro
x: Article 450 covers transformers: overcurrent protection of the transformer and its conductors, location, guarding, ventilation, and the vault construction rules for indoor installations. Sharma's day-to-day contact is the small dry-type transformer in light commercial work — a 480-to-208/120 step-down or a control transformer — where the protection table and the primary/secondary conductor rules are the working content. Vault and liquid-filled rules are later-pass material for this book. For a dry-type install: confirm primary and secondary protection against the 450.3 table for the actual voltages, confirm the secondary conductors are protected as Chapter 2 requires, and keep ventilation cl

t: Overcurrent protection for transformers
x: Section 450.3 sets transformer overcurrent protection through its tables, one for transformers over 1000V and one for 1000V and below, with the required protection depending on voltage, whether protection is primary-only or primary-and-secondary, and the transformer's impedance where the table calls for it. Primary-only protection is permitted only within the table's limits; beyond them, both sides must be protected. The percentages are table lookups for the specific case — do not carry one remembered percentage to a different voltage or impedance. Work the table for the case in front of you and write the case (voltage class, impedance, primary-only or both) on the worksheet. If the impedanc

t: Transformer ventilation — and no storage on top
x: Section 450.9 requires transformers to be installed so air can circulate and carry heat away, and the 2020 edition expanded its marking provisions so the horizontal top surfaces of covered dry-type transformers are marked against being used for storage. A transformer is a heater by design losses; blocking its vents or stacking boxes on it raises its temperature and shortens its life. Ventilation is an installation requirement, not a housekeeping preference. Keep the manufacturer's clearances on all vented faces and treat the top of a dry-type transformer as equipment space, never a shelf. On a commercial service call, photograph and report storage stacked on a transformer rather than just mo

t: A transformer needs a disconnecting means
x: Section 450.14 requires a disconnecting means for transformers, located either in a readily accessible location within sight of the transformer or in a remote location, with the article's exceptions (which include certain small transformers such as Class 2 and similar limited cases). Where the disconnect is remote, it must be lockable in the open position and the transformer must be marked with the disconnect's location, so a person servicing the transformer can find and secure its source. The 2020 clarifications to this section are about exactly that remote case. On a dry-type install, decide the disconnect location with the transformer location, not after. If the disconnect ends up remote,

t: Phase converters — article intro
x: Article 455 covers phase converters, the equipment that lets three-phase motors run from a single-phase supply. It addresses marking, conductor sizing for the single-phase input, and disconnect requirements, with sizing tied to the largest motor or load the converter serves. Sharma meets converters rarely, on small commercial and agricultural-type jobs at the edge of its territory; this first pass gives the article its place and scope. A converter is sized to its load, not to the building service. Get the motor data for everything the converter will ever run at once, and give that list to the office before quoting the install.

t: Capacitors — article intro
x: Article 460 covers capacitors installed on electrical systems, most often for power-factor correction on commercial services and large motor loads. Its working rules concern conductor ampacity (capacitor circuits are sized above the capacitor's rated current), overcurrent protection, disconnecting means, and the stored-energy discharge that makes a capacitor keep a charge after it is switched off. That stored charge is the safety point of the article: a disconnected capacitor is not automatically a dead capacitor. Treat capacitor terminals as live until discharged and verified with a meter. Allow the discharge device its time, then test — never assume. Include the capacitor's kvar and voltag

t: Resistors and reactors — article intro
x: Article 470 covers resistors and reactors used on electrical systems, such as starting resistors for motors and current-limiting reactors. Its themes are clearance from combustible material (these devices make heat by design), enclosure and guarding, and conductor sizing for the duty. Sharma encounters this equipment mainly inside larger commercial gear rather than as field-installed material, so this first pass is a scope page. Heat is the installation: keep the clearances and ventilation the listing requires, and do not enclose a resistor bank in a way its manufacturer did not intend. If a reactor or resistor shows heat discoloration on a service call, report it rather than just resetting

t: Storage batteries — article intro
x: Article 480 covers storage battery installations: the battery systems that back up services, feed UPS equipment, and increasingly pair with solar and generator work. Its working rules address disconnecting means, overcurrent protection, wiring to battery circuits, and the ventilation and spill concerns that depend on battery chemistry. The article works alongside the energy-storage rules in Chapter 7 (Article 706), which govern the system as a whole — 480 is about the battery installation itself. Identify the chemistry and the system listing before you wire anything: vented, sealed, and lithium systems have different room and protection needs. Put the battery disconnect where it is identifie

t: Battery disconnects — DC is its own problem
x: Section 480.7 sets the disconnecting methods for battery circuits, reorganized and expanded in the 2020 edition as battery requirements were gathered back into Article 480 from Article 706. The field point that matters most: interrupting DC is harder than interrupting AC, because DC has no natural current zero to help an arc die. A switching device must be rated for the DC voltage and current it will actually break; an AC-only device is not assumed suitable, whatever its amp rating says. Read the DC rating on any battery disconnect, fuse holder, or breaker before it goes in, and confirm polarity markings on polarized DC devices. If the rating plate does not mention DC, the device does not go

t: Battery interconnections (moved into 480 in 2020)
x: Section 480.12 carries the battery interconnection requirements that the 2020 edition moved into Article 480 from Article 706: the conductors and connections that join cells and batteries into a bank, sized for the maximum current the bank can deliver and made with terminals and methods suited to the battery system. Battery banks can deliver enormous fault current at very low impedance, so connection quality — correct lugs, correct torque, protected runs — is a safety item, not a neatness item. Manufacturer instructions for the specific battery system govern the details the article leaves to the listing. Torque interconnection hardware to the battery manufacturer's specification and record i

t: Equipment over 1000 volts, nominal — article intro
x: Article 490 covers equipment operating over 1000 volts nominal: medium-voltage switchgear, conductors' termination practices, and clearances for the gear Sharma's crews do not normally install but may work around on commercial and utility-adjacent sites. It closes Chapter 4 in official order. Nothing in Sharma's residential work is installed under this article, and no Sharma field employee works on over-1000V equipment under this book — such work is referred to qualified medium-voltage contractors. Your job with 490 equipment is recognition and respect: identify it, keep clear of it, and never open, rack, or test it. If a job appears to require work on the medium-voltage side, stop and take

t: Hazardous (classified) locations — the starting point
x: Some areas hold enough flammable gas or vapor, combustible dust, or ignitible fibers in the air that a normal spark or hot surface could start a fire or explosion. Article 500 is the foundation for those areas: it explains how a location gets classified, how materials are grouped, which protection methods exist, and what equipment markings mean. Articles 501 through 516 then give the working rules for each kind of location. Before any work in a suspect area, find the classification drawing or ask the engineer and the AHJ what the classification is. If nobody can tell you the class, division or zone, and group, stop — that answer decides every wiring method and every fitting that follows.  Sh

t: How locations are classified — class and division
x: Classification starts with what the hazardous material is and how likely it is to be present in an ignitible amount. Class I covers gases and vapors from flammable or combustible liquids, Class II covers combustible dusts, and Class III covers easily ignitible fibers and flyings. Division 1 means the hazard can be present during normal operation, while Division 2 means it is normally contained and shows up only when something fails or operates abnormally. Read the class and division off the classification documents for the exact room or area, not the whole building — one bay can be classified while the next is not. Treat a Division 1 boundary line on the drawing as a hard wall for wiring met

t: Material groups
x: Within each class, materials are sorted into groups by how easily they ignite and how much pressure an explosion can build. Class I groups run A through D and Class II groups run E through G, with the earlier letters generally the more severe materials. Equipment has to be identified for the specific group in the location, not just for the class. Check the group letter on the plans against the group letters on every luminaire, motor, and enclosure nameplate before installation. A fitting approved for Group D does not automatically cover Groups A, B, or C.

t: Protection techniques
x: This section lists the accepted ways to keep electrical equipment from igniting the surrounding atmosphere. The familiar ones are explosionproof enclosures that contain an internal explosion, dust-ignitionproof enclosures that keep dust out, purging and pressurizing that hold clean air inside, intrinsic safety that limits circuit energy below ignition level, oil immersion, and nonincendive designs for the less severe division. Each technique only counts where the section and the equipment marking allow it. Match the technique on the equipment to the technique the design calls for — do not substitute a dust-ignitionproof box for an explosionproof one because it looks similar. Keep enclosure b

t: Equipment suitability, marking, and temperature
x: Equipment for a classified location has to suit the exact class, division, and group where it sits, and gear approved for Division 1 may also serve in Division 2 of the same class and group. Nameplates carry the class, division or zone, group, and a temperature marking that shows the hottest surface the equipment can reach. That temperature marking has to stay below the ignition temperature of the gas, vapor, or dust involved. Read the full nameplate, including the temperature code, before setting equipment — a correct class and group with the wrong temperature code is still a failed install. Photograph nameplates on classified work for the job record.

t: Class I locations — gases and vapors
x: Article 501 gives the wiring, sealing, and equipment rules for Class I locations, where the hazard is flammable gas or liquid vapor. It is the article behind fuel-handling rooms, some process areas, and the classified pockets inside garages and hangars covered later in this chapter. Seals that stop gases traveling through conduit, and threaded metal raceways, are everyday themes here. If a Sharma job enters a Class I area, work only from the classified drawing and the method Mike Holt has reviewed. Do not carry house or light-commercial habits — NM cable, ordinary boxes, unsealed conduit — across the boundary.

t: Class II locations — combustible dusts
x: Article 502 covers Class II locations, where combustible dust is the hazard — think grain, feed, and some manufacturing dusts. The goals are keeping dust out of enclosures, keeping surfaces cool enough not to ignite a dust layer, and wiring methods that do not let dust accumulate on live parts. Dust thickness on equipment is part of the hazard picture, not just dust in the air. Ask what dust is present and its group before choosing equipment, and plan on dust-tight style enclosures where the article calls for them. Clean dust off equipment before opening enclosures in these areas.

t: Class III locations — fibers and flyings
x: Article 503 covers Class III locations, where easily ignitible fibers or flyings are handled or stored but are not normally suspended in the air in ignitible amounts — textile and woodworking style hazards are the classic examples. Rules focus on keeping fibers away from hot or arcing parts and on enclosures that limit entry. It is the least severe of the three classes, but it is still a classified location with its own wiring rules. Treat lint and fiber buildup around motors and luminaires as a code problem, not housekeeping. Use only the wiring methods and equipment the article permits inside the classified boundary.

t: Intrinsically safe systems
x: Article 504 covers intrinsically safe systems, where the circuit itself is limited to energy levels that cannot ignite the atmosphere, even under fault conditions. These systems live mostly in instrumentation and control wiring for classified areas. Separation from ordinary power wiring, identified cables, and the control drawing are the heart of the article. Never mix intrinsically safe conductors with regular power conductors in the same raceway or box unless the control drawing and the article allow it. Keep the light-blue identified wiring and separation distances the design shows.

t: Zone 0, 1, and 2 locations — the zone system for gases and vapors
x: Article 505 is the alternative zone classification system for gas and vapor hazards, used more in industrial and international-style designs. Zone 0 is where an ignitible atmosphere is present continuously or for long periods, Zone 1 where it is likely in normal operation, and Zone 2 where it is unlikely and short-lived. Equipment carries zone-specific markings and protection types that do not read the same as class and division markings. Do not assume a Division-rated fitting and a Zone-rated fitting are interchangeable — read the marking for the system the design uses. When the plans classify by zone, this article, not 501, is the rulebook.

t: Zone 20, 21, and 22 locations — zones for dusts and fibers
x: Article 506 extends the zone system to combustible dusts and ignitible fibers or flyings. Zone 20 is the most severe, with ignitible dust present continuously or often, Zone 21 is likely in normal operation, and Zone 22 is unlikely or short-lived. It pairs with Article 505 the way Article 502 and 503 pair with 501. As with 505, follow the zone marking on the equipment and the classification drawing. If a dust area is classified by zone instead of division, work from this article with Mike Holt reviewing the method.

t: Hazardous locations — specific occupancies gateway
x: Article 510 is the short gateway article that points from the general classified-location rules to the specific occupancies that follow it in this chapter. Commercial garages, aircraft hangars, fuel dispensing, bulk storage, and spray operations each get their own article because each one pre-decides common classifications for that occupancy. When one of those articles applies, it works together with Articles 500 through 503. When a job is one of the named occupancies, start with its own article to see what classification has already been decided for you. Then use 500 through 503 for the wiring and equipment rules inside the classified parts.

t: Commercial garages — repair and storage
x: Article 511 covers places that service or repair self-propelled vehicles that run on flammable liquids or gases — auto repair shops, dealership service bays, and similar light-commercial work Sharma actually bids. Gasoline vapor is heavier than air, so the classification story is mostly about the floor, pits, and the space just above them. Parking-only garages are treated differently from repair garages, and if fuel is dispensed on site, Article 514 joins in. First question on any garage bid: is it repair or parking only, major or minor repair, and is there a pit or fuel dispensing? Those answers set the classification before anyone prices conduit and fittings.  S-01: commercial branch circu

t: Classification of garage areas
x: This section sorts garage spaces using tables that turn on three questions: major or minor repair, whether the area is the floor, a pit, or the ceiling, and whether the required ventilation is provided. In major repair garages the floor area up to 18 inches is commonly a Class I, Division 2 location, pits are Division 1 or Division 2 depending on ventilation, and ceiling areas can be classified for lighter-than-air gases when ventilation is absent. Parking and storage garages with no repair work are not required to be classified. Work the three questions in order for each space and write the result on the takeoff — do not classify the whole building by its worst room. Keep ordinary receptacl

t: Wiring and equipment inside the classified areas
x: Inside the parts of a garage that 511.3 classifies, wiring and equipment follow the Class I rules of Article 501. Portable lighting used in those areas has to be identified for the location or arranged so it cannot be used inside the classified space. The practical message is that the classified pocket is wired like any other Class I, Division location, even though the rest of the shop is ordinary. Price and rough classified pockets with Article 501 methods — threaded metal raceway, seals, and listed fittings — not with shop-standard materials. Keep portable trouble lights for classified areas in the identified type only.

t: Wiring and equipment above the classified areas
x: Above the classified floor band, the article relaxes to a defined list of fixed wiring methods such as metal raceways, Type AC or MC cable, manufactured wiring systems, and certain listed cables. Equipment that can arc or spark and sits within 12 feet of the floor above a classified area has to be enclosed or guarded so hot particles cannot fall into the classified zone. Fixed luminaires over classified areas, traffic lanes, or where vehicles could strike them carry their own height and protection conditions, with 12 feet the key dimension in the common cases. Measure heights from the floor, not from the slab finish you wish you had, and confirm the 12-foot line before hanging luminaires ove

t: Underground wiring in garages
x: Underground wiring in a commercial garage borrows the underground rules written for motor fuel dispensing in Article 514. Buried runs under a repair floor sit below a space where fuel can spill and vapors can travel, so the raceway type, sealing, and emergence points are treated like fuel-dispensing underground work. Ordinary direct-burial habits from site work do not carry over. When a garage job has under-slab runs, detail them on the takeoff as 514-style underground work and confirm the method with Mike Holt. Do not let the slab pour happen before the underground method is settled.

t: Special equipment in garages
x: This section collects requirements for particular garage equipment, including battery charging areas and equipment for charging electric vehicle batteries in the repair environment. Charging can produce its own ventilation and classification concerns on top of the garage's general classification. It is a short section, but it is the one to open when a charger or charging room is in the scope. If the bid includes vehicle charging inside a repair garage, note it separately on the takeoff instead of folding it into general receptacles. Ask for the charger nameplate and the ventilation design before pricing.

t: GFCI protection in commercial garages
x: Ground-fault circuit-interrupter protection for personnel is required in commercial garages as set by the non-dwelling rules of 210.8(B). In the 2020 edition this was broadened beyond the older diagnostic-equipment and hand-tool wording, so treat essentially all receptacles in the garage as needing GFCI protection unless a specific exception applies. The rule applies whether or not the particular spot is inside a classified area. Default every garage receptacle circuit to GFCI protection at the takeoff stage and test each device at trim. Losing this line item is the cheapest inspection failure in the article to prevent.  S-07 is Sharma's residential pattern — a dual-function breaker feeding

t: Aircraft hangars
x: Article 513 classifies and wires aircraft hangars, where fuel vapors gather near the floor and in pits much as they do in garages, but around aircraft instead of cars. The floor band and pit classifications, and the wiring rules that follow them, are the core of the article. Sharma sees this rarely, but a hangar bid is never priced with ordinary commercial methods. Recognize the occupancy on the bid walk and route the takeoff to Mike Holt. The classification tables in this article decide the methods before any labor number makes sense.

t: Motor fuel dispensing facilities
x: Article 514 covers gas stations and any place motor fuel is dispensed into vehicles, including dispensing inside a repair garage. It classifies the area around dispensers and tanks, requires seals and specific underground wiring, and requires emergency disconnect controls that kill power to the dispensing equipment. Underground rules from this article are also borrowed by garages in 511.8 and by marinas for fueling docks. Fuel dispensing is specialty work: emergency shutoff location, dispenser seals, and underground method all come from the plans and this article. Flag any dispensing scope on a bid the day it is seen, not at rough-in.

t: Emergency disconnect at fuel dispensing
x: Fuel dispensing areas need clearly identified emergency electrical disconnects — the control a station attendant or firefighter reaches for when fuel is flowing where it should not. Operated, the disconnect must simultaneously open all conductors of the circuits involved, including the grounded (neutral) conductor, cutting power to the dispensing devices, to the remote pumps serving them, to the associated power, control, and signal circuits, and to the other electrical equipment in the classified area around the dispensers. Resetting after an emergency shutoff takes manual intervention, in the manner the AHJ approves. 514.11(A) also fixes where the disconnect sits: an approved location not

t: Bulk storage plants
x: Article 515 covers bulk storage plants, where flammable liquids are stored in large tanks and transferred to trucks or containers. Classifications follow the tanks, pumps, and loading areas, and the wiring rules build on Articles 500 through 501. It is industrial work Sharma would only touch with an engineered classification package. If a bulk plant appears in an invitation, the first deliverable is the classification drawing, not a price. No drawing, no takeoff.

t: Spray application, dipping, coating, and printing processes
x: Article 516 covers spray booths and rooms, dip tanks, and similar processes using flammable or combustible materials. The spray area and its surroundings carry classifications that depend on the booth construction and ventilation, and lighting through panels, interlocks, and equipment placement all have specific rules. Body shops and finishing operations are the light-commercial face of this article. A paint booth on a commercial bid pulls this article in even when the rest of the building is ordinary. Ask for the booth listing and ventilation details before pricing the booth circuits.

t: Health care facilities — the light-commercial slice
x: Article 517 covers electrical work in facilities that examine or treat patients — hospitals at the deep end, and clinics, medical and dental offices at the end Sharma is likely to bid. Its themes are redundant grounding in patient care spaces, hospital-grade receptacles at bed locations, and, for hospitals, an essential electrical system that keeps life safety and critical loads alive on a second source. This first pass covers only the small-clinic slice; hospital design belongs to engineers and later passes of this book. On a clinic or dental bid, the first question is which rooms are patient care spaces — that answer, from the plans or the facility, turns this article on. Price those rooms

t: Where Part II of Article 517 applies — and where it does not
x: Part II of Article 517, the wiring and grounding part, applies to patient care spaces in health care facilities. It does not apply to business offices, corridors, waiting rooms, and similar non-treatment areas, to sleeping rooms in nursing and limited care facilities in the way it applies to treatment spaces, or to areas used exclusively for things like immunizations, psychiatry or psychotherapy, alternative medicine, and optometry. The facility's governing body sorts spaces into patient care categories, and the category drives how strict the rules are. Get the room-by-room patient care determination in writing on the bid documents — guessing which rooms count is how a clinic job gets underp

t: Redundant grounding in patient care spaces
x: Branch circuits serving patient care spaces need two independent ground-fault return paths working together. The wiring method itself — a metal raceway, or a cable with a metal armor or sheath that qualifies as a grounding path — provides one path, and an insulated copper equipment grounding conductor run with the circuit provides the second. Receptacle grounding terminals and exposed metal of fixed equipment in those spaces connect to that insulated copper conductor, sized from Table 250.122. On a patient care rough-in, there is no NM cable and no relying on the raceway alone — pull the insulated copper grounding conductor on every branch circuit. Check that the cable or raceway chosen actu

t: Isolated ground receptacles in health care
x: Isolated ground receptacles are tightly limited in health care work because a receptacle whose ground is isolated from the local grounding system can defeat the redundant grounding that 517.13 builds. No isolated ground receptacle is permitted inside a patient care vicinity. Outside that vicinity, an isolated ground receptacle may be used only with its own insulated grounding conductor run as this section directs, in addition to the normal grounding path. If a clinic plan shows an isolated ground receptacle, check where it sits relative to the patient care vicinity before rough-in. Inside the vicinity is a stop-and-ask, not a field fix.

t: General care (Category 2) patient bed locations
x: Each patient bed location in a general care, Category 2 space needs at least two branch circuits, with at least one from the normal system and one from the emergency system where an essential system exists, and the normal circuits coming from a single panelboard. The 2020 edition sets a minimum of eight receptacles at each such bed location. Receptacles at bed locations are hospital grade, identified by the green dot marking. (The green TRIANGLE is a different mark — it denotes an isolated-ground receptacle, not hospital grade, and 517.16 restricts isolated-ground receptacles within the patient care vicinity.)13. Count receptacles and circuits per bed on the clinic takeoff, not per room — a

t: Essential electrical systems — hospitals, at a high level
x: Hospitals and similar facilities with critical care spaces need an essential electrical system: a second source of power, usually a generator, feeding separated branches — the life safety branch, the critical branch, and the equipment branch. Wiring for the essential system is kept independent of normal wiring, mechanically protected, and transferred automatically on loss of normal power. Nursing homes and limited care facilities have a scaled version in the sections that follow. This page is orientation only — Sharma does not design these systems on a first pass. If a bid shows an essential electrical system, the generator, transfer equipment, and branch separation are engineered scope — pr

t: Assembly occupancies
x: Article 518 covers buildings or parts of buildings designed or intended for the gathering of 100 or more people — auditoriums, churches, restaurants, gyms, exhibition halls, and the like. The core demand is tougher, more fire-resilient wiring in the assembly area, plus attention to the emergency systems that serve a crowd. Theaters and similar performance spaces are carved out to Article 520 instead. Ask for the occupant load of each space on a commercial bid — crossing 100 people is what turns this article on. A 60-seat café and a 300-seat hall are different wiring jobs even if the menus match.  S-01: 20 ampere minimum branch circuits on commercial work, which fits the metal raceway and MC

t: Wiring methods in assembly occupancies
x: Fixed wiring in the assembly area has to be in metal raceways or flexible metal raceways, in nonmetallic raceways encased in at least 2 inches of concrete, or be Type MI, MC, or AC cable. The method itself has to qualify as a grounding path, or the wiring has to contain an insulated equipment grounding conductor sized from Table 250.122. Nonmetallic-sheathed cable is not a fixed wiring method for the assembly area in the fire-rated construction cases this section is built around, though the section does allow the ordinary nonmetallic methods in areas not required to be fire-rated construction. Take off assembly areas in EMT, MC, or AC as the plans direct — do not carry NM pricing from a tena

t: Illumination of working space
x: Added in the 2020 edition, this short section requires illumination for the working spaces about electrical equipment installed outdoors that serves assembly occupancies. The lighting cannot be controlled by automatic means only, so a person servicing the gear is not left in the dark by a timer or sensor. Where nearby lighting already illuminates the working space adequately, no extra luminaire is required. Add a switched luminaire at outdoor service and distribution gear on assembly jobs, and check it at trim rather than discovering it at final inspection. Put the control on a manual switch, not a photocell or timer alone.  Cross-link: working space itself is 110.26 in Chapter 1; this secti

t: Theaters, audience areas, and performance spaces
x: Article 520 takes theaters, audience areas of movie and television studios, and performance areas out of Article 518 and gives them their own rules, built around stage and house lighting, switchboards, and portable stage equipment. Wiring methods echo the assembly rules, with added provisions for the portable and temporary-looking equipment that is actually permanent in a theater. Sharma would meet this on a school auditorium or church stage package, not on ordinary tenant work. Treat any stage, dimming, or performance lighting scope as engineered work and price only detailed plans. Portable stage cable and connectors follow this article, not jobsite temporary rules.

t: Control systems for permanent amusement attractions
x: Article 522 covers the control systems of permanent amusement attractions — the rides and attractions built to stay, as opposed to the traveling shows in Article 525. It deals with control circuits, disconnects, and the interface between the electrical system and the attraction's safety controls. It is a narrow article most electricians meet only on attraction work. If an attraction appears in a scope, stop at the intro level and get the manufacturer's and engineer's control package. Do not improvise ride controls from general-purpose relays.

t: Carnivals, circuses, fairs, and similar events
x: Article 525 covers temporary event power for carnivals, circuses, fairs, and similar events — rides, games, food stands, and show wiring that is installed and removed for each event. Grounding, GFCI protection, disconnects within reach of operators, and separation of ride wiring are its recurring themes. It works alongside Article 590 but adds event-specific rules that 590 does not contain. Event power is not ordinary temp power — check this article as well as 590 before quoting a fair or festival job. Operator disconnects and ride grounding are priced items, not afterthoughts.

t: Motion picture and television studios
x: Article 530 covers studios and similar locations where motion picture or television production happens, including the stage power, portable distribution, and single-conductor feeder practices that are unique to studio work. It exists because studio lighting loads and portable equipment do not behave like ordinary commercial installations. Florida production work is the only likely Sharma encounter. Studio scope is specialty scope — work from the production electrical package. Nothing in this intro authorizes studio feeder practices on ordinary jobs.

t: Motion picture projection rooms
x: Article 540 is a short article covering motion picture projection rooms and the film-handling hazards they were written for. Modern digital projection has shrunk its footprint, but the article remains in the 2020 book and in theater work where a projection room still exists. Ventilation and equipment placement in the room are its main subjects. On a theater renovation, confirm whether a projection room is in scope before assuming 518 or 520 covers the whole job. If it is, this article's room rules join the takeoff.

t: Manufactured buildings and relocatable structures
x: Article 545 covers buildings built in a factory in sections or panels and assembled on site, plus relocatable structures such as portable classrooms and jobsite offices. The electrical questions are how the factory-built sections connect together, how the completed building connects to its service, and which parts are inspected at the factory versus on site. Florida's portable classroom and modular office market makes this a live article for Sharma even though this first pass stays at intro level. On a modular or portable classroom job, get the manufacturer's connection details and the state modular insignia paperwork before pricing the site connection. This page is verified at article level

t: Agricultural buildings
x: Article 547 covers agricultural buildings and areas where excessive dust, dust with water, or a corrosive atmosphere is present — livestock confinement, dairies, poultry houses, and similar Florida rural work. Animals are far more sensitive to small voltages than people, so the article adds equipotential planes, a special site distribution arrangement, and wiring methods that survive corrosion. It modifies the normal chapters; it does not replace them. On any barn or confinement bid, ask early whether livestock will be confined on concrete — that answer pulls in equipotential planes and the distribution point. Price corrosion-resistant methods from the start instead of discovering them at in

t: Wiring methods in agricultural buildings
x: Wiring in an Article 547 building has to survive dust, moisture, and corrosion, so the section steers work toward listed damp and wet location methods, dust-tight and watertight enclosures where conditions demand them, and an insulated equipment grounding conductor when the grounding conductor runs underground outside a listed cable assembly. Part (G) sets GFCI protection: 125-volt, single-phase, 15- and 20-ampere receptacles in areas with an equipotential plane, outdoors, in damp or wet locations, and in dirt confinement areas need GFCI protection as in the non-dwelling rules. Receptacles above that voltage and size are outside that GFCI list in the 2020 clarification. Choose boxes, devices

t: Supply from a distribution point — livestock buildings
x: Livestock agricultural buildings on the same premises are supplied from a distribution point using a four-wire grounded distribution arrangement — and 547.9 expressly permits more than one distribution point on the same premises. The point of the layout is to keep neutral current from returning through the earth and through building grounding systems, which is a classic source of the stray voltage that bothers livestock. Overcurrent protection is required for the underground branch circuits and feeders leaving the distribution point. On a multi-building farm service, draw the distribution point on the site sketch and price the four-wire runs and underground protection as shown. Do not serve

t: Equipotential planes in livestock confinement areas
x: Where livestock are confined on concrete and metal equipment they can touch may become energized, an equipotential plane is installed in the floor so the animal's feet and the equipment it touches stay at the same voltage. The plane is bonded to the building's electrical grounding system with a solid copper bonding conductor of at least 8 AWG, connected with listed pressure connectors or clamps. It is required indoors and outdoors in the confinement areas the section describes. Coordinate the plane with the concrete crew before the pour — retrofitting a bonded plane after slab placement is not a real option. Keep the 8 AWG solid copper bond and its connections inspectable until they are appr

t: Mobile homes, manufactured homes, and mobile home parks
x: Article 550 covers mobile and manufactured homes and the parks that serve them, including how the home connects to its supply, the feeder between the park service and the home, and the disconnecting means at the home. Factory-built homes arrive with their interior wiring already inspected under the federal HUD program, so the site electrician's world is the service, the feeder, and the connection. The section pages that follow carry those site rules: the power supply (550.10), the disconnecting means at the home (550.11), the service equipment (550.32), and the feeder (550.33). On a mobile home job, Sharma's scope is normally the park or lot service equipment, the feeder, and the connection

t: Power supply — the home is fed by a feeder
x: A mobile or manufactured home is supplied by a feeder, not by service conductors landed in the home. 550.10(A) allows two forms: a single listed 50-ampere mobile home power-supply cord, or a permanently installed feeder of fixed wiring. Because the supply is a feeder, the panelboard inside the home is a feeder panel — never service equipment — with the neutral isolated and a separate equipment grounding conductor run back to the service equipment, on a cord connection and on a permanent feeder alike. The exception is the manufactured home on a permanent foundation that meets 550.32(B): it may be supplied directly by a service, with the service equipment in or on the home. Before rough-in, co

t: Disconnecting means at the home
x: Each mobile or manufactured home has a single disconnecting means — a circuit breaker, or a switch and fuses — at or near the point where the supply cord or the feeder conductors enter the home, in a readily accessible location. The disconnect may be combined with the branch-circuit protective equipment, so the main breaker in the home's panelboard can be the disconnect. It pairs with 550.32: one disconnect at the home itself, and the service equipment disconnect outside, within sight and within 30 ft of the exterior wall. Find and label the home's single disconnect on every set. If a home shows two mains, or the disconnect is hidden behind stored material, flag it — the occupant and the fir

t: Service equipment — in sight and within 30 ft of the home
x: Mobile home service equipment is located adjacent to the home, never mounted in or on it, in sight from the home and not more than 30 ft from its exterior wall. If the service equipment must sit elsewhere on the premises, a disconnecting means suitable for use as service equipment still has to be within sight and within 30 ft of the wall, with grounding at that disconnect per 250.32. The equipment is rated not less than 100 amperes at 120/240 volts and must allow the feeder to be connected by a permanent wiring method. Mounting height is fixed too: the bottom of the enclosure at least 2 ft above the ground, and the disconnect not more than 6 ft 7 in. above the ground or platform. A manufactu

t: The feeder — four insulated conductors, 100-ampere capacity
x: The feeder from the service equipment to the home is four continuous, insulated, color-coded conductors: two ungrounded conductors, a grounded (neutral) conductor, and an insulated equipment grounding conductor. A bare grounding conductor inside a cable assembly does not count — the ground must be insulated like the rest. Under 550.33(B) the feeder conductors must have a capacity and ampacity of not less than 100 amperes, even when the home's calculated load comes out smaller. Where the conductors are spliced, the splice goes in a suitable junction box — never inside the raceway. Pull four insulated conductors every time; standard SER with a bare ground does not make a mobile home feeder. Si

t: Recreational vehicles and recreational vehicle parks
x: Article 551 covers recreational vehicles themselves and, more importantly for site work, RV parks — the site supply equipment, receptacle configurations, and grounding for each RV lot. Park work is a feeder and pedestal job repeated many times, with GFCI and polarity details at every site. It pairs with Article 552, which covers park trailers separately. On an RV park bid, count sites and pedestal types carefully and confirm the supply equipment listing. Do not price park pedestals as ordinary receptacle posts.

t: Park trailers
x: Article 552 covers park trailers — the trailer-type units built for park placement rather than highway travel, defined around a size threshold that separates them from recreational vehicles. Its rules parallel the mobile home and RV articles for supply and connection. Confusing a park trailer with an RV or a mobile home sends the job to the wrong article, so identification comes first. Read the unit's label and paperwork before choosing between 550, 551, and 552. When the unit type is unclear, ask the AHJ rather than guessing the article.

t: Article 553 — deleted in 2020 (floating buildings now live in Article 555, Part III)
x: Article 553 no longer exists as its own article. In the 2020 NEC it was deleted and its subject — floating buildings, structures supported by water rather than by a foundation, other than boats — was folded into Article 555 as its Part III (555.50 and following). The substance carried over: the shore-to-building supply, service equipment and disconnecting means located on land rather than on the floating structure, and ground-fault protection for the supply. Work a floating building from Article 555, Part III — not from an old 553 printout. Service equipment and the disconnect for a floating building go on adjacent land, not on the floating structure. Coordinate early with the marina scope i

t: Marinas, boatyards, floating buildings, and docking facilities
x: Article 555 covers wiring and equipment at fixed and floating piers, marinas, boatyards, boathouses, and residential and commercial docking facilities, plus floating buildings in their own part of the article. The driving hazard is electric shock drowning: stray current in the water around an energized boat or dock can paralyze a swimmer without any visible warning. That is why this article layers ground-fault protection, bonding, and strict height rules over ordinary outdoor wiring. 555.1 expressly includes docking facilities associated with one-family dwellings, so a private residential dock is inside this article — not an AHJ judgment call.  Treat every marina circuit as life-safety work:

t: Electrical datum plane — heights above the water
x: The electrical datum plane is the reference height above the water below which certain equipment, connections, and receptacles may not be installed.
