For floating piers and floating facilities it is 30 inches above the water level and at least 12 inches above the deck level. Fixed facilities use their own datum definitions tied to high water and deck level in this section, so read the exact case that matches the structure before setting equipment. Establish the datum line on site with the marina operator and mark it on the pier before rough-in — then set nothing the article restricts below it. Re-check after any deck or float work that changes deck height.

t: Location of service equipment — on land, not on the structure
x: The service equipment for a floating building, dock, or marina is installed on land, adjacent to the structure it serves — never on or in the floating structure itself. A floating structure rides up and down with the water, so the service stays on solid ground, where it can be reached and worked on like any other service. Everything downstream of it — the feeders out along the pier — is supplied from that shore-side point. Set the service on land next to the dock or marina it serves and run the feeder out to the pier from there. If a plan or an existing installation shows the service mounted on a floating dock, flag it before rough-in — that location fails this section.

t: Pier power distribution — the 250-volt limit
x: Pier power distribution systems are limited to 250 volts phase to phase. The single exception is an engineered installation: where qualified personnel service the equipment under engineering supervision, the system may run above 250 volts, but never above 600 volts phase to phase. Ordinary marina and dock work is designed well under the cap, at the standard voltages — the higher band is not a field upgrade. Read the distribution voltage on the plans before ordering gear. If a pier design shows more than 250 volts phase to phase, stop and confirm the qualified-personnel and engineering-supervision conditions are actually part of the job — that call belongs to the engineer, not the crew.

t: Boat hoists — GFCI protection at dwelling docks
x: A boat hoist rated not more than 240 volts at a dwelling unit docking facility must have GFCI protection. The 2020 edition moved this rule out of 210.8(C) and into Article 555, with the rest of the dock rules. It is the lift on a house dock that raises the boat out of the water — a motor, a control, and people standing on a wet dock, which is exactly the combination the GFCI is there for. On a residential dock job, put the boat hoist on GFCI protection and test it at trim. If an existing hoist outlet has no GFCI protection, call it out to the owner — a hoist motor fault over water is the shock path this rule exists to break.

t: Warning signs — the shock hazard notice
x: A permanent safety sign is required at docking facilities, boatyards, and marinas, warning of the electrical shock hazard in the water. The sign must warn with effective words, colors, or symbols meeting 110.21(B)(1), be durable enough to withstand the environment, and be clearly visible from all approaches to the facility. At a minimum it must state: WARNING — POTENTIAL SHOCK HAZARD — ELECTRICAL CURRENTS MAY BE PRESENT IN THE WATER. This is the electric shock drowning warning, and the sign is part of the installation, not an extra. Put the sign in the job scope and photograph it at final — the job can fail inspection for a missing sign even when every circuit is right. Mount it where someon

t: Bonding at marinas and docking facilities
x: Metal parts that touch the water, metal piping, and non-current-carrying metal parts that could become energized have to be bonded back to the grounding bus in the panelboard. The bonding conductor is solid copper, insulated, covered, or bare, and at least 8 AWG. This equipotential bonding is what keeps dock metal, boat metal, and the water around them from sitting at different voltages. Bond ladders, lifts, metal framing, and piping as one system, and keep the 8 AWG solid copper bond continuous and protected from dock damage. Test continuity at trim — a bonding jumper cut by later dock work is a silent failure.

t: Disconnecting means for shore power connections (2020 section 555.36)
x: Each boat's shore power connection needs its own disconnecting means that isolates that boat from its supply. The disconnect is a circuit breaker, a switch, or both, identified to show which receptacle it controls, readily accessible, ahead of the receptacle in the circuit, and located not more than 30 inches from the receptacle it controls. Breakers or switches inside a marine power outlet can serve as this disconnect when they meet those conditions. Label every pedestal disconnect with the slip and receptacle it controls, and measure the 30-inch limit before the pedestal is set. A boater in the dark needs to kill one connection, not the whole dock.  This is the 2020 section number, 555.36.

t: Receptacles at marinas and docking facilities (2020 section 555.33)
x: Receptacles at docking facilities are mounted at least 12 inches above the deck surface and not below the electrical datum plane. Shore power receptacles have their own rules inside this section: they are part of a listed marine power outlet, installed in a listed enclosure protected from the weather, rated not less than 30 amperes, and of the pin-and-sleeve type when rated 60 amperes or more. Receptacles other than shore power get GFCI protection under 210.8, and a replacement receptacle has to meet this section too. Height, listing, and location work together — a correct receptacle set too low still fails. Set receptacle heights from the finished deck, and re-check them if decking is repla

t: Ground-fault protection — GFPE and GFCI at marinas
x: The 2020 edition reorganized this section into three clear layers. Shore power receptacles get individual ground-fault protection of equipment set to open at not more than 30 milliamperes, 15- and 20-ampere receptacles other than shore power get Class A GFCI protection for people, and feeder and branch circuit conductors supplying a dock or slip get ground-fault protection of equipment set at not more than 100 milliamperes. GFPE protects equipment and wiring at milliampere levels far above the 4 to 6 milliampere Class A GFCI trip that protects people, so the two are not interchangeable labels. Build the protection in layers exactly as the design shows — pedestal, then feeder — and record the

t: Temporary installations — jobsite power
x: Article 590 covers power and lighting installed for a limited time: construction, remodeling, maintenance, repair, and demolition work, plus decorative and holiday installations and similar short-term uses. It relaxes a few wiring methods for the temporary case but keeps the safety core — overcurrent protection, grounding, and GFCI protection for people — fully in force. Chapters 1 through 4 still apply except where this article specifically changes them. Every Sharma rough-in crew lives in this article on someone else's jobsite and on our own temp poles. Set temp power up like it will be inspected, because it can be.  S-01 does not set temp panel sizes, but Sharma temp work still uses liste

t: Time constraints on temporary installations
x: Temporary installations are permitted only for the period the work actually lasts. Construction, remodeling, maintenance, repair, and demolition power stays for that work and comes out when the work is done, holiday and decorative installations are limited to 90 days, and testing, experiments, emergencies, and similar short uses have their own limits in this section. Temporary wiring that quietly becomes permanent is a violation, not a value add. Put a removal date on the temp service paperwork when it is set. When the permanent service is energized and accepted, schedule the temp removal instead of leaving it for the next trade to trip over.

t: General requirements for temporary wiring
x: This is the working section of the article. A temporary service is installed to the service rules of Article 230, feeders and branch circuits keep the overcurrent protection of Article 240, and hard or extra-hard usage cords and cables do much of the distribution work. Receptacles on a branch circuit may not share it with temporary lighting on a construction site, receptacles in wet locations need weatherproof protection with a plug inserted, every temporary circuit needs a way to disconnect all its ungrounded conductors, lamps need guards, splices need enclosures, and cords crossing doorways and pinch points need protection. Cables and cords used as feeders or branch circuits may not lie on

t: GFCI protection and the assured grounding program
x: Receptacles that supply temporary power for construction style work need GFCI protection for personnel: the 125-volt, 15-, 20-, and 30-ampere receptacles are covered directly by 590.6(A)(1) and (A)(2); 125/250-volt receptacles join the GFCI list only under (A)(3), and only where they are receptacle outlets on a portable generator rated not greater than 15 kW, including receptacles that are part of the building's permanent wiring when they are being used for the temporary work. For receptacles outside that list, the choice is GFCI protection or a written assured equipment grounding conductor program with documented testing of cords and equipment. All receptacles used for temporary power are o

t: Overcurrent devices in temporary installations — new in 2020
x: Added in the 2020 edition, this section speaks to the reused breakers and fuses that end up in temp panels. Reused overcurrent devices have to be inspected and maintained for the reuse, and current-limiting protection is required in the higher fault current cases the section describes, such as larger temporary services. It closes the old habit of treating the temp panel as a junk drawer for retired breakers. Retire damaged or unknown-history breakers instead of cycling them into temp panels. When a temp service is large, confirm the current-limiting requirement with Mike Holt at takeoff, not at energization.  S-03 reinforces this: breakers go only in panels they are listed for, temp panels i

t: Article 600 — Electric Signs and Outline Lighting
x: This article covers signs, outline lighting, and skeleton tubing — the lighted advertising and identification equipment on commercial buildings. Its field core is simple: a proper sign branch circuit and a real disconnect at the sign. If a bid has signage, price the circuit and the disconnect, not just the sign.

t: Sign branch circuits — 20A, signs only
x: 600.5(A) requires at least one receptacle outlet in an accessible location at EACH ENTRANCE of each commercial building or occupancy that is accessible to pedestrians, supplied by a branch circuit rated at least 20A that serves no other load. The sign circuit itself is the same family of rule: a sign or outline lighting system is supplied by a branch circuit rated at least 20A that serves no other loads, other than signs and outline lighting tied to the same work. Don't hang storefront lighting or receptacles on the sign circuit.  S-01 already sets a 20A minimum on commercial branch circuits — the code and company practice land in the same place here.

t: Sign disconnecting means
x: The conductors feeding a sign, outline lighting system, or skeleton tubing are controlled by an externally operable switch or breaker that opens all ungrounded conductors. The disconnect sits where the circuit enters the sign enclosure, body, or pole; the 2020 rules in 600.6(A) also cover within-sight, lockable, and remote-location marking situations so service people and first responders can find and kill it. Stand at the sign — can you see and reach its disconnect? If it's remote, it must be marked at the sign.

t: Retrofit kits (new in 2020)
x: Converting an existing sign to new lighting technology is a listed-kit job, not a lamp swap. A general-use or sign-specific retrofit kit must be listed and labeled and must include installation instructions for field conversion of the host sign. The kit is installed per those instructions; wiring methods follow Chapter 3 (with the Class 2 path in 600.12(C), 600.24, and 600.33); parts not replaced are inspected and damaged parts are repaired or replaced; workmanship follows 110.12; and the retrofitted sign is marked per 600.4(B) — including the alert label where tubular LED lamps run on the existing sign sockets, so nobody later installs fluorescent lamps. The 600.2 retrofit definitions (host

t: Article 604 — Manufactured Wiring Systems
x: Intro: factory-built wiring assemblies — plug-together branch-circuit and feeder components — used heavily in office fit-outs. The components must be listed and used as a system, not mixed and matched between manufacturers. Sharma hits these on tenant work; keep one manufacturer's system end to end and follow its instructions.

t: Article 605 — Office Furnishings
x: Intro: electrical rules for wired office partitions and furniture systems — how powered furniture connects to the building wiring, and the limits on cord connections and interconnecting partitions. Coordinate furniture power early on office jobs; the furniture system is listed equipment, not field-built wiring.

t: Article 610 — Cranes and Hoists
x: Intro: wiring, disconnects, and controls for cranes and hoists — runway conductors, festoon wiring, and the disconnecting means that let a crane be locked out for service. Rare in Sharma's current work; recognize it and price from the article when a warehouse job includes one.

t: Article 620 — Elevators, Dumbwaiters, Escalators, Moving Walks, Platform Lifts, and Stairway Chairlifts
x: This article covers the electrical installation for elevators and similar equipment: the machine-room disconnect, the branch circuits that serve the car and the machine space, GFCI protection in pits and hoistways, and selective coordination where several machines share a feeder. Elevator work is always coordinated with the elevator contractor and ASME A17.1 — the electrical scope is defined here, the machine scope is theirs. On a job with an elevator, Sharma's piece is typically the disconnect, the car and machine-room circuits, and pit/hoistway receptacles — confirm that split in the bid, not on site.

t: GFCI protection in elevator spaces
x: All 125V, single-phase, 15A and 20A receptacles installed in pits, in hoistways, on elevator and dumbwaiter cars, in escalator and moving-walk wellways, and in the runways and machinery spaces of platform lifts and stairway chairlifts must be of the GFCI type — the protection is at the receptacle, not just a GFCI breaker upstream. Receptacles in machine rooms, control rooms, machinery spaces, and control spaces must also have GFCI protection for personnel. A permanently installed sump pump in the pit must be permanently wired or supplied by a single GFCI-protected receptacle — the blanket sump-pump exemption as printed in the 2017 edition is gone in 2020. Use GFCI receptacles (not a breaker

t: Car lighting, receptacle, ventilation, heating and air-conditioning branch circuits
x: This section puts the car loads on their own dedicated circuits, apart from the driving-machine supply. Under 620.22(A), a separate branch circuit supplies the car lights, receptacle(s), auxiliary lighting power source, and ventilation on each car, and the required car lighting must not be connected to the load side of a GFCI — a tripped service receptacle must not black out the car. Under 620.22(B), car heating and air-conditioning units are supplied by their own separate branch circuit. The overcurrent device protecting each circuit is located in the machine room or control space for that car, and neither circuit is opened by the driving-machine disconnect (620.51), so the car stays lit an

t: Disconnecting means — one per unit, lockable open only
x: Each elevator, dumbwaiter, escalator, moving walk, platform lift, or stairway chairlift gets its own disconnecting means: an enclosed, externally operable fused motor-circuit switch or circuit breaker that disconnects the driving machine. Two details are exam-and-inspection favorites: the disconnect must be lockable in the open position only — it is not permitted to be lockable in the closed position — and it must not disconnect the car lighting, receptacle, and ventilation circuits covered by 620.22, 620.23, and 620.24, which are arranged to stay energized for service work in the car. One disconnect per unit, labeled, and never let it kill the car light circuit — a serviceman in a dark car

t: Selective coordination
x: Where more than one driving machine disconnecting means is supplied by a single feeder, the overcurrent devices in each disconnect must be selectively coordinated with any other supply-side overcurrent devices, so one fault doesn't strand every car on the feeder. The coordination must be selected by a licensed professional engineer or other qualified person engaged primarily in the design, installation, or maintenance of electrical systems, and the selection — including device settings, a documentation point the 2020 edition added — must be documented and made available to those authorized to design, install, inspect, maintain, and operate the system. Enclosures containing coordinated device

t: Article 625 — Electric Vehicle Power Transfer System
x: The 2020 edition renamed this article from 'Charging System' to 'Power Transfer System' because the equipment now moves power both ways — charging, power export, and bidirectional flow are all inside the article's scope. The field core for Sharma: a dedicated branch circuit per outlet (625.40), protection at 125% of a continuous load (625.41, 625.42), a lockable disconnect above the threshold (625.43), and GFCI on every charging receptacle (625.54). Garage EV points follow Sharma's garage rules (S-07, S-01) only where they don't conflict with Article 625 — the article wins where they differ. Florida enforces NEC 2020 through the Florida Building Code, 8th Edition (2023). The NEC 2023 changes

t: Electric vehicle branch circuit — one outlet, one circuit
x: Each outlet installed for the purpose of charging electric vehicles must be supplied by an individual branch circuit, and each such circuit must have no other outlets. In the 2020 text that rule applies to every EV outlet regardless of size — the 'greater than 16A or 120V' qualifier and the exception letting one branch circuit feed multiple chargers are 2023 changes that Florida has not adopted. Two cars means two circuits under Florida's 2020 rules. Power sharing between chargers happens upstream through load management (625.42), not by doubling up a branch circuit. Florida enforces NEC 2020 through the Florida Building Code, 8th Edition (2023). The NEC 2023 changes in this article are not

t: Overcurrent protection — 125% of maximum load
x: Overcurrent protection for feeders and branch circuits supplying EV charging is sized for continuous duty at not less than 125% of the equipment's maximum load. The math the inspector expects: a 32A charger lands on a 40A device; a 48A charger lands on a 60A device; a charger set to 40A output needs at least a 50A device. Size from the charger's maximum setting, not from the car that happens to be plugged in today.

t: Rating — charging is a continuous load; load management
x: Electric vehicle charging loads are considered continuous loads for this article — that is the root of the 125% sizing in 625.41. Where a listed automatic load management system is used, the maximum equipment load on a service or feeder is the maximum load the system permits: the managed cap, not the sum of every charger's nameplate, is the figure used for the service and feeder. Adjustable equipment is figured at its setting only where the adjustment means meets the section's conditions. Load management is how a 100A or 200A service legally carries two chargers — but it changes the service calculation, never the per-outlet branch-circuit rule in 625.40.

t: Disconnecting means — over 60A or 150V to ground
x: EV charging equipment rated more than 60A, or more than 150V to ground, must have a disconnecting means that is readily accessible and capable of being locked in the open position, with the locking provision remaining in place as 110.25 requires. Equipment at or under both thresholds does not need the separate disconnect under this section. Big commercial chargers and DC fast-charge equipment cross the threshold — plan the disconnect location at rough-in, not at the final.

t: Connector storage — 18 in. indoors, 24 in. outdoors
x: Unless the equipment is listed and marked for a different arrangement, the coupling means (the vehicle connector) must be stored or located at a height of not less than 18 in. above the floor for indoor locations and not less than 24 in. above grade for outdoor locations, and positioned so it can couple directly to the vehicle. Mount the holster high enough that the connector isn't sitting in garage floor water or driveway runoff.

t: Ventilation — only where the listing requires it
x: Indoor charging locations need mechanical ventilation only where the equipment is listed as requiring ventilation for indoor use. Equipment listed for indoor charging without ventilation needs none. Where ventilation is required, it is a permanent supply-and-exhaust system vented directly to the outdoors, arranged for the vehicles being charged. Read the EVSE listing before pricing ductwork — most modern residential equipment is listed for indoor use with no ventilation at all.

t: GFCI protection for personnel — every EV receptacle
x: All receptacles installed for the connection of electric vehicle charging must be provided with GFCI protection for personnel. The requirement is in addition to the dwelling garage rules in 210.8 — a 240V charging receptacle is not exempt, and indoor locations are not exempt. The charger receptacle is the outlet being protected; the EVSE's own internal personnel protection system does not substitute for it. Treat every EV receptacle as a GFCI point, 120V or 240V, indoor or out.  Sharma note: S-07's dual-function point is a 120V device. A 240V EV circuit is not an S-07 point — meet 625.54 with the listed protection method specified for the job (Mike/Sanjay decide the device per job), and neve

t: Wet location — weatherproof enclosure
x: Receptacles installed outdoors or in wet locations for EV charging must be enclosed so they are weatherproof with the attachment plug cap inserted or removed — in plain terms, 'weatherproof while in use,' the same duty as other outdoor receptacle covers. Standard flip covers don't meet in-use duty; spec the bubble cover on outdoor charger receptacles.

t: Article 626 — Electrified Truck Parking Spaces
x: Intro: shore-power connections at truck parking spaces — pedestals, receptacles, and disconnects that let a parked truck run its cab loads without idling. Commercial/industrial work; recognize the article when a truck-stop or warehouse job specs electrified spaces.

t: Article 630 — Electric Welders
x: Intro: duty-cycle-based conductor and overcurrent rules for arc and resistance welders — the one place the Code lets you size conductors below the nameplate input current using the welder's rated duty cycle (630.11 multipliers). Shop work: get the duty cycle off the nameplate before sizing.

t: Article 640 — Audio Signal Processing, Amplification, and Reproduction Equipment
x: Intro: power and wiring rules for professional and commercial sound systems — studios, venues, houses of worship. Mostly a specialty-contractor article; Sharma touches it on commercial fit-outs with distributed audio.

t: Article 645 — Information Technology Equipment
x: Intro: special wiring allowances for IT equipment rooms that meet the article's conditions — including wiring under raised floors and the room disconnecting means. The allowances apply only when every condition in 645.4 is met; otherwise Chapters 1–4 govern as usual.

t: Article 646 — Modular Data Centers
x: Intro: factory-built data center modules treated as listed equipment with their own supply, disconnect, and grounding rules. Added in an earlier cycle (2014), not new in 2020.

t: Article 647 — Sensitive Electronic Equipment
x: Intro: the 120V, single-phase, center-tapped 60V-to-ground 'balanced' power system for audio/video production and similar noise-sensitive work, with its own receptacle and grounding rules. Rare and always engineered — never improvise one.

t: Article 650 — Pipe Organs
x: Intro: low-voltage organ action circuits, blower motors, and the separation rules between them. Church work only; recognize and route to the article.

t: Article 660 — X-Ray Equipment
x: Intro: disconnect, control, and transformer rules for medical, dental, and industrial X-ray equipment, including the momentary-rating allowances for diagnostic equipment. Healthcare work coordinates with Article 517.

t: Article 665 — Induction and Dielectric Heating Equipment
x: Intro: industrial heating equipment — shielding, grounding of high-frequency equipment, and disconnect rules. Industrial only.

t: Article 668 — Electrolytic Cells
x: Intro: cell-line working spaces, cranes over cells, and the rule that cell-line conductors and attachments are not treated as ordinary grounded systems. Heavy industrial only.

t: Article 669 — Electroplating
x: Intro: low-voltage, high-current plating supplies — busbar and conductor rules for electroplating and anodizing lines. Industrial only.

t: Article 670 — Industrial Machinery
x: Intro: the nameplate, supply-conductor, and overcurrent rules for industrial machines with combined motor and control loads — the machine's nameplate current, not a 430 calculation, drives the supply sizing.

t: Article 675 — Electrically Driven or Controlled Irrigation Machines
x: Intro: center-pivot and similar irrigation machines — collector rings, grounding, and the disconnect that must be able to stop the whole machine. Agricultural work across Sharma's rural counties.

t: Article 680 — Swimming Pools, Fountains, and Similar Installations
x: Article 680 is organized by installation type, and the first job on any pool is knowing which part you are in: Part I general rules ride with every part; Part II is permanently installed pools; Part III storable pools; Part IV spas and hot tubs; Part V fountains; Part VII hydromassage bathtubs; Part VIII pool lifts. Two systems run through all of it and must never be confused: grounding (the fault path back to the source) and equipotential bonding under 680.26 (tying everything a swimmer can touch to one potential). Florida is pool country — this is the highest-value article in the chapter for Sharma. Classify the install before pricing: a storable pool, an outdoor spa, and a permanently ins

t: Overhead conductor clearances
x: In the 2020 edition the overhead rules live at 680.9(A) with Table 680.9(A) — older sources that cite 680.8 are working from a previous edition. The clearance in any direction from the water level, the edge of a diving structure, or the base of a diving platform is 22.5 ft for the conductors the table covers. Measured from maximum water level, the clearance to an observation stand, tower, or diving platform is 14.5 ft. All clearances are measured from maximum water level, not from the deck. Read Table 680.9(A) by its rows: the figures apply to the conductor types and voltages the table lists, measured as the table directs — they are not a blanket clearance for every wire over water. Overhead

t: Underground wiring
x: Underground wiring is not permitted under a pool or within 5 ft horizontally of the inside wall unless it is necessary to supply pool equipment permitted by the article. Wiring in that zone uses the article's listed raceway methods, and equipment grounding follows the pool rules — when in doubt, route around the 5 ft band. Keep site lighting and landscape conduits out of the 5 ft band unless they serve the pool itself.

t: Motor wiring and equipment grounding conductor
x: Pool motor circuits carry an insulated copper equipment grounding conductor sized per 250.122 — and never smaller than 12 AWG, even where Table 250.122 would allow smaller. The insulated EGC (not a bare conductor in the raceway) is the pool difference inspectors look for at the equipment pad. Pull a green insulated 12 AWG minimum EGC on every pool motor circuit, whatever the breaker size.

t: GFCI protection for pool motors — re-checked
x: GFCI protection is required for outlets supplying pool motors on branch circuits rated 150V or less to ground and 60A or less, single-phase or three-phase — by receptacle or by direct connection. This was one of the figures re-checked against 2020-based sources before this chapter was written, and the v1 lookup (L-088) states it correctly: the scope is all pool motors inside those ratings, not just cord-and-plug pumps. A hardwired 240V pool pump needs GFCI protection just as much as a plug-in one — plan the protection device at design, not at the final walk.  Sharma note: like 625.54, a 240V pool circuit is not an S-07 120V DFN point. Meet 680.21(C) with the listed method specified for the j

t: Replacement pump motors
x: Where a pool pump motor is replaced, the replacement work must provide the GFCI protection 680.21(C) requires for that outlet. A service call that swaps a motor on an old unprotected circuit does not get to leave it unprotected. Service crews: a motor swap triggers the GFCI upgrade — quote it with the replacement, not as a surprise.

t: Receptacles — the 2020 lettering
x: The 2020 lettering, re-checked before writing: (A)(1) the required receptacle for a permanently installed pool — not less than 6 ft and not more than 20 ft from the inside wall of the pool, and not more than 6 ft 6 in. above the floor, platform, or grade serving the pool. (A)(2) receptacles serving pool circulation and sanitation equipment — not less than 6 ft away, grounding type, GFCI protected. (A)(3) all other receptacles — not less than 6 ft from the inside wall. (A)(4) GFCI protection for all 125V, single-phase, 15A and 20A receptacles located within 20 ft of the inside wall. (A)(5) a pool equipment room needs at least one 125V 15A or 20A receptacle and GFCI protection for receptacles

t: Lighting and fans over and near the pool
x: New luminaires, lighting outlets, and ceiling fans installed above a pool or within 5 ft horizontally of the inside wall must be at least 12 ft above maximum water level (B)(1). Existing luminaires and fans in that zone may remain where they are at least 5 ft above the water, rigidly attached, and GFCI protected (B)(3). In the band from 5 to 10 ft horizontally, luminaires need GFCI protection unless they are at least 5 ft above the water and rigidly attached (B)(4). Listed low-voltage luminaires have their own path through 680.23(A)(2) (B)(6). Screen-enclosure and lanai lights over Florida pools land in this section constantly — measure from maximum water level, not the deck.

t: Underwater luminaires
x: Underwater luminaires must be listed for the purpose and installed by niche type — wet-niche, dry-niche, or no-niche — with transformers and power supplies for low-voltage units listed for pool use under 680.23(A)(2). Units operating above the low-voltage contact limit get GFCI protection. Wall-mounted units sit with the top of the lens at least 18 in. below the normal water level unless the luminaire is listed and marked for use at a lesser depth. The light, its niche, its transformer, and its junction box are one system — check all four against the listing.

t: Junction boxes for underwater luminaires
x: A junction box tied to a conduit running directly to an underwater luminaire forming shell must be listed, labeled, and identified as a swimming pool junction box, located not less than 4 ft from the inside wall of the pool (unless separated by a solid fence, wall, or other permanent barrier), and at an elevation of not less than 4 in. above the ground or pool deck, or not less than 8 in. above maximum water level — whichever gives the greater elevation. A flush deck box is permitted only for systems at or below the low-voltage contact limit, and still at least 4 ft out. Set the deck box on the tape and the level at rough-in; 'close enough' fails on both numbers.

t: Equipotential bonding — the idea
x: Bonding around a pool is not grounding. Its job is to tie everything a swimmer can touch into one equipotential mass so there is no voltage difference between the water, the deck, a ladder, and the pump — because it is the difference, not the voltage alone, that drives current through a person. The bonding system is not required to extend back to a panelboard, a service disconnect, or a grounding electrode, and it never substitutes for the equipment grounding conductor in the branch circuit. Two systems, two purposes: the green EGC carries fault current home; the bare 8 AWG bonding grid kills voltage differences. Crews who can say that sentence pass pool inspections.

t: Equipotential bonding — what gets bonded, and how
x: The parts in 680.26(B)(1) through (B)(7) are bonded together with a solid copper conductor not smaller than 8 AWG, connected with a listed pressure connector, a terminal bar, or another listed means per 250.8(A): (B)(1) conductive pool shells — the structural reinforcing steel, or the copper conductor grid that serves as the alternate where a conductive shell's steel is encapsulated in a nonconductive compound or is not available. A nonconductive shell (vinyl, fiberglass) is not a conductive shell at all and needs no shell bonding grid; (B)(2) perimeter surfaces (next page); (B)(3) metallic components; (B)(4) underwater lighting forming shells and mounting brackets; (B)(5) metal fittings lar

t: Perimeter surfaces — the ring
x: The bonded perimeter surface extends 3 ft beyond the inside walls of the pool. Where the ring method is used, it is one or more bare solid copper conductors not smaller than 8 AWG, laid 18 to 24 in. out from the inside walls and 4 to 6 in. below the subgrade, and attached to the pool's reinforcing steel or copper grid at a minimum of four uniformly spaced points. The perimeter rule exists so the deck a wet swimmer stands on is at the same potential as the water. Set the ring before pavers or deck pour — depth and distance are both inspection points, and neither can be fixed after the deck is down.

t: Pool water bonding — 9 square inches
x: The pool water itself must be bonded. Where a bonded part (a ladder rail, a light niche, a fitting) is already in direct contact with the water, that contact does the job. Where nothing bonded touches the water, an approved corrosion-resistant conductive surface of at least 9 sq in. must be in contact with it — the familiar listed water-bonding fitting in the skimmer or pump line. All-plastic pools with vinyl liners and no metal in the water are the trap — check for the 9 sq in. contact on every job.

t: Storable pools — Parts I and III only
x: A storable pool (and a storable spa or hot tub) is governed by Parts I and III of Article 680 — and 680.26 equipotential bonding does not apply to it. The pump and equipment rules of Part III substitute for the Part II regime. Classification is the whole game: the same backyard water is a different code job depending on whether the pool is storable or permanently installed. 'Storable' is a defined term, not a synonym for above-ground: under 680.2 a storable pool is one built to be stored away, with a maximum water depth of 42 in. and walls of nonmetallic molded polymeric construction or inflatable fabric. A permanently installed above-ground pool does not meet that definition and is Part II

t: Spas and hot tubs — Parts I and IV (outdoor adds Part II)
x: Spas and hot tubs are governed by Parts I and IV, and an outdoor spa also picks up the Part II rules that Part IV references (680.42) — receptacle distances, GFCI, and bonding arrive through that door. A self-contained factory spa package still lands on an installation that must meet the article; the listing doesn't waive the field wiring rules. Outdoor spa on a lanai: run the Part II checklist (distances, GFCI, bonding) even though the tub arrived as one box.

t: Spa emergency shutoff — 5 ft, in sight, labeled
x: Spas and hot tubs (other than at one-family dwellings) must have an emergency shutoff for the recirculation and jet system: readily accessible, adjacent to and within sight of the tub, at least 5 ft away from it, and clearly labeled as the emergency shutoff. The 5 ft floor keeps a person in the water from reaching it; the in-sight rule lets a bystander find it. Hotels, condos, and amenity centers need the shutoff; a single-family backyard spa does not — know which job you're on before omitting it.

t: Indoor spas and hot tubs
x: An indoor spa or hot tub is wired under Parts I and II of Article 680 as modified by 680.43, and any Chapter 3 wiring method may be used. Receptacles [680.43(A)]: at least one 125V, 15A or 20A receptacle on a general-purpose branch circuit must be located not less than 6 ft and not more than 10 ft from the inside wall; every receptacle must be at least 6 ft from the inside walls, measured horizontally; 125-volt receptacles rated 30A or less within 10 ft of the inside walls must be GFCI protected; and a receptacle that supplies spa or hot tub equipment must be GFCI protected. Luminaires and ceiling fans within 5 ft horizontally of an inside wall must be at least 12 ft above the spa or hot tub

t: Fountains — Parts I and V
x: Fountains are governed by Parts I and V, and where people can enter the water (an interactive fountain or splash feature), the referenced Part II rules come in as well. Fountain equipment — submersible pumps, luminaires, and their supplies — is pool-grade listed equipment, not landscape-lighting stock. A 'decorative fountain' that kids can wade in is not wired like a dry-deck ornament — ask about entry before pricing.

t: Fountains — GFCI for submersible equipment
x: Under 680.51(A), GFCI protection is required for fountain luminaires, submersible pumps, and other submersible equipment, unless the equipment is a listed low-voltage system supplied through the 680.23(A)(2) path. If it lives under fountain water and runs on line voltage, it is GFCI protected — no exceptions by habit.

t: Hydromassage bathtubs — Part VII only
x: A hydromassage bathtub (the jetted tub in a bathroom) is governed by Part VII alone — it does not pick up the pool and spa parts. The unit must be on an individual branch circuit with readily accessible GFCI protection; 125V receptacles rated 30A or less within 6 ft of the tub need GFCI protection; the other electrical equipment in the room stays under Chapters 1–4 (680.72); and the equipment must remain accessible without damaging the building finish (680.73) — the access panel is a code item, not a courtesy. Master-bath remodels: dedicated circuit, accessible GFCI (a faceless device or GFCI breaker where the tub blocks access), and an access panel that actually opens.

t: Pool lifts — Part VIII
x: Part VIII covers electrically operated pool lifts (the accessibility lifts at commercial and amenity pools): listed equipment, GFCI protection for the lift circuit, and bonding of the lift into the pool's equipotential system where Part II applies. Amenity-pool ADA work: the lift is electrical scope — include its circuit and bonding in the pool price.

t: Article 682 — Natural and Artificially Made Bodies of Water
x: Intro: electrical installations in and around lakes, ponds, and similar natural or artificial bodies of water that are not pools or fountains — floating structures, docks outside Article 555's scope, and equipment near the water's edge. Florida lakefront work lands here; the shock-hazard logic follows Article 680's thinking.

t: Article 685 — Integrated Electrical Systems
x: Intro: orderly shutdown and interconnection rules for integrated electrical systems in industrial and large facilities where a single failure must not cascade. Specialty engineering territory; recognize the article.

t: Article 690 — Solar Photovoltaic (PV) Systems
x: Article 690 covers PV systems from the module terminals to the point of connection: how circuit current is figured (690.8), how conductors and overcurrent devices are sized (690.8, 690.9), maximum voltage (690.7), ground-fault and arc-fault protection (690.41(B) and 690.11; the old 690.5 number was deleted in 2020), rapid shutdown on buildings (690.12), disconnects (690.13, 690.15), and the marking that tells the next person — and the fire department — what the system is (690.56). Interconnection to the premises system runs through Article 705: the 120% bus rule lives at 705.12(B)(3)(2) in Chapter 7 and is deliberately not repeated here. Sharma's solar-adjacent work is mostly service, additi

t: Ground-fault protection (690.41(B) in 2020; the old 690.5 was deleted)
x: PV systems must be provided with ground-fault protection meeting this section: the system detects a ground fault in the DC circuits, interrupts the faulted circuit, and indicates the fault, using equipment listed for PV ground-fault protection. It is the DC-side companion to 690.11's arc-fault protection — ground faults and series arcs are different failures and one device does not cover both. On a service call, a tripped ground-fault indication inside the inverter is a find-the-fault call, not a reset-and-leave call.

t: Maximum voltage — correct Voc for cold
x: A PV string's voltage is not its nameplate total. Module open-circuit voltage rises as temperature falls, so maximum system voltage is calculated from the sum of the series modules' rated open-circuit voltages corrected to the lowest expected ambient temperature at the site, using a method 690.7(A) allows: the manufacturer's temperature coefficient of Voc from the module listing instructions, or the correction factors of Table 690.7(A) for crystalline and multicrystalline silicon modules. The corrected voltage must not exceed the rated voltage of the connected equipment (inverter input, disconnects, conductors), and maximum PV system voltage for one- and two-family dwellings is limited to 60

t: Circuit current and conductor sizing
x: PV current is figured on the article's own multipliers, not on load estimates. (A) The maximum current for a PV source circuit is the sum of the parallel module short-circuit currents multiplied by 125%. (B) Conductors are then sized at the larger of two numbers: 125% of the (A) current before any temperature correction or adjustment factors, or 100% of the (A) current after those factors are applied. Both checks must be run — either one can govern depending on the rooftop temperature and fill. Do the two-step check on paper; hot Florida rooftops make the after-correction figure govern more often than installers expect.

t: Overcurrent protection
x: Where overcurrent protection is required for a PV circuit, the device rating is not less than 125% of the maximum current figured under 690.8(A). The section also states the two-condition case in which no overcurrent device is required at all — conductors sized for the full available current and no external source able to backfeed beyond their ampacity. String fusing questions are answered by applying those conditions, not by habit. Three or more parallel strings is where the backfeed condition usually starts to bite — check it before deciding fuses are 'never needed' or 'always needed.'

t: Arc-fault circuit protection (DC)
x: PV systems with DC circuits operating at 80V dc or greater between any two conductors must be protected by a listed PV arc-fault circuit interrupter, or other listed system components providing equivalent protection. The protection must detect and interrupt arcing faults caused by a failure in the intended continuity of a conductor, connection, module, or other component in the PV DC circuits. Exception: systems not installed on or in buildings, with the DC circuits in metallic raceways or metal-clad cables, in enclosed metallic cable trays, or underground. Loose MC4-style connections are the classic series-arc source — connector discipline on the roof is what keeps this protection from ever

t: Rapid shutdown of PV systems on buildings
x: Rapid shutdown controls PV conductors on and in buildings to protect firefighters. The array boundary is 1 ft from the array in all directions. Outside the boundary — and for conductors more than 3 ft from the point of entry into the building — controlled conductors must be limited to not more than 30V within 30 seconds of initiation. Inside the boundary, the installation must use one of the section's paths: a listed PV hazard control system (PVHCS, UL 3741), or conductors limited to not more than 80V within 30 seconds, or an array with no exposed wiring methods or conductive parts and installed not less than 8 ft from exposed grounded conductive parts. The v1 lookup L-093 covers this sectio

t: Rapid shutdown initiation device
x: The initiation device must be readily accessible, must clearly indicate whether it is in the off (shutdown initiated) or on position, and may be the service disconnect, the PV system disconnect, or another listed switch. For one- and two-family dwellings, the initiation device must be located at a readily accessible location outside the building — the fire crew does not enter the house to shut the array down. On dwelling jobs, walk out front and find the initiation point the way a firefighter would — if you can't, neither can they.

t: PV system disconnecting means
x: The PV system disconnecting means must be readily accessible, indicate whether it is open or closed, be permanently marked as the photovoltaic system disconnect. Where the PV disconnect is not at the service, the directory and plaque rules of 690.56 point back to it. One obvious, labeled PV disconnect — 'somewhere in the inverter menu' is not a disconnecting means.

t: Disconnection of PV equipment
x: Equipment disconnecting means must open all ungrounded conductors from all sources — on a PV job that means the utility side and the array side, and on hybrid systems the storage side too. A disconnect that isolates the inverter from the grid but leaves it connected to a live array has not made the equipment safe to service. Before opening an inverter, verify both sides are dead — the array makes power whenever the sun is up.

t: Marking — plaques, directories, and the rapid shutdown label
x: PV systems carry permanent plaques and directories: a stand-alone system follows the directory rule of 710.10, and a system interconnected with another source follows 705.10, so the sources at a building can be found from the service equipment. Two rapid-shutdown labels apply: a permanent label on or within 3 ft of the service disconnecting means states that the system is equipped with rapid shutdown and carries the 690.56(C) diagram with the switch locations; and a reflective label on or within 3 ft of the rapid shutdown initiation device reads RAPID SHUTDOWN SWITCH FOR SOLAR PV SYSTEM, in capital letters at least 3/8 in. high, white on a red background (690.56(C)(2)). Marking is not paperw

t: Article 691 — Large-Scale Photovoltaic (PV) Electric Supply Stations
x: Intro: utility-scale PV plants of 5 MW and up — engineered installations with their own access, fencing, and documentation rules. Added in the 2017 edition, not new in 2020. Sharma does not build these; recognize the article so a plant job is never priced from residential 690 habits.

t: Article 692 — Fuel Cell Systems
x: Intro: fuel cell power systems — output circuits, disconnects, and interconnection of a chemical generator that runs whenever fuel is present. Specialty work; the disconnect and marking pages matter when one appears on a commercial job.

t: Article 694 — Wind Electric Systems
x: Intro: small wind systems — turbines, towers, and their disconnects and grounding, including the rule that the turbine itself is part of the electrical system. Rare in Sharma's counties; recognize and route.

t: Article 695 — Fire Pumps
x: Article 695 exists for one reason: the fire pump must run, even at the cost of the equipment itself. Everything in it runs backward from ordinary motor practice — sources are chosen for reliability above all (695.3), overcurrent devices are sized to carry locked-rotor current indefinitely rather than to trip (695.4), and disconnects are arranged so the pump cannot be casually shut off. Recognition level is the right depth for Sharma: this is engineered, AHJ-scrutinized work, and the pages here cover what to recognize and what never to improvise. The article does not apply to sprinkler-system pumps at one- and two-family dwellings, and pressure-maintenance (jockey) pumps sit outside its scope

t: Power sources — reliable, and sized for locked rotor
x: The fire pump supply must come from a reliable source, and the source is sized to carry the locked-rotor current of the fire pump motor(s) plus the pressure-maintenance pump motors, plus 100% of the accessory equipment load — locked rotor, not full load, is the design event. Permitted arrangements include a separate utility service arranged remote from the normal service, a tap ahead of (but not within the enclosure of) the normal service disconnect, and an on-site standby generator protected against fire damage. Where transfer equipment is used, it sits in the fire pump room (695.3(F)). Phase converters are not permitted as the supply (695.3(I)). Recognize the tap-ahead-of-the-main arrangem

t: Continuity of power — protection that refuses to trip
x: Continuity rules invert ordinary practice. A single disconnecting means is permitted where it is listed for fire pump service together with the controller (or transfer switch) it feeds. Its overcurrent device is selected to carry, indefinitely, the sum of the locked-rotor currents of the fire pump and pressure-maintenance motors plus the full accessory load, and it must be listed for fire pump use. The disconnect must be lockable in the closed position — the opposite of the elevator rule — and is identified with permanently marked letters not less than 1 in. high as a fire pump disconnect. No ground-fault protection of equipment is applied to the fire pump circuit: anything that can shut the

t: Transformers — dedicated and oversized
x: A transformer supplying a fire pump installation is dedicated to that service and sized at not less than 125% of the fire pump and pressure-maintenance motor loads, plus 100% of the accessory equipment supplied by it. Its overcurrent protection follows the same carry-indefinitely philosophy as 695.4 — the transformer protection is not allowed to become the weak link that stops the pump.

t: Voltage drop — 15% starting, 5% running
x: One of the NEC's few mandatory voltage-drop rules, and it is a calculation rule: (A) starting — the voltage at the controller's line terminals must not drop more than 15% below normal (controller-rated) voltage under motor starting conditions; (B) running — the voltage at the controller's load terminals must not drop more than 5% below the motor's voltage rating when the motor operates at 115% of its full-load current. Conductors under 695.6(B) must satisfy both their ampacity floor and these limits. Long fire pump runs get upsized for starting voltage, not just ampacity — if the pump can't start and hold, nothing else in Article 695 matters.

t: Emergency systems — the life-safety tier
x: Article 700 covers backup power that the law classes as emergency: power for getting people out and keeping them alive, such as egress lighting, exit signs, fire alarm and similar life-safety loads. A governmental agency having jurisdiction decides that a system is emergency; the owner does not get to choose the label. Emergency power has to be there fast, the wiring is kept apart from normal wiring, and the system is tested and documented. If life safety does not depend on it, you are probably in Article 701 or 702 instead. First question on any standby job: who required this system, and for what loads? The answer picks the article before you pick any gear.

t: Tests and maintenance — emergency systems
x: An emergency system is not finished when it is wired. The AHJ conducts or witnesses an acceptance test when the installation is complete, the system is tested periodically on a schedule the AHJ approves, and the equipment is maintained following the manufacturer instructions and industry standards. A written record of tests and maintenance has to be kept. Leave the owner a test log, not just a working generator. If there is no record, treat the system as unproven at inspection and at every service visit after it.

t: Capacity and rating — emergency systems
x: Emergency equipment has to be suitable for the fault current available where it connects. The system also has to have enough capacity for its emergency load, figured under Article 220 or by another method the AHJ approves. There is no user-selects-the-load shortcut here the way there is for a manual optional standby system. Check the fault-current rating on the transfer gear against the service, and do the load calculation before the generator size is promised to anyone.

t: Transfer equipment — emergency systems
x: Emergency transfer equipment has to be automatic, listed and marked for emergency use, and approved by the AHJ. It is built and installed so the emergency source and the other sources cannot be connected together by accident. An automatic transfer switch has to be electrically operated and mechanically held, reconditioned transfer switches are not allowed, the gear may feed only emergency loads, and meter-mounted transfer switches are not permitted for emergency use. The documentation rule of 700.5(E) carries no dwelling exception — unlike 702.5(C) — so the transfer equipment short-circuit rating is field marked on the outside of the gear in dwellings too. Read the listing and the marking, n

t: Signs — emergency sources
x: A sign at the service equipment tells responders and electricians what kind of on-site emergency source the building has and where it is. Nobody should have to hunt through a building during an outage to learn that a second source exists. Put the source type and location on the sign and check it against the actual disconnect location before you call the job done.

t: Surge protection — emergency systems
x: Every emergency system switchboard and panelboard has to have a listed surge protective device. This is a flat requirement of the article, not an upsell and not something to value-engineer out. Count an SPD for every emergency panelboard and switchboard on the material list, and confirm it is listed.

t: Wiring — emergency systems stay identified and apart
x: Emergency wiring is identified as emergency all the way through: boxes, enclosures, transfer switches, generators and panels are permanently marked, and emergency raceways and cables are marked as emergency at short, regular intervals. Emergency conductors also stay out of enclosures, raceways and cables that carry nonemergency wiring, with only narrow exceptions such as inside transfer equipment. Emergency receptacles are identified by a distinctive color or marking. The identification interval is concrete, not a judgment call: 700.10(A)(2) requires emergency wiring to be marked as emergency at intervals not exceeding 25 ft. And 700.10(D) adds fire protection for emergency feeders in the la

t: Sources of power — available in 10 seconds
x: When the normal supply fails, emergency power has to be available within 10 seconds. The article lists the permitted kinds of sources, from storage batteries and generator sets to a separate service and unit equipment, and it sets conditions for each one. Engine-driven sources carry on-site fuel rules, battery sources carry a minimum run-time duty at close to full voltage, and the equipment has to be located and designed so one fire, flood or act of vandalism is less likely to kill both supplies at once. The 10-second clock is the design test. Ask how the source starts, how fast load lands on it, and where its fuel or charge comes from before you argue about brands.

t: Loads on emergency branch circuits
x: Emergency circuits feed emergency loads only. A circuit that exists to keep egress lighting and life-safety equipment alive does not pick up convenience loads because there was spare capacity on paper. Walk the emergency panel schedule load by load. Anything that is not an emergency load comes off, even if the generator is big enough.

t: Emergency illumination — no single failure leaves a space dark
x: Emergency illumination covers the means of egress lighting, the illuminated exit signs and every other luminaire specified as necessary to get people out. The system has to be designed and installed so that the failure of any single illumination source cannot leave a space that requires emergency illumination in total darkness — one dead lamp, ballast or driver never blacks out an exit path. Control devices on the system have to be listed for use in emergency systems. Where discharge lighting such as HID is the sole source of normal illumination, the emergency system has to operate until normal illumination is restored, because those lamps are slow to restrike. The section also requires emer

t: Selective coordination — emergency systems
x: Emergency system overcurrent devices have to selectively coordinate with every supply-side overcurrent device, so a fault on one emergency branch opens only the device that should open instead of darkening the whole system. The coordination is designed by a qualified person and the documentation has to be available to the people who design, install, inspect, maintain and operate the system. This is an engineering deliverable, not a field guess. Get the coordination study and keep it with the job record before the gear is released.

t: Legally required standby systems — the middle tier
x: Article 701 covers standby power that a law, code or AHJ requires, but that is not classed as emergency. These systems back up loads that aid firefighting and rescue, control health hazards, or keep ventilation, smoke removal, sewage, communications and similar loads running so an emergency does not get worse. They sit below Article 700 in priority: a 700 load always outranks a 701 load on a shared source. If nobody with authority required the system, it is not 701 — it is optional standby under 702. The tell is paperwork: a code citation, a permit condition or an AHJ direction requiring standby power for named loads. No requirement, no 701.

t: Transfer equipment — legally required standby
x: Transfer equipment for a legally required standby system has to be automatic, listed and marked for that use, and approved by the AHJ, and it has to keep the standby source from being interconnected with the other sources by accident. Automatic transfer switches are electrically operated and mechanically held, reconditioned switches are not allowed, and meter-mounted transfer switches are not permitted here either. The transfer equipment short-circuit rating is field marked on the outside of the gear. Same discipline as 700: check the marking for legally required standby use before the gear is ordered, not after it is hung.  S-02 applies to gear Sharma furnishes: new transfer equipment is Si

t: Wiring — legally required standby may share raceways
x: Unlike emergency wiring, legally required standby wiring is allowed to run in the same raceways, boxes and cabinets as general wiring. The strict separation duty belongs to Article 700, and importing it into a 701 job — or forgetting it on a 700 job — are both mistakes. Know which article the job is under before you decide how to run the raceways. The wiring method follows the classification, not habit.

t: Sources of power — available in 60 seconds
x: Legally required standby power has to be available within 60 seconds of the normal supply failing — slower than the 10 seconds of Article 700, far faster than a portable generator someone drags out of a garage. The article lists the permitted source types and their conditions, including on-site fuel for engine-driven sources and battery duty where batteries are the source. One source may also carry optional loads only where capacity is truly there, or where automatic pickup and shedding protect the legally required loads first. Design to the 60-second clock and to load priority. If optional loads can starve a 701 load, the design is wrong even if the generator starts on time.

t: Selective coordination — legally required standby
x: Legally required standby overcurrent devices have to selectively coordinate with all supply-side overcurrent protective devices, so a fault on one standby branch opens the device at the fault instead of tripping devices upstream and darkening healthy standby loads with it. The coordination is selected by a licensed professional engineer or another qualified person engaged primarily in the design, installation or maintenance of electrical systems, and the selection has to be documented and made available to the people authorized to design, install, inspect, maintain and operate the system. It is the Article 700 duty at 700.32 carried one tier down. Coordination is not required between two dev

t: Optional standby systems — home and business generators
x: Article 702 covers standby systems nobody required: the homeowner who wants the fridge, well pump and a few lights through a Florida outage, or the business protecting product and comfort. Life safety does not depend on these systems, and that single fact is what keeps them out of Articles 700 and 701. The article still regulates them hard where it counts: capacity, transfer equipment that can never tie the generator to the utility by accident, signs, wiring and outdoor generator sets. Portable generators that are never connected to the premises wiring are outside this article; the moment one is connected through an inlet and transfer equipment, 702 is in play. Most Sharma generator work liv

t: Available fault current — optional standby equipment
x: Optional standby equipment has to be suitable for the fault current available at its terminals. A transfer switch with a short-circuit rating below what the service can deliver is the wrong switch, even if its amp rating matches the load. Pull the available fault current from the service gear or the utility information and match the transfer equipment rating to it before ordering.

t: System capacity — the sizing fork in Article 702
x: How big the standby source must be depends on how the load gets onto it. With manual transfer, the user chooses the load, so the source only has to carry what is intended to run at one time. With automatic transfer, nobody is standing there choosing, so the source is sized to the calculated load — figured under Article 220 or by another approved method — and it must either carry the full transferred load or be paired with automatic load management. This page and the two that follow were re-checked against 2020 sources for this edition, because the v1 wording on this section was flagged unverified. Write down which side of the fork the job is on before you size anything. 'Automatic transfer,

t: Manual transfer — the user selects the load
x: Where manual transfer equipment is used, the optional standby system has to be able to supply all the equipment intended to be operated at one time, and the user is permitted to select which loads are connected. That selection is what sets the practical size of the source: a homeowner who will run the fridge, a few lights and the well pump — and leave the range and dryer off — does not need a generator sized for the whole house. Build the intended-load list with the owner and put it in the job record. If a load is not on the list, it does not get counted, and it does not get promised.

t: Automatic transfer — full load, or load management
x: Where automatic transfer equipment is used, the standby source is sized to the calculated load, figured under Article 220 or by another approved method — for an existing installation, recorded maximum demand is one of the approved routes the code recognizes through 220.87. The system then has to satisfy one of two duties. Under the full-load duty, the source carries the entire load the automatic equipment transfers. Under the load-management duty, an automatic system manages the connected load and the source only has to carry the maximum load that management system will actually connect. Do the Article 220 calculation or pull the demand data first, then check which duty the design claims. A

t: Transfer equipment — required, listed, and built to keep sources apart
x: Transfer equipment is required to connect an optional standby source to the premises wiring, and in the 2020 code it has to be listed — a tightening over earlier editions that catches unlisted interlock hardware. One narrow exception exists: a temporary portable generator connection without transfer equipment, only where maintenance and supervision ensure qualified persons service it and the normal supply is physically isolated by a lockable disconnect or by disconnecting the normal conductors. The four duties that follow it in the section — meter-mounted switches, documentation, inadvertent interconnection, and parallel operation — get their own pages next, in the section's own order. Defau

t: Meter-mounted transfer switches
x: A transfer switch mounted between the utility meter and its enclosure has to be a listed meter-mounted transfer switch. A meter-mounted switch is manual unless it is rated in accordance with the automatic-transfer sizing duty in 702.4(B)(2) — the meter socket is not a loophole around generator sizing. Remember the contrast with Articles 700 and 701, where meter-mounted transfer switches are not permitted at all. Check with the utility as well as the code: the meter is the utility's territory, and approval there is separate from the electrical inspection.

t: Documentation — short-circuit rating marked on the gear
x: On jobs other than dwelling units, the short-circuit current rating of the transfer equipment has to be field marked on the outside of the equipment. The person maintaining or replacing that gear years later should not need the original submittal to learn what fault duty it was built for. Carry a marker and the rating from the equipment data to every non-dwelling transfer install, and photograph the finished marking for the job record.

t: Inadvertent interconnection — the heart of 702.5
x: Transfer equipment has to be suitable for the job, listed, and designed and installed so that all sources of supply can never be inadvertently interconnected in any operation of the equipment. This is the rule that kills backfeeding: a generator pushing power out through the service can energize a line a utility crew believes is dead. The listing requirement in this paragraph is the 2020 change that unlisted interlock hardware runs into. Test the finished install through every switch position, not just the normal one. The duty covers any operation of the equipment, including the sloppy one nobody planned.

t: Parallel installation — Article 705 takes over
x: Transfer equipment and power production systems that are installed to run in parallel with the normal source also have to meet Article 705. A standby source that only ever replaces the utility is a 702 job; the moment a source is meant to operate alongside the utility, the interconnection rules join the transfer rules. Ask one question on every generator quote: will this source ever run in parallel with the utility? If yes, price and wire it as a 705 interconnection too.

t: Signs — standby sources, and the power inlet sign
x: Signs close the loop that transfer equipment starts. At service equipment, a sign identifies the type and location of each on-site optional standby source — for a house, the sign sits at the 230.85 emergency disconnect and points to the permanently installed standby source disconnect or the means to shut down the prime mover. Where a power inlet is used for a portable generator, a sign at the inlet states which kind of generator system may be connected there: a separately derived (bonded neutral) system only, or a nonseparately derived (floating neutral) system only. Two different signs, two different jobs: the service sign says where the source is; the inlet sign says what kind of neutral a

t: Wiring — optional standby wiring may share raceways
x: Optional standby wiring is allowed to occupy the same raceways, cables, boxes and cabinets as other wiring. That permission is the opposite of the Article 700 rule, and it is one more reason the classification question comes first: the same physical run can be legal under 702 and a violation under 700. Use the permission, but keep the standby circuits identified in the panel directory so the next electrician knows what the generator feeds.

t: Outdoor generator sets — when a building disconnect is not required
x: For permanently installed generators and portable generators over 15 kW used outdoors, if the generator has a readily accessible disconnect within sight of the building it supplies, no extra disconnect is required at the building — provided that generator disconnect is in accordance with 445.18, and where the generator supply conductors terminate at a disconnecting means in or on the building, that disconnect meets 225.36. For a portable generator of 15 kW or less connected through a flanged inlet or another cord-and-plug connection, no disconnecting means is required at the building for the ungrounded conductors serving or passing through it. Both rules are about not duplicating a disconnec

t: Power inlets 100 A and up — listed, with an interlocked disconnect
x: Where a portable generator connects through an inlet rated 100 amps or more, the 2020 code adds two requirements on the inlet equipment. The equipment must be listed for the intended use, and it must be provided with an interlocked disconnecting means, so the inlet arrangement cannot leave the building connected the wrong way. Two exceptions soften it: the inlet device itself may serve as the disconnecting means where it is rated for that duty, and supervised industrial installations with a permanent generator space within line of sight follow their own conditions. Below 100 amps this paragraph does not apply — the 702.12(A) and (B) rules on the previous page govern instead. On a big portabl

t: Interconnected electric power production sources
x: Article 705 governs sources that operate in parallel with another source — most often a solar inverter, storage system or generator tied to a live utility service. It answers three practical questions: where may the source connect, how much current may the connection and the busbar carry, and how does everyone after you know the extra source exists. Connections land on the supply side under 705.11 or the load side under 705.12, and a power control system under 705.13 can change the math. Article 690 in Chapter 6 governs the solar array itself; this article governs its handshake with the premises wiring. Decide supply side or load side on paper first. The choice drives the overcurrent protect

t: Identification of power sources — the directory
x: Where sources are interconnected, a permanent plaque or directory at the service equipment — or another approved, readily visible location — shows where every parallel power source disconnect is. The plaque carries the caution that multiple sources of power are present, and any diagram on it has to be oriented the way the building actually sits. This is the page a firefighter or a utility worker reads; it has to be right, not approximate. Walk the building and verify every disconnect location before the plaque is made. A directory that points to where the disconnect was planned, instead of where it is, fails its only job.

t: Supply-side source connections
x: A source may connect on the supply side of the service disconnect, at the points the service rules allow, under its own set of conditions for conductor sizing, overcurrent protection and grounding. A supply-side connection steps around the panelboard busbar limits entirely, which is why it is the escape route when the 120 percent math in 705.12 will not close. It trades that freedom for service-level work: the connection is ahead of the main, so its protection and its disconnecting means have to be planned like service equipment. Price a supply-side tap as service work, with utility coordination, not as 'one more breaker.' If the busbar math fails, compare this route honestly against deratin

t: Load-side source connections — the shape of the rule
x: A source output may connect on the load side of the other source's service disconnect, at any distribution equipment on the premises. Where that equipment is fed by two sources at once and feeds branch circuits or feeders, the connection has to satisfy the sub-rules that follow: a dedicated breaker or fusible disconnect for each source, the busbar and conductor ampere-rating methods, marking of equipment that contains more than one source, breakers suitable for backfeed, and fastening where a backfed breaker could work loose. Where a power control system is installed under 705.13, the controller setting stands in for the source output current in these calculations. Work the sub-rules in orde

t: Dedicated overcurrent and disconnect — each source gets its own
x: Each source interconnection is made at its own dedicated circuit breaker or fusible disconnecting means. Two inverters do not share one breaker because the math happened to fit, and a source does not land on a breaker that also feeds a load. The dedicated device is both the overcurrent protection point and the place the source is disconnected. Count breakers on the takeoff the way the section counts sources: one source system, one dedicated device, every time.

t: The 100 percent busbar method — breaker anywhere
x: The plainest load-side method: 125 percent of the source output current, plus the rating of the overcurrent device protecting the busbar, must not exceed the busbar ampacity itself. Meet that sum and the source breaker may sit anywhere on the bus. Fail it and you do not argue with the arithmetic — you move to one of the other methods in 705.12(B)(3), derate something, or go to the supply side. Run this method first because it is the one with no position condition. Example in the lookup entries: on a 225A bus with a 200A main, this method leaves room for only a 20A inverter output, while the 120 percent method on the next page leaves much more.

t: The 120 percent rule — sources at opposite ends
x: Where two sources sit at opposite ends of a busbar that carries loads, the same sum — 125 percent of the source output current plus the rating of the device protecting the busbar — may go up to 120 percent of the busbar ampacity. The busbar still has to be sized for the connected loads under Article 220. Because the allowance depends on position, a permanent warning label goes on the distribution equipment next to the backfed breaker, warning that it is a power source output connection and must not be relocated. On the common 200A bus with a 200A main, this method allows 40A of backfeed device capacity, which is a 32A inverter output — the worked example already in v1 as L-092 and Q-063. Thr

t: The sum-of-breakers method
x: A third load-side method ignores the main breaker rating and adds up the ampere ratings of all the overcurrent devices on the panelboard — load and supply devices together, excluding the device protecting the busbar — and that total must not exceed the busbar ampacity. Equipment using this method carries permanent warning labels at the distribution equipment identifying that all sources are present. It fits panels where the breaker population, not the main, is the honest limit. Count every breaker that is actually in the panel, including the source breaker, and write the sum in the job record. A panel that passes today can fail this method after one added circuit.

t: The center-fed busbar method — one end only
x: Some dwelling panelboards are center-fed: the main breaker or main lugs sit in the middle of the busbar instead of at one end, a construction common on combination meter-and-panel equipment in some regions. This method permits a source connection at either end of that busbar, but never at both ends. The math is the familiar 120 percent check applied to the connection: the sum of 125 percent of the power source output circuit current and the rating of the overcurrent device protecting the busbar must not exceed 120 percent of the busbar rating. Because a center-fed bus can concentrate load on one half of the busbar, the option is limited to dwellings. Identify the panel construction before re

t: Power control systems — a listed controller can limit the current
x: New in the 2020 code, this section recognizes a power control system: listed equipment that monitors and limits how much current a source puts onto conductors and busbars. Where one is installed, its controller setting is treated as the source output current for the 705.11 and 705.12 calculations, so a system set to a lower limit can fit a panel the raw inverter rating could not. The section also guards the settings themselves, because the whole method stands on the setting staying where it was set. Record the controller setting in the job file and on the labels the design calls for. If nobody wrote the setting down, nobody can prove the method later.

t: Disconnecting means for sources
x: Every interconnected source needs a disconnecting means that meets this section, which in 2020 gathered the source disconnect rules into one place. The disconnect has to separate the source from the conductors of the other systems, and where a disconnect that unqualified people can reach would expose live parts when open, it has to be locked or need a tool to open. A source that can energize a panel from the far end is exactly the surprise this section exists to remove. Land the disconnect where the 705.10 directory says it is, and check the open-position condition: terminals that stay live get the warning the equipment rules call for.

t: Overcurrent protection — interconnected sources
x: Conductors and equipment on an interconnected system get overcurrent protection under this section, working with the circuit-current sizing earlier in the article and with Article 240. A conductor fed from both ends can be overcurrented from either direction, so protection is planned for the source output the same way it is planned for a utility feed. Device ratings follow the calculated source currents, with the continuous-output factor built in. Size the source output conductors and their protection from the inverter's rated output on the nameplate, not from what the array produced on a cloudy site visit.

t: Loss of primary source — the source must stop and stay off
x: When the primary source — normally the utility — is lost, an interconnected power production source has to be automatically disconnected from all ungrounded conductors of the primary source, and it must not reconnect until the primary source is restored. The duty bites even if only one line or phase of the utility supply opens. It exists so a solar array or cogeneration source can never backfeed lines that utility crews are treating as dead.
