t: Is a home-run data cable to a router a communications circuit under Article 805, or Article 725 work?
x: It depends on the system the cable serves, not the jacket. Provider communications circuits running from the demarcation point to customer communications equipment fall under Article 805 with the general rules of Article 800. Power-limited control and signaling systems, such as most access control and HVAC control wiring, are usually Article 725 work in Chapter 7.

t: When does a telephone-style circuit need a primary protector?
x: A listed primary protector is required on each communications circuit that is exposed to lightning or to possible contact with higher-voltage power conductors. The protector connects an arrester between each line conductor and ground. Circuits with no outside exposure may not trigger the requirement, which is why the entrance path matters.

t: Where does the primary protector go?
x: In, on, or immediately next to the building served, as close as practicable to where the circuit enters. Keep it out of hazardous locations and away from easily ignitible material. A short distance to the entrance also keeps its bonding conductor short, which the grounding rules reward.

t: The entering phone cable has a metal sheath and no protector bond. What are my options?
x: The metallic sheath members must be either grounded following the entrance grounding rules, or interrupted by an insulating joint or an equivalent device, as near as practicable to the point of entrance. Leaving the sheath floating is not one of the options. The same entrance idea applies to the coax shield under Article 820.
tags: cable sheath ground or insulating joint

t: Does a new house owe any communications outlet if the buyer has no provider yet?
x: Yes. New construction requires at least one communications outlet inside the dwelling, in a readily accessible area, cabled back to the service provider demarcation point. The requirement is the cabled outlet, not a live service, so rough it in even when no provider has been chosen. Older references cite this as 800.156 from before the 2020 reorganization.

t: Does Article 800's general rules govern the satellite dish article too?
x: No. Article 810 is the exception in this chapter, because its antenna rules stand alone instead of layering under Article 800. Its own section, 810.21, carries the complete bonding and grounding recipe for antenna systems. Read 810 by itself, and follow only the outside references that 810 itself makes.

t: Does every antenna mast need to be grounded?
x: Outdoor masts and their metal support structures must be grounded following 810.21. The exception is an antenna and mast sitting inside a zone of protection provided by a lightning protection system, described with a 150 foot radius rolling sphere. An ordinary house with no lightning protection system gets the mast bond, full stop.

t: How close can an antenna lead-in swing toward the power drop?
x: A lead-in attached to a building must not be able to swing closer than 2 feet to conductors of circuits of 250 volts or less. For circuits over 250 volts the clearance is 10 feet. Plan for the swung position in wind, not the still position on a calm day.

t: What size wire does a long antenna lead-in need?
x: The size steps up with length under the table in 810.16. A copper lead-in under 35 feet may be as small as 19 AWG, a run between 35 and 150 feet needs at least 14 AWG copper, and a run over 150 feet needs at least 12 AWG copper. Copper-clad steel and bronze have their own, smaller sizes listed in the same table because of their strength.

t: What is an antenna discharge unit and where does it go?
x: It is a listed device that drains static charge from the antenna system before the charge reaches the equipment inside. Each lead-in conductor from an outdoor antenna needs one, placed as near as practicable to the point of entrance, inside or outside the wall. The unit itself must be bonded or grounded following 810.21.

t: Where does the antenna bonding conductor land, and how should it run?
x: Run it in as straight a line as practicable, protect it where it can be damaged, and land it first on the intersystem bonding termination where the building has one. Without a termination, use the nearest accessible point on the building grounding electrode system or another landing point the section lists. It does not have to be insulated.

t: What size is an antenna bonding conductor?
x: Not smaller than 10 AWG copper, 8 AWG aluminum, or 17 AWG copper-clad steel or bronze. The thin copper-clad option is the messenger wire often molded into satellite coax jackets. Ten AWG copper is heavier than the 14 AWG floor used at a communications protector, because the antenna sits exposed to lightning.

t: A separate rod was driven for the dish. What else is required?
x: The separate electrode must be bonded to the building power grounding electrode system with a conductor no smaller than 6 AWG copper or equivalent. A separate electrode is allowed, but it is never allowed to stand alone. This matches the separate-electrode rule for communications entrances in 800.100(D).

t: A customer is adding a ham radio station. What grounding sizes apply?
x: Each outdoor lead-in needs a discharge unit or an equivalent static drain under 810.57. The protective bonding or grounding conductor must be at least as large as the lead-in and never smaller than 10 AWG copper, bronze, or copper-clad steel. The operating bonding or grounding conductor cannot be smaller than 14 AWG copper or its equivalent, under 810.58.

t: Does a cable TV coax entrance need a primary protector like a phone line?
x: No, a primary protector is not required for a coaxial cable entrance the way it is for an exposed communications circuit. If a protector is installed on the coax, it must be listed and applied at the point of entrance. What every coax entrance does require is grounding of the outer shield, covered in 820.93.

t: Where does the coax shield get grounded?
x: As close as practicable to the point where the coax enters the building, following the conductor rules of 820.100. The connection can be made where the cable terminates outside or just inside, and a grounded metal raceway can extend the effective point of entrance. A grounding block screwed to the wall with an empty lug does not count.

t: What are the bonding conductor numbers for a CATV entrance at a house?
x: The conductor is copper or another corrosion-resistant material, no smaller than 14 AWG, and never required to exceed 6 AWG. At a one- or two-family dwelling it must be as short as practicable and no longer than 20 feet. A separate electrode used to meet the length limit must be bonded back to the power system with at least 6 AWG.

t: The provider's outdoor coax runs 70 feet inside the house to the panel. Is that fine?
x: No. Unlisted outside plant coax may extend only 50 feet from the point of entrance inside a building before listed cable is required. Past that distance the run must be listed coax of a type permitted for the spaces it passes through. Measure the actual cable path on long custom homes, not the straight-line distance.

t: Can coax be supported from the EMT that carries the store's power?
x: No. Coaxial cable cannot be supported from a raceway containing power conductors, cannot share a raceway or box with power, and keeps at least 2 inches from power conductors unless those conductors are in a raceway or a sheathed cable assembly. Give coax its own holes and its own supports, exactly like data cable.

t: How do I recognize a network-powered broadband entrance?
x: The provider's network supplies the power for the network interface unit at the building, over the same outside plant that carries the signal. That incoming power is why this article requires primary protection and grounding at the entrance. If the interface unit is powered from a local receptacle instead, you are likely looking at a premises-powered system under Article 840.
tags: network powered broadband what is it

t: Why does network-powered broadband get protectors on its conductors?
x: Because the circuit arrives from outside plant carrying both signal and network power, exposed to lightning and to accidental contact with power conductors on the poles. Primary protection at the entrance gives that energy a path before it reaches the interface unit and the inside distribution. Treat a missing protector like a missing phone protector, as a provider-side correction.

t: What three things get grounded at a network-powered broadband entrance?
x: The cable shield, the primary protector, and the metallic enclosure of the network interface unit all get grounded. Their conductors follow the same entrance grounding recipe used across this chapter. Bonding only the shield and leaving the enclosure floating finishes just part of the job.

t: Do the broadband grounding numbers change at a house?
x: No. The broadband bonding conductor follows the chapter pattern of 14 AWG minimum, never required above 6 AWG, as short as practicable, and no more than 20 feet in a one- or two-family dwelling. A separate electrode used for length gets bonded back with at least 6 AWG. Learn 800.100 once and the broadband pages are already familiar.

t: The new house has fiber to an optical network terminal. Which article is that?
x: Premises-powered broadband under Article 840, because the terminal is powered at the premises rather than by the network. The fiber cable itself is also tied to the optical fiber rules of Article 770. Pure dielectric fiber carries no metallic path, so the entrance grounding question turns on whether any metallic member actually arrives with the cable.

t: Does a fiber entrance cable always need a bond?
x: Only where the arriving cable has metallic members, such as a shield or a metallic strength member, that require grounding. Those members are grounded following the chapter entrance pattern, as close as practicable to the point of entrance. An all-dielectric fiber cable has nothing conductive to bond, and the job record should say so.

t: How far must an outside communications drop stay from open power wiring on the building wall?
x: Specified unshielded communications wires and cables on the outside of a building must be separated at least 4 inches from open electric light or power conductors that are not in a raceway or cable assembly, subject to the alternatives in the section. This exterior rule is separate from the 2 inch indoor separation for communications cable. Check which situation you actually have before picking a number.
tags: drop wire near open power wiring

t: What is the point of entrance, and why does it matter?
x: The point of entrance is where a communications wire or cable enters the building from outside, through a wall or floor, or at the end of a grounded metal entrance raceway that extends it. Protector location, sheath and shield grounding, and the distance allowed for unlisted outside cable are all measured from this point. Settle where it is before applying any entrance rule in this chapter.

t: Can the communications bonding conductor be copper-clad aluminum (CCA)?
x: This book's position: no. The bonding and grounding conductor run under 800.100 is specified as copper or another corrosion-resistant conductive material, sized from 14 AWG up to (never required over) 6 AWG. Read honestly, the section's text neither names copper-clad aluminum nor expressly excludes it the way 250.62 names it for grounding electrode conductors — so the flat answer is an interpretation, not the section's plain words. Sharma's position in this book is to keep the communications bond copper; where it would ever matter on a job, get the AHJ's reading in writing.

t: Where is CCA allowed to terminate?
x: CCA terminates fine on 15 and 20 amp device screw terminals. Wire nuts and lugs used with CCA must be marked AL/CU. Backstab (push-in) holes are for 14 AWG solid copper only, so CCA is never backstabbed, in communications work or anywhere else. These are the same termination rules Sharma applies on the power side.

t: Does conductor metal (copper, aluminum, or CCA) change box fill or conduit fill?
x: No. Box fill under 314.16 and conduit fill under Chapter 9 Tables 4 and 5 are figured from the conductor's size and insulation, not from what metal is inside it. A 12 AWG THHN conductor takes the same fill allowance whether it is copper, aluminum, or copper-clad aluminum. Metal changes ampacity and terminations, never the fill arithmetic.

t: How are CCA conductors sized for ampacity and voltage drop?
x: For ampacity, CCA is sized on the aluminum column of Table 310.16, with minimum sizes following 310.3, which in practice means one AWG size up from copper for the same ampacity. For voltage drop, CCA's own resistance must be used, and Chapter 9 Table 8 does not list CCA values. Per-size CCA resistance is being sourced from cited manufacturer or UL data before any number is published here; until then no CCA resistance figure is stated, rather than inventing one.

t: How far can unlisted outside communications cable run inside a building?
x: 50 ft. Unlisted cables and raceways entering a building from outside are limited by 805.48: the unlisted outside-plant cable may extend no more than 50 ft (15 m) into the building before it must terminate or transition to a listed cable. Article 820's version of the same rule for coax lives at 820.48.

t: Can a Cat 6 cable carry Power over Ethernet power?
x: Yes — 840.160 (revised in the 2020 edition) is the section that lets listed communications cables carry powering circuits (PoE) alongside the data, and past 60 watts the installation ties into the ampacity rules for power-carrying cables in 725.144. Flagged unverified: the gateway is as stated, the fine structure awaits Mike's printed check.

t: How must a communications grounding conductor connect to the grounding electrode?
x: 800.100(C): connections to grounding electrodes must be made by the 250.70 methods — exothermic welding, listed lugs, listed pressure connectors, or listed clamps — and a clamp may hold only one conductor unless it is listed for more. It is the subsection the book's 800.100 sequence previously skipped.

t: How much fill is allowed for one conductor in a raceway?
x: One conductor may occupy 53 percent of the raceway's inside area under Chapter 9 Table 1. Look up that raceway's 53 percent area in Table 4 and compare it with the conductor's area from Table 5.

t: How much fill is allowed for two conductors in a raceway?
x: Two conductors together may occupy 31 percent of the raceway's inside area, the lowest of the Table 1 percentages. Two round conductors pack poorly in a round raceway, which is why this limit sits below both the one-conductor and the three-or-more percentages.

t: How much fill is allowed for three or more conductors?
x: Three or more conductors together may occupy 40 percent of the raceway's inside area under Table 1. This is the column used for most house and light-commercial pulls, and it is the basis of existing quiz item Q-067.

t: Which Table 1 percentage do I pick first in a fill problem?
x: Count every conductor in the run first, including the equipment grounding conductor, then pick the percentage for that count. One conductor gets 53 percent, two get 31 percent, and three or more get 40 percent, with 60 percent reserved for short nipples.

t: When can a raceway be filled to 60 percent?
x: A raceway nipple 24 inches or less between enclosures may be filled to 60 percent. The allowance belongs to that short nipple only, and the long runs on either side still use the normal Table 1 percentage for their conductor count.

t: How many 12 AWG THHN fit in a 1/2 in EMT nipple by fill alone?
x: At 60 percent, 1/2 in EMT offers 0.182 sq in, and one 12 AWG THHN takes 0.0133 sq in, so 0.182 / 0.0133 = 13.68, which rounds down to 13. That is a fill answer only; conductor ampacity adjustment in Chapter 3 is a separate check.

t: Is 1/2 in EMT actually a half inch inside?
x: No — trade size is a name, not a measurement. Half-inch EMT is 0.622 in inside and 0.304 sq in in total area, which is why fill work always uses the Table 4 dimensions instead of the trade-size name.

t: Does raceway type change a fill answer at the same trade size?
x: Yes. Half-inch PVC Schedule 40 is smaller inside than 1/2 in EMT — 0.285 sq in total and 0.114 sq in at 40 percent, against EMT's 0.304 and 0.122. A count that fits in EMT may not fit in PVC, so always read the row for the raceway actually being installed.

t: Is the 1/2 in EMT total area 0.304 or 0.305 sq in?
x: The v1 table carries 0.304 sq in, and one secondary source showed 0.305, so the difference is flagged rather than silently fixed. The 40 percent usable area of 0.122 sq in agrees across sources, and 0.304 should not be changed without re-checking the printed Table 4.

t: What area does one 12 AWG THHN conductor take for fill?
x: One 12 AWG THHN, THWN, or THWN-2 conductor takes 0.0133 sq in by Table 5. That single value drives the classic fill example: 0.122 / 0.0133 = 9.17, so nine fit in 1/2 in EMT at 40 percent.

t: Does insulation type change a conductor's fill area?
x: Yes. Table 5 lists area by size and insulation type, and a thicker insulation in the same AWG takes more room. If the job changes insulation type, redo the fill math with the new type's area instead of reusing the old count.

t: Which table gives the area of a bare conductor for fill?
x: A bare conductor's area comes from the conductor-properties data in Table 8, because there is no insulation for Table 5 to measure. Insulated conductors, including an insulated equipment ground, use their Table 5 areas instead.

t: What are the steps of a conduit fill calculation?
x: List every conductor including grounds, add their Table 5 areas (Table 8 for bare), pick the Table 1 percentage from the conductor count, then take the first Table 4 trade size whose usable area covers the total. Skipping the ground or using the wrong raceway row is where most wrong answers start.

t: My conductor total is just over the allowed area. Can I still use that trade size?
x: No. If the total is over the usable area at all, move up to the next trade size — the two 6 AWG plus one 10 AWG example totals 0.1225 sq in against a 0.122 limit in 1/2 in EMT, so it goes to 3/4 in. Close does not count in fill.

t: What is the most common fill mistake on a two-conductor pull?
x: Using the familiar 40 percent column for a pull that only gets 31 percent because it holds exactly two conductors. Always let the conductor count choose the percentage before any areas are compared.

t: How do I find how many same-size conductors fit in a raceway?
x: Divide the raceway's usable area at the right percentage by one conductor's Table 5 area. For 10 AWG THHN in 3/4 in EMT that is 0.213 / 0.0211 = 10.09, so 10 conductors fit.

t: Do I round a fill result up or down?
x: Round down, because a fraction of a conductor cannot be installed — 9.17 means 9 conductors. The only exception is the Chapter 9 note for all-same-size conductors, where a decimal of 0.8 or more may be rounded up.

t: When may a same-size fill result be rounded up?
x: When every conductor in the raceway is the same size and type and the division leaves a decimal of 0.8 or more — for example 8 AWG THHN in 3/4 in EMT divides to 5.82, so 6 are permitted. Mixed sizes never use this round-up; their areas are added instead.

t: How do I figure fill for mixed conductor sizes?
x: Add each conductor's own Table 5 area, count the equipment ground as its own line, and compare the sum with Table 4. There is no single division for a mixed pull, and the same-size shortcuts, including Annex C, cannot answer it.

t: Will three 1/0 THHN plus a 6 AWG ground fit in 1-1/4 in EMT?
x: No. The total is 3 x 0.1855 + 0.0507 = 0.6072 sq in, and 1-1/4 in EMT allows only 0.598 sq in at 40 percent. The next size, 1-1/2 in EMT at 0.814 sq in, is the answer.

t: Does the equipment grounding conductor count toward conduit fill?
x: Yes. An equipment grounding conductor occupies raceway space like any other conductor, and the v1 Chapter 9 notes state that grounds count toward fill. Leaving it out is the most common reason a calculation passes on paper and jams in the field.

t: What area do I use for an insulated equipment ground in fill?
x: Use the Table 5 area for that conductor's size and insulation type, exactly as for a current-carrying conductor. Only a bare ground leaves Table 5 and takes its area from Table 8.

t: Does a bare ground get counted at zero area?
x: No. A bare conductor still has metal area, taken from Table 8 for fill purposes. Counting it as zero understates the pull and repeats the classic left-out-ground mistake in a thinner form.

t: What is Annex C for?
x: Annex C is a set of pre-worked fill tables for the one case where every conductor in the raceway is the same size and type, so a count can be read off instead of calculated. It is the Tables 1, 4, and 5 math done ahead of time, and it agrees with that math — nine 12 AWG THHN in 1/2 in EMT is the shared example.

t: When can Annex C not be used?
x: Annex C cannot answer a mixed-size pull, a different insulation type than its tables assume, or a bare-ground case. Those go back to the four-step method with Tables 1, 4, and 5 — and Tables 8 for the bare conductor.

t: My Annex C count and my division disagree. Which is wrong?
x: Probably an input, not either method — Annex C and the Tables 4 and 5 division are the same math. Recheck raceway type, insulation type, conductor count, and whether a ground was included before trusting either answer.

t: What information does Table 8 give about a conductor?
x: Table 8 gives a conductor's area in circular mils, its stranding, its overall diameter, and its DC resistance at 75 degrees C in ohms per thousand feet, for copper and for aluminum. The resistance columns are what voltage-drop work is built on.

t: Do solid and stranded conductors of the same AWG have the same resistance?
x: Not exactly. Stranded 12 AWG copper is listed at 1.98 ohm/kft and solid 12 AWG copper at 1.93 ohm/kft in the v1 Table 8 data. Read the row that matches the conductor actually in hand when a voltage-drop answer is close to a limit.

t: Why does the voltage-drop formula divide by 1000?
x: Table 8 resistance is stated per thousand feet, but job lengths are in single feet. Multiplying length by ohm-per-thousand-feet and dividing by 1000 converts the table unit into the resistance of the actual run.

t: What resistance do I use for copper-clad aluminum in voltage drop?
x: CCA is not separately listed in Table 8, so the aluminum column is used only as an approximation, exactly as the v1 table notes it. Never invent a CCA resistance or present an aluminum-column result as an exact CCA value.

t: Is using the aluminum column for CCA the same rule as its ampacity?
x: They are two different uses of the aluminum column. For ampacity, Table 310.16 groups CCA with aluminum and Sharma rule S-10 sizes it one AWG larger; for voltage drop, the aluminum resistance is only a stand-in estimate, because Table 8 lists no CCA value.

t: What is the single-phase voltage-drop formula used in this book?
x: VD = 2 x L x R x I / 1000, where L is the one-way length in feet, R is the Table 8 resistance in ohm per thousand feet, and I is the actual load current. The result is in volts; divide by the system voltage and multiply by 100 for the percentage.

t: Why is there a 2 in the single-phase voltage-drop formula?
x: Current travels out on one conductor and back on the other, so it crosses the run length twice and drops voltage on both legs. Forgetting the 2 understates the drop by half and is the most common error in the whole calculation.

t: Do I use the breaker size or the actual load for voltage drop?
x: Use the actual load current the circuit carries, not the breaker rating, unless the load truly equals that rating. A 20A circuit carrying 12A drops voltage as a 12A circuit, and substituting 20A will upsize wire the job does not need.

t: How do I turn voltage drop in volts into a percentage?
x: Divide the drop in volts by the system voltage and multiply by 100. A 6.34V drop is 5.28 percent on a 120V circuit but would be only 2.64 percent on a 240V circuit, which is why long runs hurt less at higher voltage.

t: What is the voltage drop of 16A at 100 ft on 12 AWG copper at 120V?
x: Using stranded copper at 1.98 ohm/kft: 2 x 100 x 1.98 x 16 / 1000 = 6.34V, which is 5.28 percent of 120V. That is well past the 3 percent recommendation for a branch circuit, so the conductor needs upsizing.

t: How do I fix a circuit that fails a voltage-drop check?
x: Rerun the same formula with the next size's lower Table 8 resistance — do not guess how many sizes to jump. In the 100 ft, 16A example, 10 AWG still gives 3.31 percent, and only 8 AWG, at 2.07 percent, meets the 3 percent recommendation.

t: What is the three-phase voltage-drop formula in this book?
x: VD = 1.732 x L x R x I / 1000, with L one-way feet, R the Table 8 resistance, and I the load current. The 1.732 factor replaces the single-phase round-trip factor of 2 for a balanced three-phase circuit.

t: Is the three-phase formula with Table 8 exact?
x: No — it is an approximation, because it borrows DC resistance for an AC system. Large conductors, steel raceways, and power factor can move the real answer, which is the finer work Table 9 exists for, so results near a limit should be labeled and checked.

t: Are the 3 percent and 5 percent voltage-drop figures code requirements?
x: No. The 3 percent branch-circuit and 5 percent feeder-plus-branch figures are recommendations in Informational Notes to 210.19(A) and 215.2(A), not enforceable requirements. This book keeps that label on every voltage-drop page and quiz item.

t: Is a circuit over 3 percent voltage drop a code violation?
x: Not by that fact alone, because the figure is a recommendation, not a requirement. It is still a circuit that may run its load poorly — dim lights or a hard-starting motor — and a good installer fixes it by upsizing, shortening the run, or moving the load.

t: Can a 3 percent voltage-drop limit ever be enforced on a job?
x: Yes, if a source with actual authority on that job imposes it — a project specification, a contract, or a local amendment. That enforcement comes from those documents, not from the Informational Note itself, so check the job documents and the AHJ.

t: What is Table 9 used for?
x: Table 9 works with alternating-current resistance and reactance for 600V cables, giving a finer voltage-drop calculation than Table 8's DC resistance alone. Reach for it on large conductors, long three-phase runs, or any result that lands near a limit.

t: Why does this book publish no Table 9 values?
x: Because no Table 9 value was re-checked against the printed 2020 book for this pass, and the v1 calc tables do not include it. The book teaches when to use Table 9 and flags the values as unverified rather than inventing numbers.

t: What does Annex D show?
x: Annex D works the load-calculation articles end to end on example buildings: list the loads, apply the allowed demand factors, and arrive at a service or feeder size. Use it as the pattern for the order of work, and do the mandatory calculation itself in the Chapter 2 articles.

t: Where does a dwelling load calculation actually get done?
x: In Chapter 2, under the load-calculation articles — the v1 calc data carries the optional dwelling method as table 220.82. Annex D only illustrates the method with examples; it does not replace the article that governs your building.

t: Which torque value governs a lug or breaker connection?
x: The equipment's own marking or manufacturer instruction governs first, and a general recommended-torque table is used only where the equipment gives no value. Make the connection with a torque tool to that value rather than by feel.

t: Why does this book publish no Annex I torque values?
x: The annex letter and its values were not re-confirmed against the printed 2020 book for this pass, so the page teaches the order of authority — marking, instruction, then recommended table — and publishes no numbers. Check the printed book and the equipment marking on the job.

t: What does it mean that an annex is informative?
x: An informative annex explains, illustrates, or supplies reference data; it is not a mandatory requirement unless an adopting ordinance specifically adopts it. That is the same guidance status the voltage-drop percentages carry as Informational Notes.

t: Which Chapter 9 tables and annexes did this chapter hold back, and why?
x: Table 5A, Table 10, Tables 11 and 12, and every annex letter other than C, D, and I were held for confirmation against the printed 2020 book rather than written from the brief alone. There is no Table 13 or Annex K in this chapter, and nothing was invented to fill those slots.

t: Material choice in Chapter 9 calculations
x: Every conductor calculation in this chapter now states its material — copper, aluminum, or copper-clad aluminum (CCA) — before the math starts. The choice changes ampacity (Chapter 3, Table 310.16) and the resistance used for voltage drop (Table 8 here), but it does not change conduit fill or box fill, which run on conductor size and insulation only. Sharma's standard branch wire is CCA (S-10), so the material is stated out loud on every worked example instead of being assumed.

t: CCA ampacity — which column
x: Size copper-clad aluminum from the aluminum column of Table 310.16 — the table's ampacity columns cover copper and aluminum/copper-clad together, and CCA takes the aluminum side. Combined with the small-conductor caps, that lands one AWG size above copper for the same breaker (S-10). Minimum conductor sizes and the rest of the ampacity rules live with Article 310 in Chapter 3 of this book; this chapter only supplies the fill and resistance tables the sizing works from.

t: CCA resistance for voltage drop — no exact value on file
x: Table 8 does not list copper-clad aluminum, and no cited manufacturer or UL resistance value for CCA is on file for this book as of this pass — so no exact CCA resistance is published here, and none may be invented. Working practice stays what the Table 8 CCA page teaches: use the aluminum column for the same AWG as a labeled approximation, state that the voltage-drop result is an estimate, and treat any CCA-specific resistance figure from a study sheet or sales sheet as unverified until it is checked against the manufacturer's published data. Any future CCA resistance entry in this book is flagged verified=false until that check is done.

t: Where CCA terminations are OK
x: On the device side, ordinary 15 and 20 A receptacle and switch screw terminals are fine with copper-clad aluminum. Anything that clamps or splices conductors — wire connectors and lugs — must carry an AL/CU (AL-CU or CU-AL) marking; a copper-only connector is not the pick for CCA. Push-in backstab holes are the hard no: they are listed for 14 AWG solid copper only, so no CCA conductor of any size goes in a backstab hole — side screws or pigtails with a listed connector instead (S-10).

t: Conduit fill — metal does not change the answer
x: Chapter 9 Tables 4 and 5 have no column for conductor metal: fill runs on conductor size and insulation type only. Same size, same insulation, same count means the same fill result whether the conductor is copper or copper-clad aluminum — nine 12 AWG THHN fit a 1/2 in EMT either way. The metal shows up one step earlier, in sizing: when CCA's ampacity puts a circuit on a larger AWG than copper would use, run the fill math at that larger AWG, because size is what the tables read (S-10).

t: Box fill — size, not metal (314.16)
x: Box fill under 314.16 works the same way: each conductor is charged a volume allowance by its AWG size — 2.25 cu in for 12 AWG, 2.50 cu in for 10 AWG — and the metal is never asked. The result for a given set of conductor sizes is identical in copper and CCA. What changes in practice is the size itself: a 20 A CCA circuit runs 10 AWG where copper runs 12, so its conductors each carry the 10 AWG allowance and the box fills faster — the Chapter 3 box-fill table does that math.

t: Load calcs — conductor picked in the chosen material
x: A load calculation (220.82 and the other Article 220 methods) produces amperes, not a wire. The conductor is picked afterward, from Table 310.16, in the material the job is actually using: copper from the copper column, aluminum or copper-clad aluminum from the aluminum column, with the small-conductor caps applied. So the same calculated load can land on different AWG sizes for different materials — the arithmetic of the load does not change, the pick does.

t: State the material before the math
x: Field habit for every calculation in this book: say the material first — copper, aluminum, or CCA — then the size, then the table. Most wrong answers in conduit fill and voltage drop are not arithmetic errors; they are a copper assumption carried into a CCA job (or the reverse), which silently changes the AWG in the fill count and the resistance in the drop formula. Sharma runs CCA as its standard branch wire (S-10), so CCA is the assumption to state and check, not copper.

t: How is a multiconductor cable counted for conduit fill?
x: A multiconductor cable counts as ONE conductor for fill, however many conductors are inside it (Note 9 to Table 1). If the cable is elliptical rather than round, Note 2 says to use the cable's MAJOR diameter as its diameter when you work its area for the fill calculation — an oval cable is treated as a circle of its widest dimension.

t: Worked example: fill with a bare equipment grounding conductor
x: Bare conductors take their area from Table 8 dimensions (diameter), not from Table 5. Example: four 12 AWG THHN (4 × 0.0133 = 0.0532 sq in) plus one bare 12 AWG ground. A solid 12 AWG conductor is 0.081 in in diameter per Table 8, so its area is π/4 × 0.081² ≈ 0.0052 sq in. Total fill = 0.0532 + 0.0052 = 0.0584 sq in — comfortably inside a 1/2 in EMT at 40% (0.122 sq in). The bare ground is small, but it is never zero: write it on the fill list as its own line.

t: How many small-appliance circuits does a kitchen need?
x: A dwelling needs at least two 20A small-appliance branch circuits for the kitchen, pantry, breakfast and dining receptacles. Countertop receptacles in the kitchen must be served by at least two of these circuits. They can't feed other outlets except the few the code allows, such as a clock outlet or the gas range igniter.

t: Does the laundry need its own circuit?
x: Yes. At least one 20A branch circuit is required for the laundry receptacle outlets, and it can't serve any other outlets. The dryer is a separate 240V circuit.

t: What's required for bathroom circuits?
x: At least one 20A circuit must supply the bathroom receptacles. That circuit can feed receptacles in several bathrooms, or it can feed everything in a single bathroom (lights, fan) as long as it serves only that one bathroom.

t: Does the garage need a dedicated 20A circuit?
x: Yes, new in NEC 2020. At least one 120V 20A circuit must supply the receptacles required in each vehicle bay of an attached garage, or a detached garage with power. That circuit can't serve outlets outside the garage, except readily accessible outdoor receptacles.

t: Where are GFCI receptacles required in a house?
x: In NEC 2020, all 125V through 250V receptacles (single-phase, 150V to ground or less) need GFCI protection in: bathrooms, garages and unfinished accessory buildings, outdoors, crawl spaces, basements, kitchen countertop receptacles, within 6 ft of a sink, boathouses, within 6 ft of a tub or shower, laundry areas, and indoor damp or wet locations. The 2020 expansion to 250V means a 240V receptacle in a garage or laundry needs GFCI too.

t: Do 240V receptacles need GFCI in a dwelling?
x: Yes, if they are in a 210.8(A) location. NEC 2020 raised the dwelling GFCI rule from 125V only to receptacles rated 125V through 250V, so a dryer or range receptacle in a laundry area, garage, or within 6 ft of a sink needs GFCI protection. A 2-pole GFCI breaker is the usual way to provide it.

t: Do kitchen receptacles that don't serve the counter need GFCI?
x: Under NEC 2020 the kitchen rule covers receptacles installed to serve the countertop. A receptacle behind a refrigerator that doesn't serve the counter is not caught by the kitchen item, but it still needs GFCI if it's within 6 ft of the sink edge. (NEC 2023 expanded this to all kitchen receptacles, but Florida is on 2020.)

t: Does the dishwasher need GFCI?
x: Yes. NEC 2020 requires GFCI protection for outlets that supply dwelling-unit dishwashers, whether hardwired or cord-and-plug.

t: Do outdoor outlets other than receptacles need GFCI?
x: NEC 2020 210.8(F) requires GFCI protection for outdoor outlets at dwellings on single-phase circuits of 150V to ground or less, rated 50A or less, other than the receptacle outlets already covered in 210.8(A). Lighting outlets have their own exception. For a one- or two-family dwelling, the Florida Building Code, Residential, 8th Edition, E3408.1 adds Exception No. 2: GFCI protection is not required for listed and labeled HVAC equipment. Other outdoor outlets in that voltage and ampere range still need it. The exception is in the residential code; commercial jobs are outside it.

t: Which rooms need AFCI protection?
x: All 120V 15A and 20A circuits feeding outlets or devices in dwelling kitchens, family rooms, dining rooms, living rooms, parlors, libraries, dens, bedrooms, sunrooms, recreation rooms, closets, hallways, laundry areas and similar rooms need AFCI protection. Bathrooms, garages and outdoors are not on the list. Sharma puts a dual-function AFCI/GFCI breaker on every 120V circuit anyway.

t: Do I need AFCI when I extend or modify an existing circuit?
x: Yes. When branch-circuit wiring in an area that needs AFCI is modified, replaced or extended, you must add AFCI protection, either a listed combination AFCI at the origin or an outlet branch-circuit AFCI at the first receptacle of the existing circuit. Extensions of 6 ft or less with no added outlets are excepted.

t: What is the 6 ft / 12 ft receptacle spacing rule?
x: In habitable rooms, receptacles must be placed so no point along the floor line of any wall is more than 6 ft from a receptacle. In practice that means a receptacle within 6 ft of each door edge and no more than 12 ft apart along the wall.

t: What counts as wall space for receptacle spacing?
x: Any wall space 2 ft or wider counts, measured along the floor line around corners but broken by doorways, fireplaces and similar openings. Fixed glass panels count as wall space; sliding panels in exterior walls don't. Fixed room dividers and railings count as wall too.

t: Do floor receptacles count toward wall spacing?
x: Only if the floor receptacle is within 18 in of the wall. Receptacles that are part of a luminaire or appliance, inside cabinets, or more than 5.5 ft above the floor don't count either.

t: How far apart do countertop receptacles go?
x: Every countertop space 12 in or wider needs a receptacle, and they must be placed so no point along the wall line is more than 24 in from one. That works out to receptacles no more than 4 ft apart, and within 2 ft of each counter end. Space behind a sink or range is handled by the code's corner and behind-sink rules.

t: How many receptacles does a kitchen island need?
x: Under NEC 2020 an island needs at least one receptacle for the first 9 sq ft of countertop or fraction, plus one more for each additional 18 sq ft or fraction. NEC 2023 changed this rule, but Florida is on 2020.

t: How high can a countertop receptacle be?
x: Countertop receptacles must sit on or above the counter, no more than 20 in above it, or be a listed countertop receptacle assembly. Receptacles hidden behind appliances or in appliance garages don't count as countertop receptacles.

t: Where does the bathroom receptacle go?
x: At least one receptacle must be within 3 ft of the outside edge of each basin, on a wall or partition next to the basin, on the countertop, or on the side or face of the basin cabinet no more than 12 in below the counter top. One receptacle between two basins can serve both.

t: How many outdoor receptacles does a house need?
x: A one-family dwelling needs at least one receptacle at the front and one at the back, readily accessible from grade and no more than 6.5 ft above grade. Each balcony, deck or porch reachable from inside also needs one, no more than 6.5 ft above its walking surface.

t: Does the laundry need a receptacle?
x: Yes. At least one receptacle outlet is required in each area designated for laundry equipment. It goes on the 20A laundry circuit and needs GFCI protection under 210.8(A)(10).

t: How many garage receptacles are required?
x: NEC 2020 requires at least one receptacle in each vehicle bay of a garage, no more than 5.5 ft above the floor. Basements and accessory buildings with power need receptacles too.

t: Does a hallway need a receptacle?
x: Yes, if the hallway is 10 ft or longer, measured along the centerline without passing through a doorway. Then at least one receptacle is required.

t: Does a foyer need receptacles?
x: Foyers that aren't part of a hallway and are larger than 60 sq ft need a receptacle on each wall space 3 ft or wider. Doorways and similar openings break up the wall space.

t: Do I need a receptacle near the AC or air handler?
x: Yes. A 125V 15A or 20A receptacle must be installed at an accessible location for servicing HVAC equipment, on the same level and within 25 ft of the equipment. It can't be on the load side of the equipment disconnect.

t: Which rooms need a switched lighting outlet?
x: Every habitable room and bathroom needs at least one wall-switch-controlled lighting outlet. In habitable rooms other than kitchens and bathrooms, a switched receptacle can stand in for the light. Hallways, stairways, attached garages and outdoor entrances need switched lighting too.

t: Do stairs need switches at both ends?
x: Yes. Where a stairway between levels has 6 or more risers, a wall switch is required at each floor level and landing level that includes an entryway, unless the lights are controlled automatically.

t: Does the attic need a light?
x: Yes, when the attic, crawl space, utility room or basement is used for storage or holds equipment that needs servicing. At least one lighting outlet with a switch at the point of entry is required, and in attics with equipment the light must be at or near the equipment.

t: How do continuous loads affect breaker and wire size?
x: A continuous load runs 3 hours or more. The branch-circuit conductors and the overcurrent device must be sized at no less than the noncontinuous load plus 125% of the continuous load, unless the breaker assembly is listed for 100% operation.

t: What size receptacle can go on a 20A circuit?
x: On a 20A circuit with more than one receptacle, either 15A or 20A receptacles are allowed. A single receptacle on an individual circuit must be rated at least the circuit rating, so a lone receptacle on a 20A circuit must be a 20A receptacle.

t: How much cord-and-plug load can a circuit carry?
x: On a 15A or 20A circuit, one cord-and-plug appliance can't exceed 80% of the circuit rating. Fastened-in-place equipment can't exceed 50% of the circuit rating when the same circuit also feeds lighting or other cord-and-plug loads.

t: What is the small-conductor rule?
x: Unless a specific code section allows otherwise (like motors or AC), the breaker can't exceed 15A on 14 AWG copper, 20A on 12 AWG copper, or 30A on 10 AWG copper. For aluminum or copper-clad aluminum it's 15A on 12 AWG and 25A on 10 AWG. These caps apply after any ampacity derating.

t: When can I round up to the next breaker size?
x: For circuits of 800A or less, when the conductor ampacity doesn't match a standard breaker size, you may use the next standard size up, as long as the conductors don't feed multiple receptacles for cord-and-plug loads. The small-conductor limits of 240.4(D) still apply.

t: Which temperature column do I use for terminations?
x: For circuits rated 100A or less or for 14 through 1 AWG conductors, use the 60°C column unless the equipment is listed and marked for 75°C. Above 100A or larger than 1 AWG, use 75°C. You can start a derating calc from the 90°C column, but the final result can't exceed the termination rating.

t: What size wire for a 200A house service?
x: For a 120/240V single-phase dwelling service of 100 to 400A that carries the whole house load, the conductors can be sized at 83% of the service rating. For 200A that's 2/0 copper or 4/0 aluminum. It only applies when no temperature correction or bundling adjustment is needed.

t: Can I use the 83% rule for a subpanel feeder?
x: Only if the feeder carries the entire load of the dwelling unit, such as a feeder from an outdoor meter-main to the indoor main panel. A feeder to a garage or partial-load subpanel must be sized from Table 310.16 at full rating.

t: How do I derate for more than three wires in a raceway?
x: When more than three current-carrying conductors share a raceway or cable for more than 24 in, multiply the ampacity by 80% for 4-6 conductors, 70% for 7-9, and 50% for 10-20. Equipment grounds don't count, and a neutral carrying only unbalanced current usually doesn't count either.

t: What's the ampacity of NM cable?
x: NM cable conductors are rated 90°C, but the cable's ampacity is limited to the 60°C column. You may use the 90°C rating as the starting point for derating, as long as the final ampacity doesn't exceed the 60°C value.

t: Can I use copper-clad aluminum (CCA) branch-circuit wire?
x: Yes, the NEC allows CCA, but it's rated in the aluminum/copper-clad aluminum column of Table 310.16 and capped at 15A on 12 AWG and 25A on 10 AWG. So it goes one size up from copper: 12 AWG on 15A and 10 AWG on 20A. Per UL guide info cited by NEMA, 15/20A receptacle and switch screw terminals are for copper or CCA (CO/ALR adds plain aluminum), but wire connectors and equipment lugs must be marked AL-CU/CU-AL; CU-only connectors aren't rated for CCA. Push-in (backstab) terminals are 14 AWG solid copper only.

t: Can I mix copper and aluminum under one terminal?
x: Not unless the terminal or connector is identified for that intermix. Copper and copper-clad aluminum aren't treated as dissimilar in 2020, but aluminum with copper or with CCA is. CCA still needs connectors and lugs marked AL-CU/CU-AL (UL ZMVV), and aluminum touching Cu/CCA in one connector needs the 'AL-CU (intermixed - dry locations)' marking. Follow the torque values on the device.

t: Do I need a torque screwdriver?
x: Yes. NEC 2020 requires an approved means, such as a calibrated torque tool, to tighten terminals where the manufacturer gives a torque value. Guessing tightness doesn't meet code.

t: How much working space in front of a panel?
x: For 120/240V residential panels (150V or less to ground), keep at least 3 ft deep of clear space in front, 30 in wide or the width of the panel (whichever is more), and 6.5 ft high or the height of the equipment. The door must be able to open at least 90 degrees.

t: Can anything be installed above or below the panel?
x: The space equal to the panel's width and depth, from the floor to 6 ft above the panel or to the structural ceiling, is dedicated to electrical equipment. Pipes, ducts and other foreign systems can't be in that zone. Sprinkler protection is allowed.

t: Can a panel go in a closet or bathroom?
x: No. Overcurrent devices can't be in clothes closets or near easily ignitible material, and in dwellings they can't be in bathrooms. Garages, laundry rooms and utility rooms are common locations.

t: How high can the top breaker be?
x: The center of the grip of the highest breaker handle in its on position can't be more than 6 ft 7 in above the floor or working platform. Equipment next to the motor it serves and similar cases have exceptions.

t: What does the panel directory need?
x: Every circuit and every circuit modification must be clearly identified by its specific purpose or use on the directory at the panel. Labels can't depend on things that will change, like 'Bob's room', and spare positions must be marked as spares.

t: Is surge protection required on a house service?
x: Yes, new in NEC 2020. Every service supplying a dwelling unit needs a Type 1 or Type 2 surge-protective device, either built into the service equipment or right next to it. It's also required when the service equipment is replaced.

t: Do I need an outdoor emergency disconnect?
x: Yes, new in NEC 2020. One- and two-family dwellings need an emergency disconnect at a readily accessible outdoor location. It can be the service disconnect (meter-main), a separate disconnect, or another listed option, and it must be marked 'EMERGENCY DISCONNECT' along with whether it's the service disconnect.

t: What is the minimum service size for a house?
x: The service disconnect for a one-family dwelling must be rated at least 100A, 3-wire. Size the actual service from the load calculation in Article 220.

t: Where does the service disconnect go?
x: The service disconnect must be at a readily accessible location, either outside or inside nearest the point where the service conductors enter the building. Keep service conductors inside the house as short as possible.

t: How many service disconnects are allowed?
x: Each service may have up to six disconnects, but in NEC 2020 they must be in separate enclosures or separate sections, not six main breakers inside one panel. Most houses use a single main.

t: How close can a service drop be to a window?
x: Overhead service conductors need at least 3 ft of clearance from windows that open, doors, porches, balconies, ladders, stairs and fire escapes. Conductors run above the top of a window are exempt.

t: What size grounding electrode conductor?
x: Size the GEC from Table 250.66 by the largest service conductor. For example, 2/0 copper or 4/0 aluminum service conductors need a 4 AWG copper GEC. But a GEC that only goes to ground rods doesn't need to be larger than 6 AWG copper, and one that only goes to a concrete-encased electrode doesn't need to be larger than 4 AWG copper.

t: Is one ground rod enough?
x: A single rod is only enough if you prove it's 25 ohms or less to earth. Otherwise you need a supplemental electrode, usually a second rod at least 6 ft away. Most contractors just drive two rods instead of testing.

t: How do I install a ground rod?
x: The rod must be at least 8 ft long and have at least 8 ft in contact with soil. Drive it vertically; if you hit rock, drive it at an angle up to 45 degrees, or bury it in a trench at least 30 in deep. The top must be flush or below grade unless the clamp is protected.

t: What is a Ufer / concrete-encased electrode?
x: It's at least 20 ft of 1/2 in or larger rebar, or 20 ft of bare 4 AWG or larger copper, encased in at least 2 in of concrete in a footing in contact with earth. If one exists in the footing, it must be used as part of the grounding electrode system.

t: Which electrodes have to be bonded together?
x: Every electrode that's present at the building, such as metal water pipe in contact with earth, concrete-encased electrode, ground ring and building steel, must be bonded together into one grounding electrode system. Rods are added when needed.

t: Where are neutral and ground bonded?
x: Neutral and ground are bonded only at the service disconnect with the main bonding jumper. Downstream subpanels keep neutral and ground separated, with the neutral bar isolated and the bonding screw removed.

t: What size equipment ground for a circuit?
x: Size the equipment grounding conductor from Table 250.122 by the breaker rating: 14 Cu for 15A, 12 Cu for 20A, 10 Cu for 30-60A, 8 Cu for 100A, 6 Cu for 200A. If you upsize the hot conductors for voltage drop, the EGC must be upsized proportionally.

t: Does the water pipe need bonding?
x: Yes. Interior metal water piping must be bonded to the service enclosure, grounded conductor at the service, GEC, or electrode, sized from Table 250.102(C)(1). Other metal piping like gas, which could become energized, is bonded by the circuit EGC of the equipment likely to energize it.

t: What is the intersystem bonding termination?
x: An intersystem bonding termination is a device at the service that gives communications, CATV and satellite installers a place to bond. It must be accessible, outside the panel, and have room for at least three conductors.

t: How deep do I bury wiring?
x: Typical minimums: direct-burial UF cable 24 in, PVC conduit 18 in, rigid metal conduit 6 in, and residential 120V 20A or less GFCI-protected branch circuits 12 in. Depth is measured to the top of the cable or raceway; driveways and other locations have their own values in Table 300.5.

t: How far from the stud edge must a hole be?
x: Holes bored in wood framing for cable must be at least 1-1/4 in from the nearest edge of the stud. If you can't keep that distance, protect the cable with a steel plate at least 1/16 in thick.

t: How much wire do I leave in a box?
x: Leave at least 6 in of free conductor at each box, and in boxes with an opening smaller than 8 in, at least 3 in must extend outside the opening. Conductors that pass through a box without a splice are exempt.

t: How do I calculate box fill?
x: Add up volume allowances from Table 314.16(B): each insulated conductor counts once at its own size, internal clamps count as one, and each device yoke counts as two based on the largest conductor on that device. Equipment grounding conductors use the 2020 count in 314.16(B)(5): up to four count as one volume based on the largest ground, and each ground past four adds one quarter of that volume. The total cannot exceed the box volume. The metal does not change the allowance.

t: How far into the box does the NM sheath go?
x: The cable sheath has to extend at least 1/4 in inside the box past any cable clamp. With single-gang nonmetallic boxes, the cable must be fastened within 8 in of the box and the sheath still goes 1/4 in in.

t: What box do I need for a ceiling fan?
x: Where wiring is installed in a habitable room ceiling at a spot that could support a ceiling fan, the box must be listed for fan support. Fan boxes are marked for the weight they can carry, and fans heavier than 70 lb need the box marked for that weight.

t: How often do I staple NM cable?
x: Secure NM cable at least every 4.5 ft and within 12 in of each box, cabinet or fitting. Cables run through bored holes in framing count as supported.

t: Where can't NM cable be used?
x: NM cable can't be used in wet or damp locations (including raceways underground or outdoors), in exposed areas subject to damage, as service-entrance cable, or embedded in concrete. It's normally used in one- and two-family dwellings and in other buildings of construction types allowed by 334.10.

t: Do I need a neutral at a switch box?
x: Yes, in most cases. A neutral must be provided at switch locations that control lighting loads, so smart switches and occupancy sensors can be installed later. Exceptions apply when a raceway allows adding one later or the box is accessible from an unfinished space above or below.

t: How high can a switch be?
x: The center of the switch handle in its highest position can't be more than 6 ft 7 in above the floor or working platform. Sharma's standard height is 48 in to center when the plan doesn't say.

t: Where are tamper-resistant receptacles required?
x: In dwelling units, all 125V and 250V nonlocking 15A and 20A receptacles must be listed tamper-resistant. Exceptions include receptacles more than 5.5 ft above the floor, part of a luminaire or appliance, or a single/duplex receptacle for appliances not easily moved in dedicated space.

t: Which receptacles must be weather-resistant?
x: All nonlocking 15A and 20A, 125V and 250V receptacles in damp or wet locations must be listed weather-resistant. In wet locations they also need an extra-duty, weatherproof in-use cover that seals whether or not a plug is in.

t: How close can a receptacle be to a tub or shower?
x: New in NEC 2020, receptacles can't be inside a zone 3 ft horizontally and 8 ft vertically from the top of the bathtub rim or shower threshold, including directly over the tub. In bathrooms too small for that, the receptacle may go on the farthest wall opposite the tub.

t: What do I do when replacing an old receptacle?
x: Replacements must meet current rules: GFCI where GFCI is now required, AFCI protection where the area now requires it, and TR or WR where required. A two-prong ungrounded receptacle can be replaced with a GFCI-protected receptacle marked 'No Equipment Ground'.

t: Can a receptacle face up in a countertop?
x: No, not unless it's a listed receptacle assembly for countertop or work-surface use. A standard receptacle can't be installed face-up in a counter or work surface.

t: What light can go above a tub or shower?
x: No cord-connected, chain-, cable- or cord-hung luminaires, track lighting, or ceiling fans are allowed within 3 ft horizontally and 8 ft vertically from the tub rim or shower threshold. Luminaires inside that zone that are subject to shower spray must be listed for wet locations.

t: What lights are allowed in a clothes closet?
x: Use LED or incandescent fixtures with a completely enclosed light source, or fluorescent fixtures; open or partly enclosed lamps aren't allowed. Surface-mounted enclosed incandescent/LED fixtures need 12 in of clearance from the storage space, while surface fluorescent and recessed fixtures need 6 in. LED or fluorescent fixtures identified for it may go inside the storage space.

t: How do I size a water heater circuit?
x: A fixed storage water heater of 120 gallons or less is treated as a continuous load, so the branch circuit must be rated at least 125% of the nameplate. A 4500W heater at 240V is 18.75A, times 125% is 23.4A, so a 30A breaker on 10 AWG copper.

t: Does a disposal or dishwasher need a disconnect?
x: Every appliance needs a disconnecting means. For cord-and-plug appliances, the plug and receptacle are the disconnect if accessible. Hardwired appliances need a breaker that's lockable or within sight. Cord lengths for disposals and dishwashers are set by 422.16(B).

t: Can a range hood be cord-and-plug connected?
x: Yes. A range hood can be cord-and-plug connected with a flexible cord identified for it, 18 to 36 in long, plugged into a receptacle supplied by an individual branch circuit, located to avoid damage.

t: How do I size the AC breaker and wire?
x: Read the nameplate. Size the conductors to at least the Minimum Circuit Ampacity (MCA), and use a breaker no larger than the Maximum Overcurrent Protection (MOCP or max fuse/breaker) marked. For AC equipment, 240.4(D) doesn't cap the breaker on small wire because Article 440 governs.

t: Where does the AC disconnect go?
x: The AC disconnect must be readily accessible and within sight of the condenser or equipment. It can be mounted on the unit but not on panels designed to be removed for service, and it can't block the nameplate.

t: How is electric strip heat sized?
x: Fixed electric space heating is treated as a continuous load. Size the branch-circuit conductors and overcurrent device at no less than 125% of the total heating load including blower motors. Use the air handler nameplate MCA/MOCP when it's given.

t: Does an EV charger need its own circuit?
x: Yes. Outlets for EV charging must be on an individual branch circuit with no other outlets. Under 625.41 the circuit and breaker are sized at 125% of the charger's maximum load because charging is continuous. For example, a 48A charger needs a 60A circuit.

t: Does an EV receptacle need GFCI?
x: Yes. New in NEC 2020, every receptacle installed for EV charging needs GFCI protection, regardless of location or voltage. Hardwired EVSE has its own built-in protection.

t: Where must the pool receptacle be?
x: At a dwelling with a permanent pool, at least one 125V 15A or 20A receptacle must be between 6 ft and 20 ft from the inside wall of the pool, and no more than 6.5 ft above the floor or grade. All 15/20A, 125V receptacles within 20 ft of the pool need GFCI.

t: What is pool equipotential bonding?
x: All metal parts of the pool structure, perimeter surfaces, metal fittings, pump motors and water must be bonded together with solid copper 8 AWG or larger. The perimeter bonding is 18 to 24 in from the inside walls of the pool, 4 to 6 in below subgrade. This bond is not a grounding path to the panel.

t: Does the pool pump need GFCI?
x: Yes. Outlets supplying pool pump motors on branch circuits rated 150V or less to ground and 60A or less, single- or 3-phase, need GFCI protection, whether the pump is hardwired or cord-and-plug.

t: What is required for a standby generator transfer switch?
x: An optional standby generator connected to the house wiring must use transfer equipment that prevents the generator and the utility from being connected at the same time. That can be a transfer switch or a listed interlock kit. Never backfeed without one.

t: How big must the transfer switch and generator be?
x: With manual transfer, the generator must handle the loads you expect to run at the same time. With automatic transfer, it must carry the full load connected to the transfer switch, or use load management to limit it.

t: Does a home generator need an outdoor shutdown?
x: Yes, new in NEC 2020. For permanently installed generators at one- and two-family dwellings, an emergency shutdown device must be outside the dwelling at a readily accessible location. Generators over 15 kW also need a remote emergency stop outside the enclosure.

t: What is the 120% rule for solar?
x: When a solar inverter backfeeds a panel at the opposite end from the main breaker, 125% of the inverter output current plus the main breaker rating can't exceed 120% of the busbar rating. Example: a 200A bus with a 200A main allows up to 40A of backfeed (32A inverter output). The backfed breaker needs a 'do not relocate' warning label.

t: Does rooftop solar need rapid shutdown?
x: Yes. PV circuits on or in buildings need a rapid shutdown function to reduce shock hazard for firefighters. The initiation device is at a readily accessible location, typically next to the service disconnect.

t: Where do smoke alarms go?
r: N/A (FBC-R R314.3; building code, not NEC)
x: Under the residential building code: in each sleeping room, outside each separate sleeping area near the bedrooms, and on every story including basements. Mount and space them per the manufacturer and NFPA 72.

t: Do smoke alarms need to be hardwired and interconnected?
r: N/A (FBC-R R314.4, R314.6; building code, not NEC)
x: In new construction, smoke alarms must get primary power from the building wiring with battery backup, and they must be interconnected so one sounding sets them all off. Interconnection can be wired or listed wireless. Note the circuit feeding them in a bedroom area still needs AFCI under NEC 210.12.

t: When are CO alarms required?
r: N/A (FBC-R R315; F.S. 553.885; building code, not NEC)
x: In Florida, CO alarms are required in new homes with a fuel-burning appliance, fireplace or attached garage. Place them outside each sleeping area per the building code. Combination smoke/CO alarms are acceptable when listed.

t: What height do receptacles go at?
x: The NEC doesn't set a standard receptacle height for general receptacles. Sharma standard: when the plan is silent, 18 in to the BOTTOM of the box; when the plan states a height, the plan governs. Countertop receptacles are limited to 20 in above the counter by code.

t: Do we install GFCI receptacles?
x: No. Sharma practice is a dual-function AFCI/GFCI breaker (e.g., Siemens Q120DFN/Q115DFN) on every 120V circuit. Points marked GFI on the plan get a standard tamper-resistant receptacle protected by that DFN breaker. Code allows GFCI by breaker or receptacle; both satisfy 210.8.

t: Box fill
x: Every conductor, clamp, device and ground takes up space in the box, counted in cubic inches by wire size. Count each insulated conductor once. Under the 2020 rule in 314.16(B)(5), up to four equipment grounding conductors count as one volume based on the largest ground, and each ground past four adds one quarter of that volume. Internal clamps count as one, and each device yoke counts as two, based on the largest wire on that device. Compare the total against the box's marked volume. Copper, aluminum, and copper-clad aluminum do not change the volume — the AWG does.

t: Conductor ampacity
x: Ampacity comes from Table 310.16 by wire size, material, and temperature column. Copper-clad aluminum is read in the aluminum column — the table has no CCA column (Sharma rule S-10). 110.14(C) keeps many terminations on the 60°C column unless they are marked 75°C, and 334.80 keeps NM cable from finishing above the 60°C column. 240.4(D) still caps the breaker: 14/12/10 AWG copper at 15/20/30A, and 12/10 AWG aluminum or CCA at 15/25A.

t: Conduit fill
x: Conductors may fill at most 53% of a conduit's internal area for one conductor, 31% for two, and 40% for three or more. Use conductor areas from Table 5 and conduit areas from Table 4. Equipment grounds count as conductors for fill.

t: Voltage drop
x: Not a hard code limit, but the code's informational notes recommend no more than 3% drop on a branch circuit and 5% total for feeder plus branch. Long runs need bigger wire: VD = 2 × K × I × L ÷ circular mils (K = 12.9 copper, 21.2 aluminum). Use the calculator in this app.

t: Branch circuits & receptacle spacing
x: Along a wall, no point may be more than 6 ft from a receptacle, so spacing is 12 ft apart maximum, and any wall run 2 ft or wider gets one. Hallways 10 ft or longer need at least one receptacle. Kitchens, bathrooms, laundry and garages each have their own required circuits — see the room checklists.

t: AFCI & GFCI protection
x: GFCI protects people from shock in wet and risky locations: bathrooms, kitchens, garages, outdoors, laundry, basements and more. AFCI protects against arc faults in living areas — bedrooms, living rooms, kitchens, laundry and similar rooms. Sharma rule: every 120V breaker is dual-function AFCI/GFCI, so both protections live at the breaker.

t: Service & panel working clearances
x: Electrical equipment needs working space: at least 3 ft deep in front, 30 in wide (or the equipment width if wider), and 6.5 ft of headroom. That space stays clear — it is not storage. Panels in homes also cannot go in bathrooms or over stair steps.

t: Grounding & bonding
x: Grounding connects the system to earth through the grounding electrode system (rods, water pipe, concrete-encased electrode); bonding connects metal parts together so faults trip the breaker fast. The main bonding jumper ties neutral to ground at the service only — never downstream. Keep grounds and neutrals separated in subpanels.

t: Service & feeder sizing
x: For a house, the optional method of 220.82 adds general lighting at 3 VA per square foot, 1,500 VA for each small-appliance and laundry circuit, and the nameplate of fastened appliances. The first 10 kVA of that sum is at 100% and the rest at 40%. Then add the single larger heating or cooling choice from 220.82(C). Space heat is 65% when fewer than four units are separately controlled, and 40% when there are four or more. Heat and cooling are not added together. Use the load calculator, then confirm against the printed section.

t: Pools & spas
x: Pools have their own world: equipotential bonding of everything metal near the water, GFCI protection for receptacles and equipment, strict distances for receptacles (6 ft minimum from the water's edge for general receptacles) and for overhead lines. Never treat pool work like ordinary outdoor work.

t: Solar PV
x: Solar systems need listed disconnects, rapid shutdown for rooftop arrays, and labels at the disconnect and the service. When the solar breaker sits at the opposite end of the bus from the main, 705.12(B)(3)(2) lets 125% of the inverter output current plus the breaker that protects the bus total as much as 120% of the bus rating, and that backfed breaker needs a label that it must not be moved. A different method, 705.12(B)(3)(3), caps the sum of the breaker ratings at the bus rating itself, not at 120%.

t: EV chargers
x: EV charging is a continuous load — size the branch circuit at 125% of the charger's rating. A 48A charger needs a 60A circuit. The load also counts at 100% (or 7,200 VA minimum) in service load calculations.

t: Generators & transfer switches
x: Optional standby systems must use a transfer switch or interlock so the generator can never backfeed the utility. Permanently installed generators need a disconnect and clear labeling; portable generator connections need a listed inlet and interlock or transfer equipment. Never a male-to-male cord, ever.

t: Smoke & CO alarms
x: Florida requires smoke alarms inside every bedroom, outside each sleeping area, and on every level; CO alarms where fuel-burning appliances or attached garages exist. In new work they are hardwired, interconnected, with battery backup. Placement on ceilings or high on walls, away from kitchens and bathrooms that cause false alarms.

t: HVAC disconnects
x: AC equipment needs a disconnect within sight of the unit, sized from the nameplate: branch-circuit protection follows the nameplate MAX fuse/breaker, and conductors follow the nameplate MIN circuit ampacity. The nameplate wins over generic tables — always read MCA and MOCP off the unit.

t: Commercial branch circuits
x: Commercial work: 20A minimum on every branch circuit (12 AWG copper minimum). No 15A branch circuits on commercial jobs.

t: New gear is Siemens
x: All new gear (panels, meter-mains, breakers, disconnects) is Siemens.

t: Match the existing panel
x: In an existing Square D panel, use Square D breakers listed for that panel. Don't mix brands.

t: Wall receptacle height
x: Receptacles: 18 in to the BOTTOM of the box when the plan is silent. When the plan states a height, the plan governs.

t: Switch height
x: Switches: 48 in to the center of the box when the plan is silent.

t: Microwave circuit — PENDING
x: PENDING RULING. The microwave gets its own dedicated 20A circuit. Mike Holt has not ruled the wire: 12 AWG copper versus 10 AWG CCA. Until that ruling, do not treat either size as the company standard. Both can meet 240.4(D) — 12 AWG copper is capped at 20A, and 10 AWG CCA is capped at 25A. The lead decides for the job. If the plan or the nameplate states a size, that statement governs.

t: Dual-function breakers
x: Every 120V breaker is a dual-function AFCI/GFCI breaker. Points marked GFI on the plan get a standard tamper-resistant receptacle protected by that breaker. The crew does not pick a GFCI receptacle for protection.

t: Dryer circuit
x: Dryer circuit: Siemens Q230GF, 30A 2-pole GFCI breaker. Ground-fault protection is required for the 125–250V laundry receptacle under NEC 2020 210.8(A).

t: Meter and panel back to back
x: Meter and panel go back to back where the house allows: meter outside, panel inside directly behind it. The 110.26 working space in front of the panel still has to be there.

t: Wire — copper and CCA
x: Branch circuits are copper by default: 14 AWG on 15A, 12 AWG on 20A. When copper-clad aluminum (CCA) is used, go one AWG size larger (12 AWG on 15A, 10 AWG on 20A), because Table 310.16 rates CCA in the aluminum column. Ordinary 15/20A device screw terminals are fine with CCA. CO/ALR is for plain aluminum. Wire nuts and lugs for CCA must say AL-CU. Push-in holes are 14 AWG solid copper only. Never backstab. The lead picks the wire. The microwave wire is not part of this default — it is PENDING under S-06.

t: Garage outlet height
x: Garage outlets at 48 in to center. This height is a Sharma tab rule. It is not S-04 or S-05.

t: Outdoor outlet height
x: Outdoor outlets at 24 in above grade. This height is a Sharma tab rule. It is not S-04 (wall receptacles, 18 in to the bottom of the box).
